#608. Tech Report: Nine-Pound Eagles Seem to Be Hunting 60-Pound Baboons in Africa—Hinting the Predators May Have Gone After Our Ancestors, Too

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (881 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Tech Report: Nine-Pound Eagles Seem to Be Hunting 60-Pound Baboons in Africa—Hinting the Predators May Have Gone After Our Ancestors, Too

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Eagles are formidable aerial predators capable of taking down animals much larger than themselves, including primates.
  • Sources indicate that new research suggests otherwise.
  • The findings add to scientists’ understanding of predator-prey relationships.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Eagles are formidable aerial predators capable of taking down animals much larger than themselves, including primates. But scientists have long believed that eagles tend to go after smaller primates, generally weighing less than 30 pounds.

Sources indicate that new research suggests otherwise. Scientists have found evidence of Verreaux’s eagles hunting full-grown olive baboons weighing nearly 60 pounds, which they describe in a study published November 18 in the American Journal of Biological Anthropology.

The findings add to scientists’ understanding of predator-prey relationships. But they also raise the intriguing newly introduced possibility that eagle attacks might have influenced human evolution. Some of our ancestors, such as Australopithecus afarensis, weighed about as much as modern baboons, so it’s plausible that eagles went after them, too, millions of years ago. The threat of these attacks, researchers posit, might have affected how early humans communicated and cooperated with one another.

Recent findings suggest that in February and March 2025, primatologists went looking for olive baboons on the Ennedi Plateau, a remote area in northeastern Chad filled with sandstone cliffs, gorges and rock formations. They were hoping to collect genetic samples so they could chart the history of the baboons’ movement across Africa.

In a recent development, but the focus of their expedition took an unexpected turn when they stumbled upon an olive baboon skull with a distinctive hole at the back of one of the eye sockets—clear evidence that a razor-sharp eagle talon had speared the primate’s head. The researchers had noticed Verreaux’s eagles soaring overhead, but it hadn’t occurred to them that the birds might be going after the baboons.

During that initial trip, they recovered the remains of nine olive baboons, including eight adult males. Two of the skulls had talon-shaped puncture marks, while one shoulder blade was covered in what appeared to be talon scratch marks. In June 2026, they found another skull and partial skeleton, which also showed signs of eagle predation.

The study authors can’t definitively rule out scavenging. But “the severity of punctures is suggestive of lethal interactions through a killing grip,” they write in the paper.

Sources indicate that further supporting the idea that Verreaux’s eagles were actively hunting the baboons, not just scavenging their remains, the scientists noted how groups of baboons responded whenever the birds got close, based on previously published observations. As soon as Verreaux’s eagles came into view, the primates started warning each other with alarm calls and taking cover. The baboons didn’t behave this way when other significant birds of prey were nearby, suggesting they viewed the Verreaux’s eagles—which typically max out at about nine pounds—as legitimate threats.

Sources indicate that “At first, the idea of eagles hunting adult male baboons seemed to exist on the thin edge of possibility, until it didn’t,” study co-author Nathaniel Dominy, a primatologist at Dartmouth College, says in a statement. “Our skepticism slowly gave way to acceptance. The evidence was convincing.”.

It has been revealed that the scientists estimate that, when they were alive, the baboons whose remains they initially discovered weighed approximately 49 pounds on average. But the one found in 2026 appears to have been much heavier, possibly weighing as much as 58 pounds. That’s well within the range of early hominin species: “Lucy,” the famous A. afarensis individual who lived in what is now Ethiopia roughly 3.2 million years ago, is believed to have weighed about 62 pounds.

According to recent reports, the only known case of an eagle hunting and killing an ancient hominin is the Taung Child, reports Live Science. The A. africanus individual is estimated to have been about 3 at death, and their skull contains puncture marks at the bottom of the eye sockets.

According to recent reports, scientists know that our ancestors were vulnerable to attacks from ground-based predators like crocodiles and hyenas. But the fresh findings suggest they might also have needed to be on alert for ambushes from the sky.

That could have affected their behavior. Modern primates that live in areas with predatory eagles tend to move around in large groups made up of various primate species. “That means extra competition for the food—but the benefits of the added protection seem to be worth the cost,” lead author Catherine Hobaiter, a primatologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland, tells Live Science’s Owen Jarus.

Sources indicate that perhaps our ancestors deployed a similar strategy, learning to cooperate, rather than compete, with other hominin and primate species because they discovered there’s safety in numbers. They might also have evolved other adaptations in response to potential eagle attacks, such as calling out to warn others or living in places where they could easily hide.

Scott McGraw, a primatologist at Ohio State University who was not involved with the study, tells the Washington Post’s Meghan Bartels he isn’t surprised by the findings, as birds of prey, commonly called raptors, are “extraordinary predators.”.

“As long as there have been primates, there have been raptors killing and eating them, and that’s been going on for 55 million years,” McGraw adds.

Sarah Kuta is a writer and editor based in Longmont, Colorado. She covers history, science, travel, food and beverage, sustainability, economics and other topics.

#606. An Isolated Group of Amazonian Hunter-Gatherers Made a Rare Request for Help From Outsiders, Raising Concerns About Forest Degradation

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (930 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

An Isolated Group of Amazonian Hunter-Gatherers Made a Rare Request for Help From Outsiders, Raising Concerns About Forest Degradation

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (930 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for decades, the Awá, an Indigenous tribe in the Brazilian Amazon rainforest, has lived in almost complete isolation from the modern world.
  • The Awá individuals, some of whom carried spears or wore necklaces and headdresses, made contact with a government agency that supports Indigenous peoples and the Guajajara, a larger, non-isolated Indigenous group that lives adjacent to the Awá.
  • In a recent development, the interaction lasted for several hours, Stephen Gibbs reports for the London Times, though the two groups spoke different languages, rendering communication almost impossible.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for decades, the Awá, an Indigenous tribe in the Brazilian Amazon rainforest, has lived in almost complete isolation from the modern world. That changed on November 16, when a group of around 20 men, women and children emerged from the forest’s edge.

The Awá individuals, some of whom carried spears or wore necklaces and headdresses, made contact with a government agency that supports Indigenous peoples and the Guajajara, a larger, non-isolated Indigenous group that lives adjacent to the Awá. Both reside in Brazil’s Arariboia Indigenous Territory in the northeast state of Maranhão. Guajajara members captured photos and videos of the encounter, which have been shared by the London-based Indigenous advocacy group Survival International.

In a recent development, the interaction lasted for several hours, Stephen Gibbs reports for the London Times, though the two groups spoke different languages, rendering communication almost impossible. Near the end, the Guajajara shared yams with the Awá, who took the offering and, smiling, retreated among the trees.

However, Guajajara spokesperson Olimpio Santos Guajajara warns this should not be taken as a heartwarming story but as a worrying sign about the sustainability of the Awá’s voluntary isolation.

According to recent reports, “We were trying to avoid contact with them,” he tells Brazil’s Globo television network, per the London Times. Since the late 1980s, the national government has followed a no-contact policy regarding isolated tribes like the Awá, allowing the Indigenous peoples to remain away from modern society at their discretion. “Unfortunately, today they felt forced to come and make contact,” Santos notes.

Sarah Shenker, head of Survival International’s Brazil office, notes the pressures of illicit deforestation, cattle ranching and hunting might be pushing the tribe to its limits, forcing them to emerge from isolation to survive.

Recent findings suggest that “They’ve shown so clearly for so long that they don’t want contact with outsiders,” she tells the Upcoming York Times’ Zane Irwin. “The fact that they’ve come out now does indicate they’ve probably felt forced to. … Because their lives are so intricately related to the forest, it would be impossible to completely separate the pressures on the land.”.

The Brazilian government has designated certain swaths of the Amazon, including Arariboia, as protected Indigenous land. But as deforestation and farm development have increased, these small territories are one of the few places still home to the Amazon’s historic hardwoods, Shenker tells the Times.

Thanks to conservation efforts and renewed enforcement, deforestation is slowing in Brazil. Still, estimates suggest that nearly 20 percent of the Amazon, which spans several South American countries, has been destroyed since the 1970s, and the forest can’t handle much more.

At least 196 uncontacted tribes live in ten countries worldwide, according to Survival International. Roughly 95 percent reside in the Amazon rainforest.

In recent years, hunters, loggers and ranchers have increasingly encroached upon the Awá territory. They previously cut down over 34 percent of one legally protected Awá reserve. Survival International claims the Brazilian government has hardly responded to these intrusions. In its place, a team of Guajajara people known as the Forest Guardians has taken to defending the Arariboia territory, and several members have died during these conflicts.

Repeated hunting and deforestation pose significant strain to the Awá way of life. The tribe survives off the forest, hunting wild boar, deer, monkeys and fish, and gathering fruit and honey, according to the Times. The forest is also central to the people’s medicinal and spiritual practices. But this is only possible in an “ever-smaller island of Amazon rainforest, surrounded by destruction,” says Caroline Pearce, director of Survival International, in a statement.

When the Awá made contact with the Guajajara village, the effects of this habitat loss were clear: Uirá Garcia, an anthropologist at the Federal University of São Paulo who has studied the isolated tribe for 20 years, tells Globo that some members of the group looked “exceptionally thin,” per the London Times. This was particularly concerning given the timing of the encounter in the middle of the Amazon’s rainy season—typically a time of abundance in the forest.

Sources indicate that experts also worried that contact with the modern world may pose serious health risks to the Awá. They have not received any vaccinations or built immunity to common viruses like influenza, measles and chicken pox, making them vulnerable to any pathogens present in the Guajajara population. Introduced diseases are presently the primary killer of isolated tribal people.

According to recent reports, to guard the Awá from further exposure, the Brazilian government agency dedicated to protecting Indigenous peoples has enacted an emergency contingency blueprint. It includes restricting outsider access to the area surrounding where the group members emerged, the London Times reports.

It has been revealed that past estimates have put the total Awá population at roughly 450 people—only around 100 of whom still live in complete isolation from the rest of the world, separated into a few small, mobile bands. As one of the globe’s last nomadic hunter-gatherer tribes, they draw intense interest from the scientific community and general public alike. But, Shenker says, the tribe is better off remaining somewhat of a mystery.

“We would rather not have images and not have video footage of the uncontacted Awá,” she tells Steven Grattan from the Associated Press, “when that means that they are living in the way that they choose in their forest, able to get on with their lives, hunting, fishing, gathering.”.

Gabby Shell is an editorial intern with Smithsonian magazine.

The PopSci Proven sticker printer that cuts its own work.

I tested the Cricut StickerPix Print + Cut in October, and setup took less than 10 minutes. The Essential Bundle is $249.00 (was $299.00). It’s a dye-sublimation printer with a blade inside, so it prints a 4 x 7-inch sheet and then kiss-cuts each sticker without slicing through the backing. A few of my stickers survived an accidental trip through the dishwasher. It only works with Cricut’s own paper and ink packs, so plan on buying refills. It earned a PopSci Proven award, and my full StickerPix Print + Cut review covers the paper costs and the quirks.

The same printing tech without the blade, for $130 less.

Cricut lists more than 100 compatible materials for it, and it can cut Smart Materials up to 12 feet long without a mat, which is the reason to pick it over a Joy if banners or large decals are in your looks.

A palm-size press for the spots a significant one can’t reach.

Shoes, stuffed animals, seams and the gaps between shirt buttons are all bad places for a full-size heat press. The Cricut EasyPress Mini in Raspberry is built for them, and it’s $39.00 (was $49.99). Cricut gives it three heat settings, a ceramic-coated plate, an insulated base to rest it on and an automatic shutoff. It’s also the least expensive machine in this post.

#601. Breaking: Great horned owl survives 70 miles stuck in a moving truck

Breaking: Great horned owl survives 70 miles stuck in a moving truck

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (479 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In March, we reported on a bobcat who endured a four-hour surgery on two broken legs after getting hit and dragged by a car, after her head had gotten stuck in the car’s grill.
  • “This is a very unusual case, as most animals that are hit by a tractor-trailer die due to their injuries or are killed instantly,” Tracie Young, director of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center tells Popular Science.
  • Recent findings suggest that the wildlife center’s team received a voicemail from cargo and freight tech giant Old Dominion Freight Line, saying that one of their drivers in Pennsylvania had hit an owl.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In March, we reported on a bobcat who endured a four-hour surgery on two broken legs after getting hit and dragged by a car, after her head had gotten stuck in the car’s grill. During a strangely similar scenario, the same wildlife center in Pennsylvania recently treated a great horned owl (Bubo virginianus) who also got jammed in the front of a vehicle. But this one was dragged along for 70 miles.

“This is a very unusual case, as most animals that are hit by a tractor-trailer die due to their injuries or are killed instantly,” Tracie Young, director of Raven Ridge Wildlife Center tells Popular Science.

Recent findings suggest that the wildlife center’s team received a voicemail from cargo and freight tech giant Old Dominion Freight Line, saying that one of their drivers in Pennsylvania had hit an owl. When they called back, they discovered that the owl was alive and had gotten stuck in the truck’s air dam. The company’s maintenance team was able to remove the owl, but something was clearly wrong with the bird because it couldn’t fly away.

The wildlife team told them to place the injured animal in a dark and quiet place. Ultimately, transport volunteers were able to transfer the owl to Raven Ridge, where the team had waited to receive the patient past the wildlife center’s closing hours. Its feathers were a mess, but the staff was shocked to find no broken wings or legs, nor open wounds. The owl had just injured its left eye.

According to recent reports, but when they called back the next day, “the story got even more incredible,” according to the wildlife center. The driver had felt the collision, but she didn’t know that the owl had gotten stuck on the truck, so she’d continued driving all the way back to the terminal.

“The distance from the spot where the owl was hit to the terminal was 70 miles,” the team wrote.“The owl was stuck headfirst in the fiberglass air dam for 70 miles at 65 miles per hour. It’s truly the luckiest owl we’ve ever seen.”.

It has been revealed that staff brought the hardy survivor to their vet for an eye exam, which revealed blood and swelling in the injured eye. The wildlife team is now monitoring the bird’s recovery.

According to recent reports, “The owl is doing great, and the left eye that sustained the damage is also healing. After we move the owl outside into a flight cage, we will make sure that the owl can sustain flight, that there are no obvious underlying complications, and that it can find the food placed in its cage,” Young concludes.

The goal is to ultimately release it close to where the collision occurred.

#600. For the First Time, Astronomers Witnessed a Giant Star Gobble Up Its Smaller Stellar Companion

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (626 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

For the First Time, Astronomers Witnessed a Giant Star Gobble Up Its Smaller Stellar Companion

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that in 2023, astronomers realized that a red giant star in our neighboring Andromeda galaxy was doing something strange.
  • In a recent development, the researchers rushed to observe the phenomenon, and they sifted through older data to piece together what had happened.
  • Industry observers note that the eruption, called AT 2025abao, occurred because the two stars shared what’s called a common envelope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in 2023, astronomers realized that a red giant star in our neighboring Andromeda galaxy was doing something strange. Sure enough, two years later, the astronomical object exploded.

In a recent development, the researchers rushed to observe the phenomenon, and they sifted through older data to piece together what had happened. Analyses suggest the huge star had gobbled up its smaller stellar companion, marking the first direct observation of this kind of star merger. The findings were described November 18 in the journal Nature.

Industry observers note that the eruption, called AT 2025abao, occurred because the two stars shared what’s called a common envelope. Some stars approaching the end of their lives balloon to a huge size, entering a giant phase. As an object expands, its outer layer of gas—or envelope—engulfs anything orbiting it, resulting in odd interactions.

However, common envelopes are tough to observe because they happen over relatively short timescales of months to years, and usually, just a few stars exist in this phase at a time within a galaxy, writes Jason Nordhaus, an astrophysicist at the Rochester Institute of Technology who did not participate in the work, in commentary accompanying the study.

Experts estimate that nearly a third of all stars go through a common envelope phase at some point during their lives, reports New Scientist.

Sources indicate that to investigate the strange event, which occurred in October 2025, researchers obtained data captured just 47 days later by NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope. They also had follow-up observations from other ground- and space-based instruments, as well as data from roughly the past 30 years, which revealed the big star had started brightening in 2018.

Using all that data, the team was able to “reconstruct what happened with quite significant confidence,” Sven Buder, an astrophysicist at the Australian National University who did not participate in the study, tells the Australian Broadcasting Corporation’s Jacinta Bowler.

Recent findings suggest that computer simulations hinted that the two stars had orbited each other for millennia. Before the eye-catching explosion, the primary star—dubbed “Major Bao” after the eruption’s name—had become enormous. It was seven times more massive, 350 times the radius and 18,000 times brighter than our sun. Its companion, “Little Bao,” on the other hand, probably contained 0.7 times the mass of our sun and was smaller and fainter.

In a recent development, the smaller star spiraled into the bigger one’s envelope, and the two objects took about seven years to unite, which is quite quick in astronomical terms. The merger occurred when the red giant dragged its companion into its core, resulting in a dramatic event resembling “a bomb exploding inside a living star,” study co-author Kishalay De, an astrophysicist at Columbia University, indicates in a statement.

“We were able to see all different phases of this process—we were able to see the quiescent system, we were able to see the moment the stars touched each other, we were able to see the inspiral, and we were able to see the significant outburst in 2025,” lead author Viraj Karambelkar, also an astrophysicist at Columbia University, tells Latest Scientist’s Leah Crane. “So we now know how this process works far better than we ever had before.”.

Now, however, the system is too dusty for scientists to observe the aftermath directly, and it will likely remain so for years, reports Science News’ Meghan Bartels. In the meantime, Karambelkar notes they can work to “catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

Margherita Bassi is a freelance journalist and trilingual storyteller. Her work has appeared in publications including BBC Travel, Discover magazine, Live Science, Atlas Obscura and Hidden Compass.

#598. Tiny egg-eating snake discovered in Ethiopia

Tiny egg-eating snake discovered in Ethiopia

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that biologists have discovered multiple latest species of egg-eating snakes slithering through the forests near southeastern Ethiopia’s Bale Mountains.
  • “Three other species in this genus are still waiting in line,” Arthur Tiutenko, a study co-author and herpetologist at Germany’s Friedrich-Alexander University of Erlangen–Nuremberg (FAU), said in a statement.
  • It has been revealed that many snakes will snack on an egg if the opportunity presents itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that biologists have discovered multiple latest species of egg-eating snakes slithering through the forests near southeastern Ethiopia’s Bale Mountains. Although researchers only described the white-throated egg-eater (Dasypeltis albigularis) in their study recently published in the journal Herpetozoa, they promised that information on additional finds is on the way.

“Three other species in this genus are still waiting in line,” Arthur Tiutenko, a study co-author and herpetologist at Germany’s Friedrich-Alexander University of Erlangen–Nuremberg (FAU), said in a statement.

It has been revealed that many snakes will snack on an egg if the opportunity presents itself. But for a handful of species, it’s all eggs, all the time. These nonvenomous snakes solely eat shelled embryos, and largely exist in Africa and some portions of India. To devour their meals, egg-eating snakes have evolved a set of very clever biological tricks. First, their back bones extend all the way into their esophagus and function like a saw to slice open shells. From there, the snake’s neck muscles contract and funnel the egg contents down its throat. Once finished, the reptile simply spits out the cracked shells.

In a recent development, however, Tiutenko’s team almost missed D. albigularis entirely. At first glance, the snake looks extremely similar to a species called the montane egg-eater (Dasypeltis atra). A closer inspection revealed some key differences—a patch of white scales extending down its stomach earned its “white-throated” moniker, while the skin between each scale has a distinctly blue shimmer. Other egg-eating snakes can rub their scales to create a rustling noise that startles foes, but only the D. albigularis females do the same—and they do it silently.

Sources indicate that don’t envision python-sized snakes chowing down on chicken eggs though. D. albigularis is less than eight inches long, weighs only 0.05 ounces, and is about as thick as a knitting needle. This means the snakes only have eyes for particularly tiny eggs from various diminutive birds. Luckily, their regional home is full of options.

“That may also be the reason why egg-eating snakes only live in Africa, and in particular in a small area in the southwest corner of the Arabian peninsula,” added Tiutenko.

#596. Rembrandt's 'Night Watch' Is Teeming With Life. Researchers Reveal a Hidden World of Microbes All Over the Masterpiece

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (992 w)
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Rembrandt's 'Night Watch' Is Teeming With Life. Researchers Reveal a Hidden World of Microbes All Over the Masterpiece

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (992 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For nearly four centuries, viewers have admired the bustling militia figures frozen in oil paint on Rembrandt van Rijn’s 1642 masterpiece, The Night Watch.
  • In a recent development, researchers from the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia (which claims to be the world’s only museum dedicated to microbes) are collecting 60 samples from 10 different areas of the painting to catalog its surface microbiome.
  • “This is the first time The Night Watch, or any work of art, has been analyzed in this way, and we’ve found bacteria that appear on human skin and in soil, and are even associated with plants,” Eline van Bloois, a microbiologist at Artis-Micropia tells El País’ Isabel Ferrer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For nearly four centuries, viewers have admired the bustling militia figures frozen in oil paint on Rembrandt van Rijn’s 1642 masterpiece, The Night Watch. Now, scientists in Amsterdam have revealed that the iconic canvas is teeming with an invisible, living world of its own.

In a recent development, researchers from the Rijksmuseum and ARTIS-Micropia (which claims to be the world’s only museum dedicated to microbes) are collecting 60 samples from 10 different areas of the painting to catalog its surface microbiome. Early laboratory cultures have turned up myriads of common bacteria and one puzzling outlier: Microbacterium saccharophilum, a bacterial species first identified in 2013 at a sugar refinery in Japan.

“This is the first time The Night Watch, or any work of art, has been analyzed in this way, and we’ve found bacteria that appear on human skin and in soil, and are even associated with plants,” Eline van Bloois, a microbiologist at Artis-Micropia tells El País’ Isabel Ferrer.

Sources indicate that the ongoing investigation is featured in “The Night Watch Lives,” an exhibition at ARTIS-Micropia running through May 2027. Centered around a life-size reproduction of Rembrandt’s painting marked with numbered sampling dates, the display showcases living bacterial colonies growing inside glass-encased Petri dishes.

“To get that close to the painting was very scary,” van Bloois tells Hyperallergic's Noëlle de Leeuw. “After all, it's a piece of art that is so well-known to so many people.”.

The microbial census forms a upcoming chapter of “Operation Night Watch,” the Rijksmuseum’s sweeping research and conservation initiative rolled out in 2019. Inside a glass chamber in the museum’s Gallery of Honor, conservators are currently working in full view of visitors to painstakingly remove a yellowed layer of varnish applied in the 1970s. It’s a delicate process, using organic-fabric gauze, small tissues and tiny amounts of solvent that will take years to complete.

Decades before Dutch microbiologist Antonie van Leeuwenhoek first described microorganisms in the 1670s, Rembrandt was already using chemistry to protect his work against microscopic threats. Previous Operation Night Watch analyses revealed that Rembrandt had applied a layer of lead-laden oil beneath the primer to shield the painting from moisture and mold in Amsterdam’s damp buildings. The canvas was later trimmed in 1715 to fit inside Amsterdam City Hall and has suffered numerous conservation treatments and deep cleanings roughly once every 50 years.

Did you know? Operation Night Watch.

Since 2019, Operation Night Watch has made several other breakthroughs. Researchers restored the trimmed edges of the painting with artificial intelligence and discovered a hidden sketch beneath the paint with advanced X-ray imaging.

In a recent development, “Thirty or 40 years ago, nobody could have imagined you’d be talking to a chemist or biologist about The Night Watch,” Rijksmuseum director Taco Dibbits stated during a press conference, Hyperallergic reports. “And I think precisely because this research is broadening—the fact that the humanities and the exact sciences are collaborating—it also leads to it becoming more widely embraced.”.

To sample the 400-year-old surface safely, conservators and lab technicians gently pressed small, sterile cellulose discs against both varnished and unvarnished sections of the canvas. Those discs were transferred to Petri dishes and incubated in ARTIS-Micropia’s laboratory until invisible microbes multiplied into visible colonies, which an external lab then identified.

The team has completed only half of its six planned sampling trips to the Rijksmuseum so far, with 20 identified microbes right now on display and another 10 still incubating. Researchers expect to collect all 60 samples by February.

In a recent development, among the familiar microbial residents detected so far are Staphylococcus epidermidis and Micrococcus luteus, harmless bacteria routinely found on human skin that help hydrate it and defend against pathogens, Amsterdamian’s Dana Marin reports. The team also isolated plant-root and soil species, including Kocuria palustris, Kocuria rhizophila and Lysinibacillus sphaericus, a resilient bacterium capable of surviving harsh environments rich in heavy metals.

In a recent development, none of those, however, baffled scientists quite like Microbacterium saccharophilum, which turned up on a section where old varnish had already been stripped away. Originally isolated from soil at the Ensuiko Sugar Refining plant in Yokohama, Japan, the microbe has no obvious connection to a Dutch Golden Age canvas.

“We’ve seen very little sugar in Rembrandt’s painting so far, and it’s best not to speculate, but it’s possible that the Saccharophilum isn’t as old as the canvas,” van Bloois tells El País, adding that scientists currently have no way to determine when any of the bacteria arrived.

Industry observers note that museum visitors often wonder whether any microbes lingering on the paint might date back to Rembrandt himself. “Ideally, you want to have the bacteria of Rembrandt: this is the Holy Grail,” Katrien Keune, the Rijksmuseum’s head of science, tells the Art Newspaper’s Senay Boztas. Yet Keune tells Amsterdamian that centuries of restoration make finding traces of the master unlikely, noting that the surface largely reflects museum staff and visitors shedding skin cells and saliva droplets.

Even without a direct biological link to Rembrandt, researchers hope the project helps rehabilitate the public image of microbes, pointing out that far less than 1 percent of known species cause disease in humans or animals. “It's good to give microbes some love as well,” van Bloois tells the Art Newspaper.

“The Night Watch Lives” is on view at ARTIS-Micropia in Amsterdam through May 2027.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that resilience and perseverance was on full display in Alaska this summer. The park rangers at Tongass National Forest in the southeastern corner of the state spotted an unnamed black bear (Ursus americanus) with a broken arm. Even with this injury, the tough bear still managed to catch the fish running through Anan Creek. For this grit, the rangers awarded the bear with the 2026 Grin & Bear It Award.

It has been revealed that “We don’t know how the injury happened, but we’re impressed by the bear’s resilience,” the rangers write. “In other wild places the injury may have been a death sentence, but the abundance of Anan gives this bear a chance.”.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the annual Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Industry observers note that the largest national forest in the United States, Tongass covers most of southeastern Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area also includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears. One of the hotspots is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

According to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears like the one with the broken arm and eight brown bears (Ursus arctos). Similar to their portly counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to feast on salmon and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear here has their own behaviors and quirks.

It has been revealed that the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behavior.

  • Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Click to tell Google to prioritize Quanta and see more of the best coverage of science and math in your search and AI results.

One evening in the fall of 1969, a team of researchers sent a historic message from a computer in Los Angeles to one in Menlo Park, California. Or rather, they sent part of the message: the “L” and “O” in “LOGIN.” The first transmission over the first link in Arpanet, the prototype for the modern internet, lasted all of two characters before the network crashed.

Computer networks have grown much more reliable since that first test nearly 60 years ago. But we also demand a lot more of them. When you watch a movie online, the video data gets divided into a series of tiny “packets” that hop between way stations called routers on their way to your computer. Links between routers sometimes fail. One reason our videos aren’t constantly glitching out is that each router has a thorough contingency plan — a set of rules for redirecting packets in case a link goes down.

Sources indicate that if a large outage cuts off every path between two points, there’s no way a packet can get through. But ideally, a network would be able to withstand any pattern of link failures short of this worst-case scenario. Researchers call this property “perfect resilience.” For over a decade, computer scientists have sought to understand what kinds of networks can be made perfectly resilient under realistic conditions.

According to recent reports, now, in a paper that was presented at the Symposium on Theory of Computing in June 2026, two researchers have settled the question with a comprehensive proof. They indicated that there are exactly four minimal network structures that can thwart perfect resilience. In networks that lack these structures, you can always concoct rules that will reliably deliver packets from any source to any destination, regardless of which links fail.

Sources indicate that “It’s a very elegant contribution,” stated Michael Schapira, a computer scientist at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem who was not involved in the result. “It’s pretty rare that you get a complete understanding of something.”.

In a recent development, imagine you have a network of routers in which each device can direct data packets bound for any other point in the network. You can then ask yourself: What instructions should the routers follow?

According to recent reports, one simple approach would be to map out the shortest path between every pair of points in the network, and then give each router a copy of the map. If the network ever changes — if even a single link fails — start over and do it again.

Sources indicate that in principle, this strategy will ensure that every packet reaches its destination. In practice, it’s far too slow. Calculating shortest paths is inherently a “global” problem — it requires knowledge of the entire network. In a real-world network, that calculation might take up to a few seconds. But each router has to act fast, in a fraction of a millisecond or less. That means routers must direct packets using only locally accessible information, such as the status of links to their immediate neighbors.

Industry observers note that this restriction makes the problem of perfect resilience much more complicated. Without any global coordination between routers, packets might get trapped in loops.

Industry observers note that in a 2012 paper, Schapira and five other researchers formally defined perfect resilience and devised a mathematical model to study when it’s achievable. They assumed that routing rules must have a simple form. A router can decide in which direction to send each upcoming packet using only three factors: the packet’s destination, the link it arrived on, and which neighboring links have failed. The rules can’t depend on the path that a packet has taken so far, since routers don’t have access to this information.

With these assumptions, the researchers aimed to capture “something very close to how networks actually operate,” mentioned Brighten Godfrey, a computer scientist at the University of Illinois, Urbana-Champaign who co-authored the 2012 paper.

In 2020, Stefan Schmid and his colleagues proved a partial result about the reliability of communication networks.

Godfrey, Schapira, and their colleagues showed that in this model, perfect resilience isn’t always achievable. They did so by finding a single example of a network layout that can’t be made perfectly resilient. No matter what set of routing rules you choose, there’s always a pattern of link failures that will cause some packets to get stuck in a loop.

According to recent reports, but the network they identified was fairly complicated. Was it a rare example? Or is perfect resilience impossible in many other networks as well?

The 2012 paper caught the attention of Stefan Schmid, a networking researcher now at the Technical University of Berlin. He toyed with the perfect-resilience problem on and off for years, but his first real progress came in 2020, when he and his colleagues made a connection to a topic in mathematics called the theory of graph minors.

Sources indicate that computer scientists have long studied the mathematical properties of real-world networks by modeling them as graphs — webs of nodes connected by lines called edges. Imagine that you start with a graph, then repeatedly simplify it using three basic operations: You can delete a node, delete an edge, or merge pairs of connected nodes. The graphs that you can obtain by combining these operations are known as the minors of the larger graph.

These operations never make it more likely that packets will get routed in endless loops. If a graph is perfectly resilient, then so are all of its minors.

You can reverse this logic and understand the behavior of large, complex graphs using the properties of their simpler minors. An iconic result in graph theory, called the Robertson-Seymour theorem, tells you what you can learn from this kind of reversal. Applied to network resilience, the theorem states that there’s only a finite number of minors that are not perfectly resilient — every larger graph that lacks perfect resilience reduces to one of these so-called forbidden minors. If you can identify the full set of forbidden minors, you’ll have a complete understanding of when perfect resilience is achievable.

Unfortunately, the Robertson-Seymour theorem doesn’t tell you how many forbidden minors there are, or how to find them. “We know such a finite set exists,” said Matthias Bentert, a theoretical computer scientist at the Technical University of Berlin and Schmid’s collaborator on the fresh paper. “But we don’t know, does it contain one or two graphs, or does it contain 100,000 graphs?”.

Matthias Bentert, an expert in the math of graph theory, teamed up with Schmid to complete a comprehensive proof.

The researchers wanted to find the complete set of forbidden minors and prove that no others existed.

In their 2020 paper, Schmid and his colleagues identified two simple graph minors that prevent perfect resilience, but then they got stuck. Schmid suspected they’d need a collaborator with more expertise in graph theory to make further progress. Three years later, he met Bentert at a research retreat, and they worked together briefly on a different problem. In 2025, when Bentert was wrapping up a postdoctoral fellowship in Norway, Schmid invited him to join his group in Berlin.

“It was a really perfect match,” Schmid remarked. “Matthias made a lot of very fast contributions on a couple of our problems.” Perhaps he’d help make quick work of the perfect-resilience problem, too.

Bentert swiftly identified a third forbidden minor. He then decided to see how far he could get by attacking the problem from the other direction. Perhaps if there were no additional forbidden minors — if the three they had found were the complete set — then he could prove that all graphs that lacked these three could be made perfectly resilient.

The strategy worked, but not in the way he had hoped. “I found that, actually, I cannot show it, because it’s not true,” Bentert said. He had discovered a fourth obstruction.

So now they had four forbidden graph structures. Were there more? Bentert tried the same strategy again: Prove that all graphs that lacked these four minors could be made perfectly resilient. The strategy worked, this time because he really had found the full set.

The four forbidden graph minors.

Recent findings suggest that bentert hadn’t expected the answer to be so simple. “I would have stopped if I reached 50 or so, but that it’s really only four was a little bit of a surprise to me,” he said.

Sources indicate that of course, knowing that perfect resilience is theoretically achievable for any given network is only useful if you know how to choose the right routing rules. Fortunately, Schmid and Bentert’s new result also yields a fast algorithm for finding these rules, which turn out to take a similar form in any network. They’re all based on a trick for escaping mazes: Simply take a right turn at every intersection. The only networks where a maze navigation–based approach fails are those containing one of the four forbidden minors. For those networks, changing the rules won’t help.

It has been revealed that with their new result, Schmid and Bentert have fully resolved the perfect-resilience problem as it was originally posed in 2012. But the solution isn’t all good news. Even though there are only four graph structures that obstruct perfect resilience, the fact that they’re so simple means that many networks will have them as minors. Dense networks with many connections are especially likely to lack perfect resilience — an ironic outcome, given that adding more links to a network is the most straightforward way to make it more reliable.

“The more connectivity you have, the more possible subgraphs there are,” Godfrey said. “I wouldn’t be surprised if many real-world networks do not have a solution for perfect resilience.”.

That may not be a deal-breaker: In some communication networks, resilience isn’t as critical as high speed and low congestion, two factors that Schmid and Bentert’s rules don’t take into account. And in cases where resilience is crucial, Schmid and Bentert’s result may not be the end of the story. They now blueprint to study how the situation changes if each packet can carry a record of the last few nodes it visited. Bentert is optimistic that this approach could make perfect resilience achievable for a broader range of networks, yet still remain feasible in the real world.

It has been revealed that “Maybe some very freaky networks will not be perfectly resilient” even in a modified version of the problem, he said. “But everything that will ever be designed by a human or a machine will be.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that some 2,000 years ago, an elite individual associated with the nomadic Xiongnu Empire was buried in style in what is now northeastern Mongolia.
  • Sources indicate that despite this impressive exterior, the tomb’s interior is surprisingly small and shallow.
  • Sources indicate that the National Museum of Korea, the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia recently completed a four-year excavation of the burial, which is known officially as Tomb 160.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some 2,000 years ago, an elite individual associated with the nomadic Xiongnu Empire was buried in style in what is now northeastern Mongolia. Their tomb, measuring nearly 240 feet in length (about four-fifths the height of the Statue of Liberty), is the largest of its kind discovered in the East Asian country to date.

Sources indicate that despite this impressive exterior, the tomb’s interior is surprisingly small and shallow. But it was packed with treasures that shed new light on the Xiongnu people’s links to such far-flung foreign powers as the Roman Empire and the Lelang Commandery, an administrative division of China’s Han dynasty that was based in what is now Korea.

Sources indicate that the National Museum of Korea, the Institute of Archaeology at the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia recently completed a four-year excavation of the burial, which is known officially as Tomb 160. It’s located in Duurlig Nars, a Xiongnu burial ground with some 300 graves.

It has been revealed that did you know? UNESCO recognition.

Archaeologists recovered 413 artifacts from the tomb, including a glass cup believed to be of Roman origin, a gourd-shaped silver pendant that once adorned a horse’s harness, a lacquered chariot and 15 jade pieces modeled after Han funerary goods.

Recent findings suggest that the pendant resembles accessories found in Lelang tombs in modern-day North Korea, but unlike those ornaments, it boasts a crystal at its center. The jade objects, meanwhile, were fashioned in irregular shapes with intricate designs carved onto their surfaces, setting them apart from the disc-shaped bi prized by the Han as symbols of heaven.

Sources indicate that “This excavation clearly shows that the Xiongnu of 2,000 years ago were linked to a broad exchange network reaching from Rome to the Korean Peninsula,” the National Museum of Korea says in a statement, per a translation by Seoul Economic Daily. “We expect it to serve as a turning point in expanding the field of Korean archaeology into Eurasia.”.

The rich range of objects buried alongside the deceased testifies to their high status. Although the researchers have yet to identify the grave’s occupant, they proposal to conduct a DNA analysis of teeth and hair recovered from the individual’s coffin to determine their sex and age.

To construct the tomb, ancient laborers built an elevated terrace enclosed by nine layers of stacked stones. The central chamber of the grave extends to a depth of nearly 50 feet, making it significantly smaller than comparable Xiongnu tombs in central Mongolia, whose depths reach more than 70 feet. The excavation team suggests that this downsized interior reflects societal shifts in the late first and second centuries C.E., when the tomb was built. At the time, the Xiongnu Empire was declining, with internal disagreements and external pressure from the Han military weakening the once-great pastoral confederation.

It has been revealed that the Xiongnu thrived in Central Asia between the third century B.C.E. and the second century C.E., wielding control over vast swaths of territory “without building cities, forming central bureaucracies, devising a writing system or mobilizing masses of farmers to produce food,” Bruce Bower wrote for Science News in 2023. In recent years, scholars have revealed an array of insights on the Xiongnu that challenge long-held perceptions of the group as “barbaric” invaders.

In 2023, for example, a paper published in the journal Science Advances suggested that elite Xiongnu women traveled to the empire’s frontiers to shore up alliances with powerful locals. “They are representatives of the imperial clan that ruled the empire,” study co-author Bryan Miller, an archaeologist at the University of Michigan, told Live Science’s Tom Metcalfe. “You’ve got these marriage alliances spanning the whole empire, even in these local communities.”.

Recent findings suggest that speaking with Science News, Miller added, “This must have been an empire organized around moving populations. Xiongnu elites were savvy politicians who delegated power to keep the empire together.”.

Meilan Solly is a senior associate digital editor at Smithsonian magazine, where she oversees the online history section and writes about everything from archaeology to the British royal family. Solly’s specialties are Tudor England, Renaissance and modern art, and World War II.

Psychedelic therapies may improve decision making

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, psychedelics such as ketamine and psilocybin continue to show promise as alternative treatments for mental health issues like anxiety and depression.
  • In a recent development, the team’s experiment was straightforward.
  • According to recent reports, while the untreated rodents performed moderately well, they often made mistakes like returning to a specific location no matter the light cue.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, psychedelics such as ketamine and psilocybin continue to show promise as alternative treatments for mental health issues like anxiety and depression. Although they’re commonly associated with mind-altering trips and sometimes confounding experiences, recent research indicates small doses may provide an opposite outcome. In a study published today in the journal Science Advances, researchers show that psychedelics may actually improve decision making in certain situations.

In a recent development, the team’s experiment was straightforward. After supplying lab mice with small amounts of ketamine or psilocybin, neuroscientists exposed them to a simple, sensory-based training exercise. Each mouse was tasked with identifying which of two sites contained a reward based on light pulses emitted from either location. Researchers then compared their decisions with a control group of mice who didn’t receive either psychedelic.

According to recent reports, while the untreated rodents performed moderately well, they often made mistakes like returning to a specific location no matter the light cue. However, the mice treated with ketamine or psilocybin appeared to rely less on repetition and more on sensory observations. As a result, they had fewer errors and found the location more effectively.

“These findings reveal how psychedelics reduce the reliance on habits and repetitive choices, which may explain part of their therapeutic effect,” Benjamin Scott, a Boston University psychologist and study co-author, remarked in a statement.

According to recent reports, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) have remained the most commonly prescribed anxiety and depression medications for decades, but they often come with caveats. Patients usually take SSRIs for weeks before experiencing any relief, and they must take them consistently for indefinite periods of time. Meanwhile, about 30 percent of people with depression are resistant to SSRIs, which makes treatment much more difficult. Another benefit is that the effects of ketamine and psilocybin are much easier to map in the brain compared to SSRIs, even after a half century of research.

“We know a great deal about how psychedelics affect the nervous system,” stated Scott.

In a recent development, on a molecular level, psychedelics bind to receptors on neurons, protective neural cells called glia, and likely other cells. Once attached, the effects compound throughout the brain by altering cellular activity, circuits, and neuroactivity. Psilocybin works with serotonin receptors to influence how information is processed. In contrast, ketamine is a dissociative psychedelic that functions as an antagonist to specific receptors.

“The discovery we report in this paper is that these two drugs have similar pro-cognitive effects, at least in mice performing a simple task,” Scott explained. “Both drugs strengthen the influence of sensory evidence on choices and reduce the effect of bias.”.

The study’s authors do note some potentially negative effects, as well. Although a mouse’s accuracy improved, the correct decisions sometimes came more slowly than before they took the psychedelics. Scott remarked this may logically translate to impacts on human reaction times, which could be a problem during activities like driving a car or playing sports. Despite this, the team is still confident in what psychedelics have already accomplished for patients, as well as what that could mean in the future. Scott cited existing evidence of patients reporting noticeable, long-lasting improvements after a single dose of psilocybin.

“This is dramatically different than today’s first-line drugs for depression,” he added.

#587. China grid-connects world’s first artificial-cavern CAES plant

China grid-connects world’s first artificial-cavern CAES plant

💡 Key Takeaways
  • 1 compressed air energy storage (CAES) station in Yumen, Gansu province, achieved its first grid connection on November 16, marking what its developer describes as the world’s first grid-connected CAES facility using purpose-excavated underground rock caverns.
  • The project was developed by China Energy Digital Technology Group, a subsidiary of China Energy Engineering Corporation, which is responsible for its investment, construction, and operation.
  • Rated at 300 MW/1,800 MWh, the facility is designed for an eight-hour charging cycle and six hours of continuous discharge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China’s Yuanchu No. 1 compressed air energy storage (CAES) station in Yumen, Gansu province, achieved its first grid connection on November 16, marking what its developer describes as the world’s first grid-connected CAES facility using purpose-excavated underground rock caverns.

The project was developed by China Energy Digital Technology Group, a subsidiary of China Energy Engineering Corporation, which is responsible for its investment, construction, and operation.

Rated at 300 MW/1,800 MWh, the facility is designed for an eight-hour charging cycle and six hours of continuous discharge. Total investment reached approximately CNY 2.5 billion ($368 million), with projected annual electricity generation of 600 GWh.

It has been revealed that its defining feature is an engineered underground air storage system. Four interconnected chambers were excavated approximately 110 meters below the surface in hard rock, creating a pressurized storage space of around 200,000 cubic meters. The system has a design pressure of 18 MPa.

It has been revealed that the plant employs non-combustion, adiabatic CAES technology. During charging, electricity drives compressors that pressurize air, while heat generated during compression is recovered and stored. During discharge, the stored heat reheats the compressed air before expansion through turbines, eliminating the need for supplementary natural gas combustion.

According to molten-salt supplier Shandong Huayang Dier Chemical, the thermal system combines low-melting-point ternary molten salt with pressurized hot water to recover and store heat at different temperatures. Lower- and medium-temperature compression heat is stored in pressurized water tanks, while higher-temperature heat is transferred to molten-salt tanks. During discharge, both media release heat in stages to reheat the air before expansion. The developer also reports using shared heat-exchange equipment during charging and discharging, reducing equipment duplication.

The developer reports a round-trip electrical efficiency of 72%, although sustained operational data have not yet independently confirmed the figure.

Industry observers note that the artificial-cavern approach addresses a geographical constraint on CAES deployment. Salt caverns offer relatively economical underground storage but require suitable geological formations. Excavating and sealing chambers in competent hard rock could broaden site selection, although geological conditions and construction costs remain key considerations.

Recent findings suggest that yumen lies within the Hexi Corridor, a major wind and solar development region in northwest China. The plant is intended to absorb surplus renewable electricity during off-peak periods and return it to the grid when demand rises, providing multi-hour balancing capacity.

Sources indicate that china has been expanding its large-scale CAES fleet. At least six projects rated at 100 MW or above have been reported as grid-connected, including the 600 MW Huai’an salt-cavern station, the 700 MW Jintan Phase II project, 300 MW facilities in Yingcheng and Feicheng, the 100 MW Zhangjiakou demonstration project and Yuanchu No. 1.

It has been revealed that according to an October 2026 report by the Energy Storage Application Branch of the China Industrial Association of Power Sources, 13 CAES projects were under construction, totaling 4.95 GW/23.95 GWh. Separately, industry figures cited in November indicated more than 36 GW of projects in preparation as of the first quarter of 2026, with nearly 100 project filings nationwide.

The figures highlight China’s growing CAES pipeline, although many proposed projects remain subject to financing, geological assessments and commercial viability. For Yuanchu No. 1, long-term efficiency, cavern integrity and operating costs will determine whether artificial-cavern technology can be replicated economically.

#586. Latest Update: Yosemite needs your help tracking river otters

Latest Update: Yosemite needs your help tracking river otters

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (356 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Yosemite National Park is home to all of these natural wonders and more.
  • Recent findings suggest that even for experienced rangers and biologists, North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are difficult to monitor.
  • Industry observers note that additionally, one otter can travel five to 10 miles a day along rivers and streams, making them difficult to track.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

El Capitan. Glowing waterfalls. Half dome. River otters. Yosemite National Park is home to all of these natural wonders and more. The plucky and playful mammals have officially been spotted in the population park in Northern California—and park rangers want the public’s help to monitor them.

Recent findings suggest that even for experienced rangers and biologists, North American river otters (Lontra canadensis) are difficult to monitor. They have a very high metabolism, and can eat about 15 to 20 percent of their body weight in a single day. They spend a lot of their time looking for prey, including fish, crayfish, crabs, frogs, birds’ eggs, and even some reptiles like turtles.

Industry observers note that additionally, one otter can travel five to 10 miles a day along rivers and streams, making them difficult to track. According to the California Department of Fish and Wildlife, river otters’ range stretches all of Northern California’s five coastal counties from Oregon down to San Francisco Bay, the Sierra Nevada Mountains from Mariposa County north, and large parts of the inland northern valley. Yosemite National Park itself has over 1,700 miles of streams, so that’s a lot of wet ground to cover when looking for otters.

Park rangers are asking the public to note the location, date, and time of any river otter sightings in Yosemite. Written sightings can be reported in the comments section of this Facebook post or the park’s contact us form. Any videos or photos can be shared through a direct message on Instagram.

“Your observations can help us better understand how otters roam and use Yosemite’s waterways,” the rangers write.

River otters are not endangered, but they have had a rocky history. During the 19th and 20th centuries, they were extensively hunted and trapped for their fur and many were removed from their natural range. Decades of conservation and reintroduction efforts are currently helping populations to recover. California’s population is considered fairly stable, but they are still at risk from further habitat destruction and water pollution.

#584. The Search for a Top Dark Matter Candidate Was Losing Hope. Then Came a Potential Signal. Will It Be Enough to Energize the Struggling Field?

The Search for a Top Dark Matter Candidate Was Losing Hope. Then Came a Potential Signal. Will It Be Enough to Energize the Struggling Field?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory is not a bad place to fret over the state of your career.
  • The lab also descends into the Gran Sasso mountain, forming one of the world’s largest underground research centers.
  • In a recent development, for the past few decades, scientists have been hunting for dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up 85 percent of the matter in our universe.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that italy’s Gran Sasso National Laboratory is not a bad place to fret over the state of your career. The lab’s panoramic views of white-capped mountains and endless greenery are nearly inescapable. Physicists fuel their work with sharp espressos, rather than the watery coffee many Americans accept.

The lab also descends into the Gran Sasso mountain, forming one of the world’s largest underground research centers. Nestled beneath 4,600 feet of rock is an array of particle detectors. Thanks to the mountain’s thick skin, these instruments are shielded from cosmic rays, the high-energy particles produced by black holes, exploding stars and even our own sun. In the quiet depths of this laboratory, physicists hope to pick up on much more elusive particles—including dark matter.

In a recent development, for the past few decades, scientists have been hunting for dark matter, the invisible substance that makes up 85 percent of the matter in our universe. One primary target has been weakly interacting massive particles, or WIMPs—a hypothesized candidate for dark matter that passes through normal matter with barely a trace. Massive underground detectors like those at Gran Sasso are leading the search.

In a recent development, but no one has definitively found a WIMP, so no one is sure that they exist—and challenges to spotting them are building. As detectors get more sensitive, upcoming background signals are beginning to cloud them, reducing the odds of catching WIMPs. Funding is growing more precarious, leaving many wondering how many years this endeavor has left.

When I visited the lab in May, the mood among some of these physicists was muted. “Of course, we were a bit more depressed,” reflects physicist Paolo Salomone, laughing. Despite his clear enthusiasm for the dark matter hunt, Salomone, a strikingly blue-eyed University of Chicago postdoctoral scholar, knew he was entering a field some might diagnose as terminal.

Then, in September, a pinprick of hope emerged. An American lab also searching for WIMPs released a preprint paper detailing a single—but intriguing—data point, rising above the expected background signals. Maybe, just maybe, it was dark matter.

Salomone was on vacation in Corsica when his phone started blowing up. Text notifications from physicist friends streamed in, asking him if he’d seen the news. “I was there on the beach trying to look at my phone, trying to zoom in on the plot,” he claims. Watching the faraway excitement, he says, “I felt like I was missing out a lot.”.

The finding was not a definite dark matter detection—one data point isn’t nearly enough to count as a discovery. Still, the result spawned headlines across the globe, a torrent of preprint papers and newfound hope for many physicists in search of WIMPs.

Sources indicate that the question, now, is what’s next. Will this life raft be enough to overcome the field’s growing challenges? And will the few other detectors with similar sensitivity—most notably, one at Gran Sasso—be able to replicate the signal?

It has been revealed that nearly a century ago, Swiss astronomer Fritz Zwicky noticed a group of galaxies with some moving so rapidly that they should have escaped the cluster’s gravity and flown apart. He theorized that some invisible material was gluing them together. Since then, scientists have accrued more evidence for this dark matter: stars speeding precipitously fast around a galaxy’s rim; unexpectedly strong gravitational lensing, in which distant light is bent by extreme gravity.

Recent findings suggest that to explain it all, astrophysicists dreamed up WIMPs in the 1980s. As far as subatomic particles go, these would be relatively massive. In theory, they glide through space, on occasion lightly interacting with matter. Physicists have a pretty good sense of the density of dark matter scattered throughout our universe, but not much more about it. “It opens the possibility of having a lot of light particles or very few heavy particles,” says Salomone.

According to recent reports, directly detecting WIMPs, then, could clue us into the mass of individual dark matter particles and the number of them floating around, as well as how strongly these particles interact with normal matter. But finding them has been a challenge. Not only are physicists searching through a vast plain of possibilities, but they’re also looking for incredibly rare interactions that require extreme care in detection.

The smallest impurities can anger a detector. To illustrate the point, Marcello Messina, the technical coordinator for Gran Sasso’s XENONnT experiment, brought up the humble banana. While we don’t tend to think of a banana as radioactive, the fruits are rich in potassium, leading to a tiny shower of particle decays. “A banana can completely destroy our data table,” he said.

Messina was my guide for the day at Gran Sasso, driving me six miles through one of Italy’s longest tunnels and into the mossy interior of the mountain. He led me through the lab’s sterile halls, ending up at his even more sterile detector.

Messina’s XENONnT experiment is a hulking cylinder that holds a chamber of nearly 9.5 tons of xenon—mostly liquid—inside. The hope is that when a WIMP flies into the detector, it jostles one of the large and stable xenon atoms, which would in turn shoot out electrons and a light ray, alerting sensors to the strange particle’s presence.

XENONnT, which has been collecting data for around six years, is the strapping great-grandchild of the team’s original 2006 prototype. “XENON, for almost all its life, provided the most sensitive results,” Messina told me. “It was definitely leading the field.” Today, a few more rivals—like the American detector—have emerged.

It has been revealed that we walked past another device that looked like a gigantic red Lego: a new detector Salomone is helping to build, DarkSide-20k, which will use a chamber of around 55 tons of argon instead of xenon. This enormous detector will reach a similar sensitivity to XENONnT and is set to begin collecting data in 2028.

In a recent development, despite their materials’ purity, physicists expect some level of background fuzz—mainly radioactive decay products—and predict what that will look like. Sometimes, though, this “background” can behave in unexpected ways, so physicists must have a high bar for what anomalies in their data to take seriously.

Messina demonstrated me a kind of memento mori for physicists: the latest generation of the DAMA experiment, which made a claim of dark matter detection that has been dismissed by most of the community.

In 1997, DAMA, which is made up of sodium iodide crystals, detected a signal that varied yearly, swooping in every summer—just as dark matter was expected to do. But while the team has continued to stand by their results, other experiments later ruled this out.

After DAMA’s false alarm, “I think people are just very cautious now,” says Ina Sarcevic, a physicist at the University of Arizona.

Industry observers note that despite the fear of more detector-cried-wolf scenarios, many physicists swiftly pulled together theories to explain September’s announcement of a possible detection, Sarcevic says. The signal came out of South Dakota’s LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment, which is at the moment the world’s largest WIMP detector.

Physicist Richard Gaitskell, LZ’s spokesperson, has been searching for dark matter for nearly 40 years, starting with a detector “barely bigger than the top of my thumb,” he indicates. LZ, on the other hand, is a nine-foot-tall cylinder containing around 11 tons of xenon, packed within a 20-foot-tall outer structure.

To take advantage of LZ’s whopping size and sensitivity, Gaitskell says, the team “decided to really aggressively push” beyond the usual search parameters.

The longstanding assumption in these experiments has been that WIMPs swoop in at relatively low energies and bounce off the xenon like billiard balls. In this case, when a WIMP collides with a xenon nucleus, it scatters the atom’s protons and neutrons in what’s called a “coherent” manner, where their resulting energies add up, amplifying the signal. But if WIMPs were to barrel in at higher energies, the particles would scatter in a trickier way to track.

Industry observers note that it was the switch to searching for these higher-energy collisions that led to LZ’s unusual detection. The signal also hinted that particles of dark matter would be quite heavy and collide with matter in a different way than many expected. Rather than rebounding like billiard balls, the WIMP may lose some energy (and mass) in the crash, exiting as a different, slimmer form of dark matter.

Recent findings suggest that notably, this detection couldn’t be explained by known forms of background events, like stray neutrons. The signal, then, could be dark matter, but it may also be a previously unknown type of background.

In announcing this event, Gaitskell says, the team was looking for input from the wider community, as they continue to pore through their own data. And input he did receive.

Recent findings suggest that amid the excitement and wave of preprint papers, though, many have retained a sense of caution. Messina notes he was initially skeptical of the single data point. “The immediate reaction was, ‘Come on, one event?’” he says. But he recognized XENONnT’s potentially crucial role in the next step toward discovery.

Given their detector’s comparable sensitivity, the team is now rushing to replicate the finding, looking through the past two years of their own data for signals that chime with the American detection. Or they could find nothing.

Either way, Messina would like to let the team’s data analysis do the talking, rather than get too excited now. They hope to release a paper in the next few months. “Data matters,” Messina claims. “All the rest is fake.”.

When Messina led me around in the spring, he wasn’t optimistic about the future of his field. He was continuing to support the search for dark matter with XENONnT, but he had also been devoting time to detecting neutrinos, another kind of subatomic particle generated by stars, radioactive decay and the Big Bang. “Many people like me are thinking, ‘You know what, I want to investigate different fields,’” he said.

Some WIMP proponents point out that even though the detectors haven’t found one of these fabled particles, they have made a less obvious kind of progress over the decades. In their searches, scientists have ruled out many potential WIMP masses and densities, ticking away at the options and possibly making it easier to zero in on their true properties in the future.

But to many onlookers—including the funding bodies that control cash flow—the lack of clear progress in particle physics has been disappointing. “It’s quite hard to convince politicians to support you if you have a significant discovery each 30 years,” Messina stated.

In a recent development, on top of the current fragile science funding ecosystem in the United States, he wasn’t sure how much more time WIMP detection had. He doubted the proposed next-generation detector, XLZD—which would dwarf LZ and XENON and merge the collaborations—would move forward.

Sources indicate that after LZ’s finding, though, Messina’s tune has changed. While he still stresses the uncertainty that this signal will lead to a discovery, he believes it has imparted “some momentum” back into WIMPs.

Many physicists still see more promise in other dark matter models—the hypothetical WIMPs might not be the best (or only) explanation.

According to recent reports, ben Safdi, a theoretical physicist at the University of California, Berkeley, claims that LZ’s detection may well be dark matter, but his initial excitement has waned. At first, the signal seemed to match an existing theory for WIMP behavior, but several preprint papers—including one of his—challenged this idea. “My personal belief that it is dark matter has gone down,” he says.

Safdi divides his research between WIMPs and a different dark matter candidate called axions. These theorized particles would move in a “continuous, almost fluid” wave through the universe, he says. Individually, axions would be super light—much less massive than WIMPs—but together, they could account for the missing mass of dark matter.

Recent findings suggest that attention to axions has surged as people have grown tired of WIMPs. While Safdi still thinks the WIMP hunt is worth continuing, “my heart is in axions,” he claims.

Did you know? Other strategies to find WIMPs.

It has been revealed that even if interest in WIMP detection is revitalized, technological challenges remain. One specter still haunting the field is a fog of neutrinos that’s threatening to descend on the instruments.

With increased sensitivity, the detectors are starting to pick up the constant swarm of neutrinos. These tiny particles don’t interact much with matter—trillions move through your body every second—but they can clutter data taken by detectors that are precise enough to notice them. As this neutrino fog wafts in, potential WIMP signals could get lost in the haze. XENONnT reported its first glimpses of the fog in 2024.

According to recent reports, this isn’t a huge problem for the detectors yet, and not everyone agrees it will be soon. But once neutrinos start meaningfully gumming up the signal, scientists don’t know what they’ll do.

Ronald Walsworth’s group is experimenting with a workaround: tracing the direction of incoming particles. WIMPs are expected to flood in like a “headwind” against the solar system’s path through the galaxy, he notes. On the other hand, a lot of neutrinos emanate from the direction of the sun, produced by the churn of fusion.

A sea of liquid xenon functions “like an antenna,” states Daniel Ang, a quantum scientist in Walsworth’s group. The flash of light only clues scientists into a particle’s collision—not the direction it rode in. So to trace a signal’s source, physicists might have to take a whole upcoming approach.

Walsworth decided to try this by using a more glamorous substance: diamonds. From his previous work, he knew that when particles cut through diamond crystals, they leave behind a finely detailed track—so their incoming direction is clear. “That’s the grandiose idea we had,” indicates Walsworth, a quantum physicist at the University of Maryland.

But the team has only tested their blinged-out detector on a small scale, and getting the funds to go bigger will be a challenge—especially given the “sagging of enthusiasm” for WIMPs, Walsworth notes.

Industry observers note that once Salomone, the postdoc, got back from vacation, his excitement about LZ’s signal was slightly tempered by his boss, he notes. “He was, of course, more skeptical and less enthusiastic than me.”.

Industry observers note that but even among Salomone’s liquid argon detector community, scientists are paying serious attention to the result. His collaboration has a regular meeting, which only one or two dozen people usually show up to. But at a recent one, some 100 people attended. Even people who never participated were interjecting with ideas, he states.

Salomone’s workdays are much like before, continuing to help build the DarkSide-20k detector, placing orders for special screws and popping over to the café for an espresso. But he feels a renewed excitement about the theory behind his daily tasks.

Sources indicate that “You’re still doing what you were doing before but with a different mind-set,” he notes. “Spending more time trying to read papers, spending more time trying to be even a better physicist, so that’s what I’m really happy about.”.
