A rare triple-star system near Earth ‘should not exist’

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers searching for fresh exoplanets recently found something much stranger—a rarely seen triple-star system located only 28 light-years away from Earth.
  • Sources indicate that “The system should not exist,” Patrick Dufour, a University of Montreal astrophysicist and study co-author, stated in a statement.
  • Industry observers note that dufour’s team first noticed the perplexing triple-star system while scanning for exoplanets using highly sensitive equipment mounted on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope near the dormant volcano of Mauna Kea.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers searching for fresh exoplanets recently found something much stranger—a rarely seen triple-star system located only 28 light-years away from Earth. If that weren’t odd enough, two of its three stellar components are dense, depleted white dwarfs. A study recently published in the Astronomy & Astrophysics Journal details an oddball trio that is so perplexing that researchers still aren’t quite sure how it formed in the first place.

Sources indicate that “The system should not exist,” Patrick Dufour, a University of Montreal astrophysicist and study co-author, stated in a statement. “We have no clean explanation for how it got here.”.

Industry observers note that dufour’s team first noticed the perplexing triple-star system while scanning for exoplanets using highly sensitive equipment mounted on the Canada-France-Hawaii Telescope near the dormant volcano of Mauna Kea. Astronomers were specifically looking for subtle discrepancies in the movements of distant stars, which often indicates that there are orbiting planets nearby.

But when it came to one particular red dwarf, the data simply didn’t make sense. Rather than delicate shifts in motion, researchers recorded velocity swings at speeds nearing 10 miles per second. This effect was too much for a single planet to cause, and after years of additional observations, astronomers determined that whatever the unseen subject was, it possessed a mass greater than half the sun.

“The object’s unusual combination of high mass and dim light left only one plausible explanation: it was the remains of a dead star,” explained Charles-Antoine Parent, a University of Montreal astronomer and study co-author.

Possible suspects included a neutron star and even a secret black hole, but some assistance from the Gemini North telescope also on Mauna Kea finally confirmed its identity: a close-orbiting white dwarf. This complicated the situation. Astronomers previously discovered another white dwarf circling the red dwarf at a much greater distance. Taken altogether, that made three stars existing in a single system. The grouping is now known as Welopō‘ai, a Hawaiian phrase that roughly translates to “path of family traits” in reference to the stars’ shared relationships. According to researchers, no other comparable example can be found within 100 light-years of Earth.

However, Welopō‘ai still doesn’t quite add up. The red dwarf’s nearest companion was about 40 percent more massive than our sun prior to transforming into a white dwarf. When it did, it would have expanded hundreds of times its original size. Previously documented systems featuring these dynamics entailed the two stars falling into an even tighter orbit, or even merging. Despite this, Welopō‘ai’s red dwarf is still there and in a strikingly stable, wide orbit with the closest white dwarf. The team now prepares to continue observing their discovery to learn as much as possible about the triple-star system, and possibly figure out how it formed in the first place.

“Discoveries like this remind us that our own cosmic neighborhood still contains remarkable surprises,” added study co-author and astronomer, Étienne Artigau.

#581. One of Hilma af Klint's Amazingly Rare Abstract Paintings Sold for a Record $12.7 Million at Auction. But Should It Have Been on Sale at All?

One of Hilma af Klint's Amazingly Rare Abstract Paintings Sold for a Record $12.7 Million at Auction. But Should It Have Been on Sale at All?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • On Thursday, a rare abstract painting by Swedish artist Hilma af Klint sold for a staggering $12.7 million at auction, raking in nearly 16 times its estimated worth.
  • In a recent development, ser III No.
  • According to recent reports, “She calls her work a message for humanity.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Thursday, a rare abstract painting by Swedish artist Hilma af Klint sold for a staggering $12.7 million at auction, raking in nearly 16 times its estimated worth. Painted in 1920, Ser III No. 5 is the first of af Klint’s abstract works to go to auction in over three decades, according to a statement from Bukowskis, the Stockholm-based auction house. But some critics say the sale defies the artist’s original intent.

In a recent development, ser III No. 5 epitomizes af Klint’s late-career abstractions, exploring the idea of balance through its black-and-white background broken by a series of colorful, stacked geometric shapes. The painting works on “an intimate scale, steeped in af Klint’s mystical visual language,” Min Chen writes for ArtNet.

According to recent reports, “She calls her work a message for humanity. There’s the balance of materialism but also spirituality,” Rachel Villari, author of Hilma af Klint’s Atom and The Tree of Knowledge, explains to NPR’s Rob Schmitz. “She was doing it as a way to convey a message for a future generation, [and] I believe we are that generation now”.

Af Klint created her first abstract work in 1906 and over the course of her career amassed more than 1,200—but almost none have ever sold. Unlike many of her modern art contemporaries, af Klint refused to show off her works beyond her intimate circle.

It has been revealed that for af Klint, her work was a way of connecting with a higher power; instead of hanging in a museum or private collection, she hoped her paintings would one day fill the walls of a temple. “For Hilma, this is a holy body of work,” Erik af Klint, the artist’s great grand-nephew and the board chair of the Hilma af Klint Foundation, tells Hyperallergic’s Rhea Nayyar.

Throughout her life, af Klint’s work was limited to a small, “spiritually interested audiences,” per the foundation’s website. Upon her death in 1944, af Klint, who never married or had children, bequeathed her collection to her nephew under the condition the public wouldn’t see them for at least 20 years. “The world, she believed, wasn’t ready for them,” Smithsonian’s Ellen Wexler wrote in May.

It has been revealed that for decades, her works languished in relative obscurity until a 2018 Guggenheim exhibition propelled her into the public eye. Art historians deemed her to be the world’s first abstract artist, reclaiming the title from Wassily Kandinsky, and the 2022 biopic Hilma brought her story to the massive screen.

Sources indicate that but, even as interest in af Klint’s life and work rose, collectors couldn’t get their hands on any of her abstract pieces. The foundation still owns almost all of her pieces and guards them tightly. “Her spirituality and her mysticism are so appealing to people, but she’s been out of reach for so long,” Louise Wrede, head of Bukowskis’ art department, tells the Wall Street Journal’s Kelly Crow. Erik af Klint, in particular, has resisted calls to share, monetize or sell the work, Hyperallergic reports, believing the art should be available as a complete body of work to those seeking a spiritual experience.

Ser III No. 5 is one of the few exceptions. In 1992, an entity related to the foundation tried to sell four of Klint’s works to little avail, the Journal reports. In 1995, an unnamed collector purchased two, including Ser III No. 5, which his heirs recently decided to list for auction. Still, the final sticker price likely came as a surprise. Its high-end estimate was $800,000. Af Klint’s previous auction record, set in 2019, was a mere $165,825 for a 1931 watercolor titled The Power of the Spleen.

Villari tells NPR that af Klint’s resurgence in the artworld—coupled with the inaccessibility of her pieces—likely contributed to the pumped up price: “That makes it even more desirable to people who can afford to buy her work because what would you want more than the impossible painting that you’re not supposed to have or can’t have?”.

Af Klint first began painting abstracts as a spiritual project. While in art school, she and four other young, female artists formed a group called “the Five,” devoted to spiritual beings they called the High Ones, per Bukowskis. Her first abstract series, The Paintings for the Temple, comprised 193 paintings dated from 1906 to 1913, each a fragment of an ideal spiritual temple.

According to recent reports, did you know? A collaborative project.

Experts suggest af Klint wasn’t the only artist behind The Paintings for the Temple. She often worked closely with the other members of the the Five, including Anna Cassel, who is thought to have been painted some of the projects’ pieces.

Industry observers note that soon, she was introduced to Rudolf Steiner, an Austrian guru who founded the anthroposophy movement, which centers around the idea that the human consciousness can perceive spiritual worlds. In 1920, she began her next project, 85 geometric works including Ser III No. 5 meant to interpret the anthroposophy creed.

Villari tells NPR that it is hard to understand af Klint’s pieces, including Ser III No. 5 on their own. “I believe that her work should be kept together as a whole, and that they should be shown sequentially,” she says. “I know, from my own research, that looking at her work from beginning to end, you can see that it’s a progression of this message that they’re conveying.”.

It has been revealed that free-On-Board (FOB) China mainstream module prices edged lower this week, weighed down by continued price weakness in lower-efficiency modules, as manufacturers clear inventories ahead of a stricter module efficiency standard taking effect on Jan. 1, 2027.

Recent findings suggest that according to the OPIS Global Solar Markets Report released on Nov. 17, the Chinese Module Marker (CMM), the OPIS benchmark assessment for TOPCon modules below 645 W from China, fell 0.93% on the week to $0.106/W FOB China, after five consecutive weeks unchanged at $0.107/W.

Forward prices for Q1 2027 loading tracked the weakness in the spot module market, falling 0.93% week on week to $0.106/W, while Q2 through Q4 2027 held steady at $0.105/W.

Across efficiency grades, price indications for high-efficiency TOPCon modules, defined as products above 650 W, were heard in the low $0.110s/W, while back-contact modules were heard in the low-to-mid $0.110s/W. By contrast, a Dow Jones Energy market survey showed that lower-efficiency TOPCon modules, particularly those in the 625-630 W range, were quoted in the low $0.100s/W on an FOB China basis, with prices in some regions already falling below $0.100/W.

It has been revealed that industry sources noted that manufacturers have stepped up inventory clearance efforts in the fourth quarter, anticipating weaker domestic offtake for lower-efficiency modules once the latest standard comes into effect. Under the standard, the minimum efficiency for TOPCon modules sold in China will be 23.2%, corresponding to a power output of 630 W.

Industry observers note that major producers’ inventories of lower-efficiency modules are already running low, one leading manufacturer said, as most have shifted production lines toward higher-efficiency products and average module power ratings among major TOPCon producers have reached around 640 W. Most of the remaining lower-efficiency stock sits with smaller or tier-2 players, who are undercutting prices aggressively, the manufacturer said.

Industry observers note that A top-tier integrated module manufacturer noted aggressive discounting in the lower-efficiency segment has also placed downward pressure on mainstream module prices, as procurement teams increasingly use lower-priced offers as leverage in price negotiations. The manufacturer added that while policies aimed at curbing module oversupply and regulating prices could support the market over the longer term, intense price competition among manufacturers is likely to persist in the near term.

Meanwhile, a divergence between domestic and export module prices has become increasingly evident since the start of Q4 2026.

Domestic mainstream TOPCon module prices have softened amid weakening demand, while export prices have remained comparatively resilient, with market sources noting that manufacturers’ quotations for overseas markets have largely resisted the downward trend in domestic prices.

According to OPIS data, EXW China TOPCon module prices fell by more than 1.8% since the beginning of October, while FOB China TOPCon mainstream modules remained broadly unchanged, before edging down by 0.93% this week.

Industry observers note that in domestic tenders, China Energy Engineering Corporation (CEEC) shortlisted 23 bidders for its 2026 centralized module procurement tender, covering 15 GW of TOPCon, heterojunction (HJT) and back-contact modules. TOPCon modules accounted for the largest share at 10.7 GW, with shortlisted bids of CNY 0.695-0.770 ($0.104-0.115)/W. Back-contact modules represented 3.3 GW, with six companies shortlisted and bids of CNY 0.760-0.779/W, while HJT modules accounted for the remaining 1 GW, with bids of CNY 0.717-0.752/W.

OPIS is a specialist business within Dow Jones Energy, a global energy intelligence business that brings together trusted price reporting, research and market intelligence across the energy value chain. OPIS publishes the OPIS Global Solar Markets Service, which includes pricing data for solar panels and components across Asia, Europe and the U.S., manufacturing capacity data, module forward curves, and a global solar policy tracker.

  • The latest projection represents an upward revision of 6 GW from GlobalData’s December 2025 forecast, which put Mexico’s installed solar capacity at 37.8 GW by 2035.
  • Industry observers note that the Mexico Power Market Trends and Analysis by Capacity, Generation, Transmission, Distribution, Regulations, Key Players and Forecast to 2035 report projects that Mexico’s total installed power capacity will increase from 104.2 GW in 2025 to 156 GW in 2035, representing a compound annual growth rate of 4.1%.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mexico’s installed solar capacity is expected to increase from 13.7 GW in 2025 to 43.8 GW by 2035, according to the latest report on the Mexican electricity market by research and consultancy firm GlobalData. The firm forecasts that renewables will account for 42.3% of the country’s total installed power capacity by 2035, up from 22.9% in 2025.

The latest projection represents an upward revision of 6 GW from GlobalData’s December 2025 forecast, which put Mexico’s installed solar capacity at 37.8 GW by 2035.

Industry observers note that the Mexico Power Market Trends and Analysis by Capacity, Generation, Transmission, Distribution, Regulations, Key Players and Forecast to 2035 report projects that Mexico’s total installed power capacity will increase from 104.2 GW in 2025 to 156 GW in 2035, representing a compound annual growth rate of 4.1%. Over the same period, natural gas-fired generation capacity is expected to rise from 53.4 GW to 64.8 GW.

Despite the expansion of renewables, GlobalData expects thermal power plants to continue accounting for nearly 60% of Mexico’s electricity generation in 2035, while the share of renewables in the generation mix is projected to increase from 14.5% to 31.9%. The consultancy also forecasts that electricity consumption will rise from 328.5 TWh in 2025 to 423.2 TWh in 2035, driven by industrial nearshoring, the expansion of data centers, and growing demand for air conditioning.

In a recent development, attaurrahman Ojindaram Saibasan, a power sector analyst at GlobalData, noted the 2025 Electricity Sector Law and the binding nature of the 2025-2039 Electricity Sector Development Plan (PLADESE) have reshaped Mexico’s investment landscape. The new framework guarantees the state at least 54% of the electricity injected into the grid and gives a central role to mixed-investment projects involving the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) and private companies.

Against this backdrop, the Mexican government announced in June its target of adding 22 GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030. The Ministry of Energy (Sener) recently reported the selection of 121 solar and wind projects totaling 18 GW. Meanwhile, CFE has increased planned investment in its portfolio of mixed-capital renewable energy projects to $10.6 billion. The portfolio includes 8,026 MW of generation capacity and more than 2,500 MW of energy storage capacity.

Recent findings suggest that globalData has identified a pipeline of power generation projects exceeding 45 GW, dominated by solar PV. However, it warned that transmission and distribution losses, estimated at around 11.5%, and congestion on transmission lines connecting northern Mexico with demand centers in central Mexico and the Bajío region could slow the connection of latest projects to the grid.

It has been revealed that “Mexico is not lacking in projects or resources. The pace of the transition will depend on whether the mixed-investment model can attract international developers – following years of regulatory uncertainty – and on whether the CFE can expand transmission infrastructure swiftly enough,” noted Saibasan.

  • “This efficiency breakthrough was made possible by multiple core technological innovations, including selective passivation technology for textured silicon surfaces in N-type TOPCon, a perovskite multi-component crystallization synchronization control strategy, and nanoscale interface passivation materials and light-management enhancement technologies,” the company mentioned in a statement, adding that the efficiency improvement was achieved over five months.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chinese solar module manufacturer JinkoSolar has announced that it has achieved a power conversion efficiency of 35.24% for a perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell.

Industry observers note that the manufacturer said the result was certified by the Shanghai Institute of Microsystem and Information Technology of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS). JinkoSolar previously achieved an efficiency of 34.82% with the same cell configuration.

“This efficiency breakthrough was made possible by multiple core technological innovations, including selective passivation technology for textured silicon surfaces in N-type TOPCon, a perovskite multi-component crystallization synchronization control strategy, and nanoscale interface passivation materials and light-management enhancement technologies,” the company mentioned in a statement, adding that the efficiency improvement was achieved over five months.

The company did not disclose further technical details about the cell or the efficiency improvement.

In a recent development, the current world record for perovskite-silicon tandem solar cell efficiency is held by Chinese manufacturer Longi, which achieved 35.5% efficiency in July 2026. The result, obtained with a two-terminal tandem cell, was independently certified by the European Solar Test Installation (ESTI). It surpassed Longi’s previous certified record of 34.85%, announced in April 2025.

Longi also recently reported an efficiency of 35.31% for a tandem cell incorporating specially designed self-assembled molecules. Longi previously achieved a certified efficiency of 34.85% in April 2025 and an efficiency of 34.3% for a large-area tandem cell measuring 261 cm².

In January 2026, Chinese module maker Trinasolar achieved 32.6% efficiency for a large-area tandem cell developed with Huairou Laboratory, with the result certified by Germany’s Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems (Fraunhofer ISE).

#574. High pressure drives irradiance gains across South East Asia as Sichuan misses out

General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Pv-magazine

High pressure drives irradiance gains across South East Asia as Sichuan misses out

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that october 2026 brought unusually sunny conditions across much of southern China and mainland South East Asia, with irradiance 20%+ above average in the strongest-affected areas, according to analysis using the Solcast API.
  • In a recent development, the strongest positive irradiance anomalies stretched across Yunnan, Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan, through northern Indochina and into the Philippines.
  • It has been revealed that sichuan and Chongqing were a notable exception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that october 2026 brought unusually sunny conditions across much of southern China and mainland South East Asia, with irradiance 20%+ above average in the strongest-affected areas, according to analysis using the Solcast API. Persistent high pressure over South East Asia and the South China Sea, alongside a very strong El Niño, suppressed rainfall and cloud. Sichuan and Chongqing missed much of the irradiance boost, while repeated cold fronts and Typhoon Champi interrupted the broader pattern farther north and east.

In a recent development, the strongest positive irradiance anomalies stretched across Yunnan, Guangxi, Guangdong and Hainan, through northern Indochina and into the Philippines. Rainfall was up to 6 millimeters per day below average across much of the same region, helping keep skies clearer. October rainfall in thesouthern southwest was more than 50% below normal, with drought persisting in Yunnan, southwest Guizhou and southern Guangxi. Southern and central China were also more than 1.5 C warmer than average. Hong Kong recorded its warmest October, with a mean temperature of 27.6 C. A weakernortheast monsoon and persistent high pressure helped limit the usual influx of moisture and cloud, reinforcing the sunnier pattern during a very strong El Niño.

It has been revealed that sichuan and Chongqing were a notable exception. While surrounding regions recorded positive irradiance anomalies, the basin saw slightly below-average irradiance for October. More easterly winds than usual and lower pressure over the Sichuan Basin helped keep cloud concentrated over the region, with the surrounding terrain and anomalously high pressure limiting its dispersal. The additional cloud coincided with neutral to slightly above-average rainfall in October, in contrast with the drier conditions surrounding the basin and farther south.

Recent findings suggest that farther north and east, repeated cold-air outbreaks brought periods of increased cloud and precipitation, interrupting the otherwise favourable irradiance conditions. China experienced six cold-air outbreaks during October, 2.4 more than average. These brought rain and snow across parts of northern and eastern China, with eastern Hebei and most of Beijing receiving 50–100 mm of precipitation from 15–23 October.

Typhoon Champi provided another interruption to the broader pattern. The storm formed on 11 October and reached winds near 215 km/h, affecting Taiwan, Japan and China. Cloud and rainfall associated with the system reduced irradiance as it moved through the region, with 62,400 people evacuated in Shanghai due to the conditions. October was particularly active for tropical weather overall, with eight tropical cyclones across the South China Sea and western North Pacific during the month.

According to recent reports, farther south, Sumatra and Kalimantan recorded below-average irradiance despite substantial rainfall deficits. Indonesia had recorded more than 1.06 million fire hotspots by 14 October, with widespread smoke and haze reducing incoming sunlight despite the otherwise dry conditions. Aerosol optical depth shows where the heaviest concentrations of smoke and haze occurred during the month.

Industry observers note that solcast produces these figures by tracking clouds and aerosols at 1-2km resolution globally, using satellite data and proprietary AI/ML algorithms. This data is used to drive irradiance models, enabling Solcast to calculate irradiance at high resolution, with typical bias of less than 2%, and also cloud-tracking forecasts. This data is used by more than 350 companies managing over 350 GW of solar assets globally.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Archdaily

What Happened to Parametricism? How a Style Blurred Into a Look

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Archdaily

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In September 2008, at a series of sessions organized alongside the 11th Venice Architecture Biennale under the name of the Dark Side Club, a text was presented that announced, for the first time since Modernism, a latest style for architecture.
  • It has been revealed that in September 2008, at a series of sessions organized alongside the 11th Venice Architecture Biennale under the name of the Dark Side Club, a text was presented that unveiled, for the first time since Modernism, a upcoming style for architecture.
  • Eighteen years is a long time in digital culture, and the manifesto has had an unusually long afterlife.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Written by Diogo Borges Ferreira.

In September 2008, at a series of sessions organized alongside the 11th Venice Architecture Biennale under the name of the Dark Side Club, a text was presented that announced, for the first time since Modernism, a latest style for architecture. Parametricism as Style, written by Patrik Schumacher, then a partner at Zaha Hadid Architects, called it "the great new style after modernism" and recast Postmodernism and Deconstructivism as "transitional episodes" that had prepared its arrival. What the manifesto proposed was a design logic in which every element of a project, from the urban plan down to the tectonic detail, the interior and the product, would be treated as a variable, so that form could differentiate continuously and adapt to the shifting demands placed upon it.

It has been revealed that in September 2008, at a series of sessions organized alongside the 11th Venice Architecture Biennale under the name of the Dark Side Club, a text was presented that unveiled, for the first time since Modernism, a upcoming style for architecture. Parametricism as Style, written by Patrik Schumacher, then a partner at Zaha Hadid Architects, called it "the great new style after modernism" and recast Postmodernism and Deconstructivism as "transitional episodes" that had prepared its arrival. What the manifesto proposed was a design logic in which every element of a project, from the urban plan down to the tectonic detail, the interior and the product, would be treated as a variable, so that form could differentiate continuously and adapt to the shifting demands placed upon it.

Eighteen years is a long time in digital culture, and the manifesto has had an unusually long afterlife. It was relaunched in 2016 as Parametricism 2.0: Rethinking Architecture's Agenda for the 21st Century, an entire problem of Architectural Design built on the premise that the style had been delayed by circumstance while remaining intact as a project, one presented by its publisher as "progressing beyond its experimental roots to make an impact on a broader scale" while maintaining that parametricism was "not universal, but it's sufficiently entrenched." Architecture has no shortage of manifestos, but very few of their authors are still around to be asked whether their prophecies have come true.

It was relaunched in 2016 as Parametricism 2.0: Rethinking Architecture's Agenda for the 21st Century, an entire issue of Architectural Design built on the premise that the style had been delayed by circumstance while remaining intact as a project, one presented by its publisher as "progressing beyond its experimental roots to make an impact on a broader scale" while maintaining that parametricism was "not universal, but it's sufficiently entrenched." Architecture has no shortage of manifestos, but very few of their authors are still around to be asked whether their prophecies have come true.

In a recent development, reread today, the text holds up best as a document of a particular moment, when fifteen years of digital experiment had accumulated without a theory to organize them. The argument here is that the three things it bundled together (a technique, a set of formal rules and a diagnosis of society) have since come apart, each for its own reasons, and that what survives is the demand underneath them, the idea that a style is a research program, a set of rules about what to pursue and what to refuse, and that a discipline is weaker without one. By that measure, the manifesto has been both defeated and vindicated.

By that measure, the manifesto has been both defeated and vindicated.

Related Article The Right to Be Naive: How Architecture Turned Innocence into a Position.

In 1993, Greg Lynn guest-edited Folding in Architecture, an issue of Architectural Design that read Gilles Deleuze's The Fold (first published in French in 1988) as a brief for an architecture of continuous variation. Behind it lay Bernard Cache's objectile, a term Deleuze took from him to describe an object conceived as a function, a rule capable of generating a whole family of variants. Much of what the 2008 text would claim was already present in that idea, although in the 1990s it lived inside animation software developed for the film industry, within reach of a handful of studios and schools. That changed in September 2007, a year before Venice, when David Rutten released a free Rhino plug-in called Explicit History, soon renamed Grasshopper and eventually folded into Rhino 6 in 2018 as part of the package. Within a decade, associative modeling had stopped being an avant-garde competence and become an ordinary office tool.

Behind it lay Bernard Cache's objectile, a term Deleuze took from him to describe an object conceived as a function, a rule capable of generating a whole family of variants. Much of what the 2008 text would claim was already present in that idea, although in the 1990s it lived inside animation software developed for the film industry, within reach of a handful of studios and schools. That changed in September 2007, a year before Venice, when David Rutten released a free Rhino plug-in called Explicit History, soon renamed Grasshopper and eventually folded into Rhino 6 in 2018 as part of the package. Within a decade, associative modeling had stopped being an avant-garde competence and become an ordinary office tool.

In September 2010, the researcher Daniel Davis argued that a parametric model is a means of representation with no form of its own, and that drawing the Villa Savoye in Grasshopper would not make it parametric architecture, which is another way of saying that the technique could travel without the style. The manifesto was poorly placed to answer, since it had tied the style to its instruments from the start. Among its heuristics, besides the instructions to interarticulate and to morph, it told architects to "use splines, nurbs, generative components, script rather than model", a list that places software and modeling routines among the style's principles.

According to recent reports, in September 2010, the researcher Daniel Davis argued that a parametric model is a means of representation with no form of its own, and that drawing the Villa Savoye in Grasshopper would not make it parametric architecture, which is another way of saying that the technique could travel without the style. The manifesto was poorly placed to answer, since it had tied the style to its instruments from the start. Among its heuristics, besides the instructions to interarticulate and to morph, it told architects to "use splines, nurbs, generative components, script rather than model", a list that places software and modeling routines among the style's principles.

The manifesto also explained why this style, and why now. Styles, in its account, arise from the conditions that make them necessary, and the conditions were those of "the socio-economic era of post-fordism", a heterogeneous society whose complexity would demand an architecture of continuous differentiation, whether or not anyone liked it. Measured against that standard, the record since then divides badly. The technique became universal for reasons that have little to do with post-Fordist complexity and a great deal to do with a plug-in being free and a construction economy that wanted its arithmetic checked. The forms, meanwhile, took hold mostly in very large, one-off commissions (airports, stadiums, cultural institutions), the few programs whose budgets could absorb a method in which form was settled first and structure and envelope were resolved afterwards. Beijing Daxing International Airport, designed by Zaha Hadid Architects and opened in 2019, belongs to this type at its largest-scale buildings, and it is instructive precisely because it is so hard to repeat.

Beijing Daxing International Airport, designed by Zaha Hadid Architects and opened in 2019, belongs to this type at its largest-scale buildings, and it is instructive precisely because it is so hard to repeat.

Mario Carpo offers a second reading in which the technology moves first and style trails behind it. In The Second Digital Turn, published in 2017, he treats the smooth, curving surfaces of the 1990s as the signature of a first digital age, shaped by tools that were still short of computing power, and describes what followed as a different regime, in which software has become a set of "tools for thinking" and the data-compression techniques on which earlier design depended are no longer needed. The spline was one of those techniques, a compact shorthand standing in for a list of coordinates too long to handle. If the smooth geometry owed its necessity to the hardware of a particular decade, it carried a date from the start, and digital design was already moving toward discrete parts and aggregation while the manifesto was being relaunched in 2016.

According to recent reports, read now, the manifesto is stranger than its reputation; it contains almost no description of buildings and a great deal of legislation. The apparatus comes from Imre Lakatos, the philosopher of science who argued that theories are never tested one at a time and are defended instead as programs, with a hard core that adherents agree to protect and a belt of working assumptions that absorbs the damage when evidence goes against them. Lakatos attached to the model a criterion that keeps it honest, by which a program is progressing while it keeps turning up things nobody was looking for, and degenerating once its energy goes into explaining what it got wrong. Transposed to architecture, this produces a list of techniques to pursue and a list of refusals, and it is the second that has aged most strangely (avoid repetition, avoid straight lines, avoid right angles, avoid corners).

Transposed to architecture, this produces a list of techniques to pursue and a list of refusals, and it is the second that has aged most strangely (avoid repetition, avoid straight lines, avoid right angles, avoid corners).

In a recent development, "There can be neither verification, nor final refutation merely based on its built results", the text declares of a style, which places the enterprise beyond the reach of any individual disappointment. It can look like a cheap trick, although it is roughly how any discipline shields a young idea from its own early prototypes. However, what Lakatos also provided was a way of determining when the protection had ceased to be effective; its expiry date. Eighteen years spent on the wrong side of his distinction is a long time when adoption is slower than predicted.

Of all the refusals, the ban on repetition was the most significant. Its justification has to be read from the diagnosis, which contrasted the "mass society" of modernism and its single standard of consumption with a far more heterogeneous present, and concluded, in effect, that a society which no longer consumed identical things should no longer be housed in them. That is a statement about the economy, and it depends on what the economy rewards. Embodied carbon is now measured, increasingly priced and, in countries such as France and Denmark, limited by regulation, and since a large share of it sits in structure and envelope, ordering the same element a thousand times, with less waste, faster fitting and some prospect of demounting and reuse, has come to count in a project's favor.

It has been revealed that the style's own revision came in 2017 under the name Tectonism, later described as "a sub-style within parametricism", a modest label for what is, in practice, a change of direction. Form is now meant to emerge from structural behavior and from what a robotic arm or a concrete printer can actually do, so that geometry follows the flow of forces and the reach of the machine. The term had already been explored in 1995, when Kenneth Frampton, in Studies in Tectonic Culture, used it to describe architecture as a poetics of construction, something read in the way a building meets the ground, carries its roof and, above all, joins one part to another, and set it against the scenographic, the building conceived as an image. It is a curious inheritance for a style whose founding text had legislated against precisely that kind of legibility (avoid clear-cut zones, it instructed, and never add or subtract "without elaborate interarticulations"), which comes close to banning the joint altogether. The flow of forces appears instead as ribs and striations drawn across a single continuous figure, as in Striatus, the printed concrete footbridge that Zaha Hadid Architects built in Venice in 2021 with ETH Zurich's Block Research Group, where structure turns into pattern and the engineering diagram takes over the role the render once played.

The manifesto's case for its forms was social and economic (before it was formal). Parametricism offered itself as the spatial form of a networked, self-organizing society, an order that arises from interaction without anyone drawing it up, which describes a building and, in slightly different terms, a market. In Architecture and Utopia, Manfredo Tafuri had warned that architecture's formal radicalism is routinely absorbed by the development it believes itself to be criticizing, and Douglas Spencer, in The Architecture of Neoliberalism (2016), brought that warning up to date by reading smooth, continuously differentiated space as the favored environment of neoliberal management, emancipatory in its imagery and discreet about the labor and procurement conditions that produced it. Read as determinism, the argument is easily dismissed, given how many architects have used these tools with no interest in the economics attached to them. Still, the style's most complete buildings were only possible for clients who could afford them.

Recent findings suggest that but if the social half of the case came away without anyone much noticing, the technical half has come apart more recently. Image generators trained on, among much else, two decades of published architecture now produce continuous differentiation on request, with no associative model, no parameters and no structural reasoning of any kind (a long way, it should be said, from "script rather than model"). For twenty years the parametric surface worked as a credential, telling a client or a jury that the office behind it had computational capacity and could carry the risk that came with it, and once the same surface can be produced in seconds it stops telling anyone very much. By the manifesto's own definition, a style that survives as appearance, with no research program underneath it, has become one more look among the many it had hoped to supersede.

For twenty years the parametric surface worked as a credential, telling a client or a jury that the office behind it had computational capacity and could carry the risk that came with it, and once the same surface can be produced in seconds it stops telling anyone very much. By the manifesto's own definition, a style that survives as appearance, with no research program underneath it, has become one more look among the many it had hoped to supersede.

None of this disposes of what the manifesto asked for, which was a shared project, explicit about what to pursue and what to refuse, and over the same eighteen years the discipline has in fact acquired one, from a direction the text did not anticipate. Carbon now comes with its own metrics and prohibitions and with a stronger claim on historical necessity than post-Fordism ever had, and it reached architecture from outside, through regulation and accounting, without needing a manifesto to be adopted. It tells architects what to count and what to avoid and says almost nothing about what a building should be, so that it produces compliance where the 2008 text wanted conviction. The generation of small practices that formed after 2008 has made a position out of declining to sound certain, and the sensibility that followed them has yet to settle into a doctrine, which may be why a text so easy to fault has proved so difficult to put away. The question it asked in Venice, whether architecture can still share a project about form, remains open long after its own answer stopped convincing.

According to recent reports, mexico-based COLECTIVO C733 was named the inaugural recipient of the Siza Award for public architecture, established by the Serralves Foundation. The first edition marks the 10th anniversary of the Serralves Foundation's Álvaro Siza Archive and aims to recognize architectural generosity and public-space engagement, in honor of the Portuguese architect's vision. Like Siza's body of work, the award is open to the international community. COLECTIVO C733's public infrastructure portfolio includes markets, cultural facilities, transport hubs and public landscapes across Mexico, such as Bacalar Eco-Park, Guadalupe Market, Tapachula Station, Nacajuca's Music House community center and Matamoros Market, as well as their work with Mexico's Ministry of Agrarian, Territorial and Urban Development (SEDATU) in vulnerable regions and along the U.S.–Mexico border.

It has been revealed that the Siza Award is an annual architecture prize established by the Serralves Foundation to honor socially responsible design and public architecture. It places special emphasis on architectural generosity and targets emerging practices and architects in their thirties and forties with demonstrated sensitivity to local communities, territory, and the environment. The recognition is grounded in the conviction, reflected in Siza's career, that architects are agents of change with the ability to influence democratic discourse, whether in rebuilding urban identities or promoting social inclusion. As stated by the Foundation, the newly introduced generation of architects it targets now faces the challenge "to bridge the gap between human scarcity and technological advancement, rethinking the rules of the game and exploring archetypes, materials, shelters, labor, and other ways of improving life as a whole.".

Vietnam sets rooftop solar monitoring and control acceptance procedure

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (378 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Vietnam’s state-owned national power utility Vietnam Electricity (EVN) has introduced fresh technical requirements and acceptance procedures for rooftop solar installations that export surplus electricity to the grid.
  • 1382/QĐ-EVN, issued on November 18, sets out technical specifications and a process for testing and accepting rooftop solar installations connected to EVN’s monitoring, data-collection and control systems.
  • The requirements cover rooftop solar systems designed for self-consumption that export surplus electricity to the grid and fall within the electricity manufacturer’s monitoring and control remit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Vietnam’s state-owned national power utility Vietnam Electricity (EVN) has introduced fresh technical requirements and acceptance procedures for rooftop solar installations that export surplus electricity to the grid.

Decision No. 1382/QĐ-EVN, issued on November 18, sets out technical specifications and a process for testing and accepting rooftop solar installations connected to EVN’s monitoring, data-collection and control systems. It replaces Decision No. 378/QĐ-EVN, issued on Mar. 12, 2025, and takes effect immediately.

The requirements cover rooftop solar systems designed for self-consumption that export surplus electricity to the grid and fall within the electricity manufacturer’s monitoring and control remit.

Under the specifications, installations must transmit operational data to the electricity company’s monitoring system, with inverter output updated at intervals of no more than five minutes.

Systems must also be capable of both receiving and executing remote commands to limit exported power, as well as automatically adjusting inverter output to comply with instructions from the utility.

The acceptance testing procedure includes documentation reviews, site inspections, communications testing and verification of monitoring and control signals. Utilities must also test a system’s ability to reduce exports in response to power limitation commands and check its behaviour during communications outages and faults before issuing any acceptance documentation.

EVN notes system owners are responsible for installing compatible monitoring, metering and communications equipment, providing technical documentation and coordinating with utilities during testing. Electricity companies are responsible for providing connection and communications configurations, verifying cybersecurity and monitoring functionality and conducting the acceptance tests.

It has been revealed that the decision comes as Vietnam looks to accelerate rooftop solar deployment. The Vietnamese government ordered provinces to speed up rooftop solar support policies in September. Last month, it called on provincial and municipal authorities to introduce these policies by the end of the year.

A Ministry of Industry and Trade publication released in September also outlined plans to link distributed rooftop solar, behind-the-meter battery energy storage systems and electric vehicles into flexible grid assets, moving away from basic time-of-use tariffs.

Vietnam’s solar capacity surpassed 19 GW by the end of 2025, with around 586 MW of solar added last year. The country had more than 11.45 GW of rooftop solar capacity across 134,410 installations as of the end of August 2026, according to figures from EVN.

#564. Georgia O'Keeffe Is Famous for Painting Flowers and Deserts. Why Have We Forgotten Her Obsession With American Architecture?

Georgia O'Keeffe Is Famous for Painting Flowers and Deserts. Why Have We Forgotten Her Obsession With American Architecture?

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, but while she found the scenery striking, nature was only part of the American Southwest’s aesthetic appeal.
  • “I bought the place because it had that door in the patio, the one I’ve painted so often,” she said in a 1962 interview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Georgia O’Keeffe started visiting Newly introduced Mexico in 1929, immersing herself in the state’s austere desert landscapes for months at a time. She captured her surroundings in hundreds of paintings, which are now some of her best-known works.

In a recent development, but while she found the scenery striking, nature was only part of the American Southwest’s aesthetic appeal. In the 1930s, the artist stumbled across an abandoned house in Abiquiú, which she later purchased. O’Keeffe was particularly fascinated by a large wooden door leading to the central patio, a feature she painted at least 20 times.

“I bought the place because it had that door in the patio, the one I’ve painted so often,” she said in a 1962 interview. “I’m always trying to paint that door—I never quite get it. It’s a curse—the way I feel I must continually go on with that door.”.

Industry observers note that O’Keeffe is considered one of America’s greatest artists, and general audiences are familiar with her desert landscapes and large-scale flower portraits. But now, an exhibition at the Detroit Institute of Arts spotlights a lesser-known part of her oeuvre: her enduring fascination with the built environment.

Industry observers note that “This is the first exhibit that takes a comprehensive view of architecture as a lifelong fascination for O’Keeffe,” Ben Colman, the exhibition’s curator, tells the New York Times’ Leslie Wayne. “Barns and fields and buildings are not the O’Keeffe that people think about. It’s a bit of a surprise.”.

Quick facts: Georgia O’Keeffe’s flowers.

“Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture” features nearly 40 works created between the 1920s and 1960s. The artist’s paintings are grouped into three sections, each exploring a central setting from her life: rural barns and farmhouses, New York City skyscrapers, and New Mexico homes.

In a recent development, stables, a painting of a white barn that the artist noticed during a 1932 road trip through Quebec, served as the inspiration for the exhibition. It’s the only O’Keeffe in the Detroit Institute of Arts’ collections. When Colman joined the institute in 2015, he was fascinated by its simple geometric shapes and large blocks of color. He found himself thinking about it often.

“I had such a strong pull to this picture and wanted to know more,” Colman says in an interview posted on the institute’s website. “In asking questions about Stables, I started to sketch out a broader story about O’Keeffe’s life and her engagement with architecture across her career. What began as a set of questions about the summer of 1932 turned into a larger story about the role architecture played as a recurring source of inspiration throughout the artist’s life.”.

Stables is on display in the exhibition’s first section, which reflects O’Keeffe’s childhood on a Wisconsin dairy farm, as well as her sojourns to Lake George in upstate Latest York with her husband, photographer Alfred Stieglitz.

Another highlight of this section is My Shanty, Lake George (1922). Colman describes it as “a challenge to her critics,” who struggled to evaluate O’Keeffe’s art without considering her gender.

In a recent development, “One day as I looked at the brown burned wood of the Shanty, I thought, ‘I can paint one of those dismal-colored paintings like the men. I think just for fun I will try—all low-toned and dreary,’” O’Keeffe wrote in her 1976 autobiography. When My Shanty, Lake George went on display, “the men seemed to approve of it,” she added. “They seemed to think that maybe I was beginning to paint.”.

Sources indicate that the second section showcases paintings of high-rises in Fresh York City, where the artist lived for three decades. One of the pieces on view is Brooklyn Bridge (1949), the final city artwork that O’Keeffe created before moving away. She painted it from the perspective of someone passing through the bridge’s famous archways.

“It captures a view that you only see when you’re crossing the river, when you’re in the midst of making a change yourself,” Colman states. “The artist created this painting the year that she relocated her life and home to New Mexico permanently.”.

The final section displays O’Keeffe’s paintings of Newly introduced Mexico, where she lived until her death at age 98 in 1986. These paintings capture the region’s unique adobe architecture—including ten depictions of that inscrutable patio door.

“Georgia O’Keeffe: Architecture” is on view at the Detroit Institute of Arts through January 3, 2027.

  • It has been revealed that rosemary Lonewolf has fond memories of sitting at the kitchen table with her dad and grandpa.
  • In a recent development, lonewolf, who is a member of the Santa Clara Pueblo (Tewa) tribe and based at their reservation in New Mexico, remembers a conversation when she was about 20 during which her grandpa, Camilio Tafoya, commented on spaceships.
  • It has been revealed that his statement, made in the mid-1970s, stuck with her.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rosemary Lonewolf has fond memories of sitting at the kitchen table with her dad and grandpa. The three artists would each work on their respective pottery piece, perhaps polishing an almost finished one or designing what would be carved into clay, as they chatted.

In a recent development, lonewolf, who is a member of the Santa Clara Pueblo (Tewa) tribe and based at their reservation in New Mexico, remembers a conversation when she was about 20 during which her grandpa, Camilio Tafoya, commented on spaceships. He said, “One of these days, they’re going to poke a hole in the sky,” recalls Lonewolf, who is also known by her Tewa name, Apple Blossom.

It has been revealed that his statement, made in the mid-1970s, stuck with her. Over a decade later, it inspired her to create a round, palm-size seed jar called Wings, Machines and Other Flying Things, featuring carvings of a space shuttle, an airplane, a bird, a butterfly and other airborne items. The piece also includes a Pueblo spacewalker, who sparks a conversation.

“If Native Americans went to the moon, how would we handle that?” Lonewolf says. According to her culture, the land belongs to everyone, so no one can own it. “To go and put your nation’s flag in the ground [on the moon] and claim it for your nation is foreign.”.

It has been revealed that lonewolf’s thought-provoking piece is one of more than 300 artworks showcased in the “Mighty Miniatures” exhibition at the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Indian in New York. On display from November 21, 2026, to August 20, 2027, the exhibition highlights mesmerizing tiny objects from the museum’s vast collection, including dolls, baskets, animals and homes, crafted by Indigenous artists.

“I really wanted to curate an exhibition that would bring joy, especially Indigenous joy,” says museum curator Anya Montiel, who is of Tohono O’odham descent.

Recent findings suggest that did you know? Opposite end of the size spectrum.

Lonewolf also designs large-scale structures for public art, including the Isaac Pedestrian Bridge in Phoenix, which resembles parts of a scarlet macaw—a bird prized by Pueblo peoples.

The idea for “Mighty Miniatures” struck Montiel around 2022. As she combed through the museum’s inventory of roughly 825,000 objects at its storage facility in Suitland, Maryland, to check that they were in their proper places, she regularly came across remarkably tiny items.

Industry observers note that “I would stop what I was doing, and then go to another co-worker and say, ‘Oh, my gosh, look at this,’” Montiel says. Other staff would do the same.

The collection database revealed that the museum had more than 1,300 miniatures from North, Central and South America and Hawaii.

Recent findings suggest that one part of the exhibition introduces visitors to objects at the small scale, placing minuscule models next to their full-size equivalents. Another area highlights play, showing how dolls and small versions of objects like cradleboards, traditional baby carriers, are teaching tools for children, helping them to imagine themselves as adults.

Toys “are a way to transfer Indigenous knowledge from one generation to another,” Montiel notes.

Industry observers note that watercraft and architecture are highlighted in two other sections. The first features objects including little canoes, kayaks and Hawaiian seafaring outriggers. The other is meant to show the diversity of Indigenous peoples’ homes.

Sources indicate that “I want people to know that Native people don’t just live in tepees,” Montiel claims. “We do have a tepee, but we have hogans, we have Pueblo adobe buildings, we have one from Alaska. We also have a home from South America, from the Amazon.”.

Another section helps visitors understand why some Indigenous artists create miniatures: tourism. It features shrunken-down versions of objects that would otherwise be too big for a traveler to transport. And an additional area displays some of the most intricate, tiniest works in the exhibition to showcase artistic skill. For instance, one of the objects there is a Pomo miniature basket measuring just 0.1 by 0.1 inches.

It has been revealed that montiel wants visitors to marvel at the pieces here and ask how such tiny recreations could’ve been made. “It really is gathering these works where you have these Indigenous artists who specialize in miniatures, and they are testing themselves on: ‘How small can I make something and it still look like a pot?’”.

One of Montiel’s favorite featured works is a model of an old cookstove made of woven beach ryegrass and sealskin, likely created by a Yup’ik artist in Alaska more than 100 years ago.

Sources indicate that she knew little about the piece when she first came across it. So, she reached out to stove restoration expert Brandon Pineo at the Antique Stove Hospital in Little Compton, Rhode Island, who told her it was based on an appliance made after 1875. Since the piece was acquired in 1908, Montiel was able to pinpoint the full-size stove in old catalogs at the National Museum of American History with the help of library technician Alexia MacClain.

“That’s a really beautiful piece because I think about everybody’s expertise coming together to really tell an amazing story,” Montiel indicates.

To help kick off the exhibition, the museum will host a workshop on December 12 led by miniaturist Lance Cardinal, who is a member of the Bigstone Cree Nation and based in Alberta. During multiple sessions throughout the day, Cardinal will show visitors how to craft a small version of a traditional hand drum.

It has been revealed that normally, these instruments—which are around one to two feet wide—take about two days to make, Cardinal explains. First, birch wood is steamed and curved into a ring. Deerskin is stretched over it to create the drum head, and a sinew string or ribbons of skin are used to tie everything together. The drum then gets dried over a fire. Workshop attendees will use many traditional elements, including birch strip rings and sinew thread, to make their diminutive drums, he says.

In a recent development, cardinal’s love of miniatures began in childhood. He undertook his first passion project as an elementary school student in the early 1980s, when he used construction paper to create an operational replica of the carnival that traveled to his tiny town of Calling Lake. Sinking into artistry and imagination provided an escape from difficult circumstances.

In a recent development, today, that time in his life still inspires him. Many of his miniatures evoke memories of American pop culture, including tiny models of scenes and objects from classic TV programs like “The Muppet Show,” “Sesame Street” and “Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood.” Other pieces are inspired by his Cree culture, including a model of the dog sled his family used when they went trapping and fishing and a replica of the residential school his grandparents were forced to attend.

In a recent development, “When we create something small, we go in close. … We feel safer about it because we feel like we have dominance over it,” Cardinal says. “So that’s why I did it for Indigenous things, for First Nations things, because it lets people feel safe enough to get close to a miniature tepee or to a small miniature drum without feeling scared or intimidated by it. And I think that’s really important.”.

According to recent reports, lonewolf, meanwhile, has had a hand in reinventing a traditional artform. Pueblo peoples of the American Southwest have been crafting pottery for some 2,000 years, often making practical items such as water vessels and seed-storage jars, as well as ceremonial pots.

In a recent development, the practice was generally handed down among women, from mother to daughter, as part of their household tasks, Lonewolf explains. It was unusual for her grandpa and dad to learn the skill, and they were sometimes ridiculed and called “sissies” for doing “women’s work,” she says.

But her father, Joseph Lonewolf, helped revolutionize Santa Clara Pueblo pottery, making it contemporary. At the behest of beginner collectors who wanted his artworks but couldn’t afford his roughly ten-inch pieces, he began to shrink his pottery, Lonewolf states. Scaling down some objects made his art a bit more accessible. Joseph also started to depict realistic representations of animals and his experiences as a hunter onto his pieces, rather than just geometric designs. Submitting these works to art reveals sometimes resulted in rejection and remarks like, “This isn’t Pueblo pottery.”.

Recent findings suggest that additionally, Joseph began to move traditional elements of pottery so they wouldn’t interfere with the design, such as putting the hole of a pot on the bottom rather than the top. “By taking the traditional use out of a pot, it wasn’t a pot anymore,” Lonewolf says. “When you removed the utilization … it became artwork.”.

That created a shift in people’s minds about Pueblo pottery. It didn’t need a specific purpose; people could appreciate it for art’s sake. “Nobody asks a painter, ‘Well, what is this painting for? What am I supposed to do with it?’” Lonewolf indicates. “He did break the clay ceiling in many ways.”.

Lonewolf naturally followed in the footsteps of her dad and grandpa, as well as her aunt, the noted potter Grace Medicine Flower. She grew up watching them and other family members creating with clay, eventually being handed her own pieces of squishy earth to sculpt.

Sources indicate that today, she hopes her artworks—small, large and in between—help share her people’s world. For instance, an image of a turtle on a piece can represent so much. The Rio Grande is filled with turtles, so it reflects the region. Turtle shells are also used in cultural dances: They’re strapped to the backs of men’s calves and filled with stones, so they rattle, mimicking the sound of rain.

In a recent development, “It’s not just a turtle; it’s telling the story of a culture, of what this culture and these people value,” Lonewolf indicates. She urges viewers to “take the time to look at it and ask questions about it, ask the story behind the symbols.”.

That’s what Montiel wants the entire “Mighty Miniatures” exhibition to do as well.

“Sometimes you see visitors going into a gallery, and they almost seem afraid to talk,” she indicates. So, she asked herself, “Can I create a space of joy where you are so excited by what you see that you turn to someone and say, ‘Did you see this? Have you seen that?’”.

Montiel adds, “I’m nurturing learning but also a conversation between people.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

California-based duo Proper Voltage and Unigrid have teamed up to pair voltage-control electronics with sodium-chromium oxide cells to create a 73.1 kWh backup cabinet aimed at delivering power to data centers.

Battery integration firm Proper Voltage confirmed that it has launched Salt Vault, an uninterruptible power supply (UPS) battery cabinet built around sodium-ion cells from San Diego-based Unigrid. Commercial deliveries to unnamed early-adopter data center and critical infrastructure operators are scheduled to begin in April 2027.

The system combines Proper Voltage’s software that it calls its battery operating system (bOS) with Unigrid’s sodium-chromium oxide (NCO) chemistry.

According to Proper Voltage’s product specifications, the Salt Vault High Power cabinet delivers 73.1 kWh of capacity and 333 kW of power output at a nominal 522 VDC, rated for 10,000 cycles. It operates across a discharge temperature range of -20 C to 40 C and a charge range of 0 C to 40 C. A single module in the cabinet is 6.1 kWh.

According to recent reports, the two companies are targeting a specific operational problem in AI data centers, where training and inference clusters swing from idle to peak load in milliseconds. Those repeated power transients may accelerate degradation in conventional lead-acid and lithium iron phosphate (LFP) backup batteries.

It has been revealed that proper Voltage claims its software-defined voltage control as part of its bOS regulates output across the full state of charge, allowing the sodium-ion cabinet to drop into existing UPS architectures without inverter redesigns. It can also adapt to 800 V racks, as the industry scales towards that voltage level.

No independent performance data or pricing has been disclosed.

“Performance is what drives the best models, and the battery behind them must be resilient and adaptive across every one of those demands,” noted Charlie Welch, CEO of Proper Voltage. Unigrid CEO Darren Tan said the NCO chemistry is built for high-rate pulse power and thermal stability under heavy cycling.

The launch adds to a growing push by sodium-ion developers into AI infrastructure, where fire safety and high-rate discharge may matter more than energy density.

Earlier this year, Energy Vault locked in 1.5 GWh of Peak Energy’s sodium-ion systems for its AI data center portfolio.

And, less happily, ESS Tech introduced a modular sodium-ion platform for the same market in July, before it went out of business in November.

Industry observers note that the hill to climb towards supplying hyperscalers is steep. Nvidia’s BESS qualification program only Tesla, LG, and Hitachi, underscoing how hard supply deals are for tier-one data center contracts.
