#557. In Peacock's 'Dig,' Amy Poehler Plays an Archaeologist Who Discovers an Extraordinary Statue in Greece. What Do Real Experts Think of the TV Series?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2218 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

In Peacock's 'Dig,' Amy Poehler Plays an Archaeologist Who Discovers an Extraordinary Statue in Greece. What Do Real Experts Think of the TV Series?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With their beloved NBC workplace comedy, “Parks and Recreation,” actor Amy Poehler and series co-creator Michael Schur did the impossible.
  • It has been revealed that in the new Peacock series “Dig,” Poehler plays Elise, the long-serving second in command of a university-sponsored excavation, who is eager for her boss, Neville (Hugh Laurie), to retire.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Dig” is based on Kate Myers’ 2023 novel, Excavations, which Poehler brought to Schur for potential adaptation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With their beloved NBC workplace comedy, “Parks and Recreation,” actor Amy Poehler and series co-creator Michael Schur did the impossible. They turned the thankless work of civil servants in the fictional small town of Pawnee, Indiana, into an endearing laugh riot. Now, the pair want to do the same for a workplace that couldn’t be farther from Middle America: an archaeological dig site in Greece.

It has been revealed that in the new Peacock series “Dig,” Poehler plays Elise, the long-serving second in command of a university-sponsored excavation, who is eager for her boss, Neville (Hugh Laurie), to retire. After Elise and three of her female colleagues uncover a generation-defining artifact, they unexpectedly find themselves embroiled in an international conspiracy.

Recent findings suggest that “Dig” is based on Kate Myers’ 2023 novel, Excavations, which Poehler brought to Schur for potential adaptation. The writer jumped at the chance to explore his fascination with the ancient world and the people charged with rescuing it from obscurity.

Schur had previously brushed up on his Greek knowledge while filming the final episode of his NBC philosophical comedy, “The Good Place.” Shooting scenes in the Athenian Agora, he was struck by how much ancient history coexists alongside the present-day city.

“You walk around Athens and you just turn to your left, and there are some still-extant columns from a structure that was built in the fourth century B.C.,” he says. “It’s incredible.”.

It has been revealed that while working on “Dig,” Schur realized that the field of archaeology is similar, in a way, to the work performed in municipal buildings in small towns around the world. It’s essential and often underappreciated.

Sources indicate that “This slightly arcane discipline that not that many people go into, that isn’t very glamorous and doesn’t make people famous and rich, it’s such a vital thing,” he notes. “It’s such a humanist thing. It’s people trying really hard to help us understand who we are and how we got here and where we came from. That work is so noble to me that I just thought it would make for a good TV show.”.

Here’s what you need to know to differentiate between fact and fiction ahead of the series’ arrival on Peacock on November 23.

In a recent development, when Joseph Rife, a classicist and social historian at Vanderbilt University, was hired as the historical consultant on “Dig,” he stuck to what he knew: overseeing university-sanctioned digs in Greece. “I love working with undergraduates in the field, teaching them about the importance of the past firsthand, giving them that unique, immersive experience of living overseas and doing advanced research,” he claims. “This show is both a story about how we deal with the past and how we find ourselves. It was for me, at least, because I’ve worked in Greece since 1990, when I was an undergraduate.”.

Industry observers note that multiple generations of archaeologists are represented in “Dig.” But the story starts with a upcoming batch of undergraduates arriving for a summer program at the fictional Simantikos dig site, which is home to the ruins of a coastal village dated to the 12th century B.C.E. “I talked to the producers about the flow of a work site, and what roles students play, because some people are pushing wheelbarrows, while others are working with sieves to look for artifacts in the dirt, and others are actually digging,” Rife says.

As Elise explains to the upcoming arrivals in the first episode of “Dig,” archaeology is hard work.

“Undergraduates are always your labor on an excavation,” says Maria Liston, an emeritus skeletal biologist and archaeologist at the University of Waterloo in Canada. “You’ll have some Greek workmen, too, who are dealing with more skilled and potentially more dangerous tasks. But the nitty-gritty labor is undergraduates, and good excavations work hard to teach them and help them get better.”.

Need to know: The inspiration behind Excavations.

In a recent development, when Liston watched the trailer for the series, she was impressed by the showrunners’ realistic representation of excavation trenches and the conditions faced by archaeologists. (Liston wasn’t involved in the creation of “Dig,” but she has participated in excavations in Greece since 1987.).

“The shade canopies and the equipment in the background” caught Liston’s eye, she recalls. “Every generation claims the current diggers have it much cushier than we did. But it’s true. We never got shade. Now that is standard. Those built shelters are because insurance companies and university lawyers don’t like it when you have people dropping from heat exhaustion.”.

It has been revealed that liston also took note of the stray dogs that frequent the Simantikos site in “Dig.” “Do not feed the dogs—ever,” Elise says in the show’s trailer. In real life, Americans rarely listen to such warnings. “Athens has lots of stray dogs, and they all get named, and they do get fed,” Liston says.

It has been revealed that although “Dig” keeps the exact location of the Simantikos dig site vague, Rife claims that there was no confusion behind the scenes. “It’s in southern Greece, the Peloponnese, which is a region where we have some of the oldest and richest Greek sanctuaries,” he explains.

In a recent development, what audiences see on screen, however, isn’t exactly authentic to the region: “It’s way too green,” Liston notes. “There is way more rainfall where this is being filmed than in southern Greece.” (The bulk of the show was filmed in California, with some exteriors recorded on location in southern Italy and Athens.) She adds: “It’s very dry there, very arid—not desert exactly, but rain is something that only falls in the winter and fall. The shots of those excavation trenches, the soil and all the trees” are more characteristic of northern Greece.

Sources indicate that within the “Dig” universe, the Simantikos excavation is clearly a permanent endeavor. But an American dig site can’t just pop up on a whim anywhere in Greece, which restricts foreign countries to three independent dig sites at a time, plus three in collaboration with local archaeologists.

“For the most part, you get a permit to excavate for three years,” Liston says. “In theory, it’s renewable for two more years, but then you go to the back of the queue. Each foreign school can also be granted three survey permits, so that means you’re out walking the ground, picking up stuff on the surface, but you’re not digging.”.

Recent findings suggest that permanent dig sites are far rarer. Prominent examples include the French School at Athens’ work in Delphi, the German excavations at Olympia, and the American digs at ancient Corinth and the Athenian Agora. Corinth claims one of the United States’ three permits. But the country’s enduring presence at the ancient gathering place in Athens stems from a separate process.

In a recent development, greek legislators granted the U.S. permission to excavate the agora in 1929—a permanent greenlight made possible, in part, by the significant financial contributions of John D. Rockefeller Jr., the American philanthropist. The agora is still an active excavation site today, operating under the auspices of the American School of Classical Studies at Athens. “Everyone else gets angry at the Americans because we technically have four excavation permits,” Liston says.

Recent findings suggest that in the premiere episode of “Dig,” Elise cautions her latest group of undergraduate students that they will likely spend their summer sifting through dirt, only to find “old Nazi stuff and boring pottery” shards. This assessment rings partly true, according to Liston. She notes that artifacts dating to Nazi Germany’s occupation of Greece are rare today, mostly because metal detectors have made it easier for civilians to scavenge the upper layers of dirt. But pottery fragments are the most common finds by weight and volume.

In a recent development, many depictions of archaeology in popular culture, including the Indiana Jones franchise and the movie The Mummy, suggest that excavations unearth groundbreaking artifacts every day. That simply isn’t the case. “Most people would go through their entire careers without ever finding even a piece of a statue,” Liston says. “A piece of a clay figurine is about as good as it gets most of the time.”.

Industry observers note that in Excavations, Elise and her team are decidedly luckier: They find a trophy referencing Hera, the Greek goddess of marriage, women, family and childbirth, which seemingly confirms their suspicion that Simantikos once hosted an all-female athletic competition that predated the ancient Olympic Games. The TV adaptation of Myers’ novel goes even bigger, with Elise revisiting a previous dig site to find an enormous, fully intact statue of Hera.

It has been revealed that “It’s a cult statue, or what we often refer to as a colossal statue,” notes Rife, who researched writings and lettering of the time to create an inscription on the base of the figure. “It is a larger-than-life-size rendering of the goddess. It would have been a visual, physical focus for people who came to worship and offer sacrifices to the goddess but also a kind of metaphor or a symbol of the divine presence herself.”.

The choice of Hera is certainly no coincidence. Her presence in the book and the Peacock series is a notable metaphor for the female friendships that anchor the story: In “Dig,” Poehler’s Elise works closely with Clare (Antonia Thomas), the head preservationist at the dig site’s lab; Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan), a flighty former student who returns to Simantikos after a five-year absence; and Patty (Fina Strazza), a Midwestern farm girl and Neville’s newest undergraduate assistant.

In a recent development, the quartet’s find is understandably extraordinary in the series, and it sets off a chain of events that brings both hilarity and high-stakes danger. For real-life archaeologists, however, “it is extremely rare to find intact statues, in part because the early Christians made sure they didn’t stay intact,” Liston notes. “At the very least, they broke off their heads, but they also tended to turn them into lime plasters. You break it up into chunks, you burn the marble and you make plaster out of it.”.

It has been revealed that in a twist straight out of fiction, archaeologists at Corinth recently discovered two oversize, Roman-era marble statues of Asklepios, the Greek god of healing, and Hygieia, the Greek goddess of health. The exceptionally well-preserved figures “would have symbolized the restorative powers of bathing and cleanliness,” excavation leader Christopher Pfaff writes in a newsletter.

Industry observers note that while “Dig” is first and foremost a comedy about the act of excavation, the show also wades into the question of what happens after an artifact is found. In Greece, dig sites are meticulously monitored and cataloged each day in accordance with permits granted by the Ministry of Culture, meaning it would be difficult for Elise and her colleagues to sneak away and make a landmark discovery, as they do in the series.

Recent findings suggest that “There is a representative of the Greek Archaeological Service on site at all times, who has to talk to all of the trench supervisors every single day,” Liston states. “They are taking notes and reporting to the ephor, the regional supervisor, on a daily or weekly basis.”.

Moreover, if a discovery of great magnitude isn’t reported immediately, it can result in dire consequences for the person who concealed it. “If you hide a find, you would likely be arrested, or at best deported and never let back in the country and never [allowed to] work in Greek archaeology again,” Liston indicates.

Beyond those stakes, archaeologists have to consider the threat posed by looters and black-market antiquities dealers. “If you find something like that statue [of Hera] and you can’t get it out of the ground that night, you have to keep people at the site to watch it,” Liston says. “Normally, the ephor may demand that there be a police presence there. But at the very least, you’ve got to have people there because it will [otherwise] get stolen.”.

Rife states that one of the reasons he wanted to be involved in the series is to shed light on the challenges faced by archaeologists. “Dig” getting its hands dirty (metaphorically speaking) means more eyes on these scholars’ diligent work.

Recent findings suggest that “This is a small field, the study of ancient Greece,” he indicates. “It’s a field of humanistic study, and in the world today, it is as important as ever to study the past, to learn from it and to preserve this cultural heritage. As a professor who sits in Middle Tennessee and teaches students in a classroom, I am absolutely thrilled to see this brought to life in a popular medium, because it can only help people learn more about the importance of the past and the work.”.

  • China has started operating a 195 km hydrogen pipeline connecting Darhan Muminggan United Banner with Baotou, Inner Mongolia, reported Xinhua News Agency.
  • ACME Group has reached a final investment decision (FID) on a $3.6 billion green ammonia project in Odisha, India, with an annual production capacity of 760,000 tons.
  • Recent findings suggest that researchers in Chile have found that green hydrogen produced from curtailed solar electricity could achieve a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) as low as $5.58/kg, compared with $7.27/kg for the most competitive wind projects.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has started operating a 195 km hydrogen pipeline connecting Darhan Muminggan United Banner with Baotou, Inner Mongolia, reported Xinhua News Agency. The pipeline has an approved annual transport capacity of 100,000 tons of hydrogen, potentially increasing to 240,000 tons. Developed by Inner Mongolia Huadian Huameng Pipeline, the infrastructure will connect renewable hydrogen production facilities in northern Baotou with industrial consumers in the south. Pipeline transport could reduce hydrogen delivery costs from about CNY 13 ($1.83)/kg by tube trailer to approximately CNY 3/kg, according to Xinhua. China has been expanding its hydrogen transport infrastructure to connect renewable energy resources with industrial demand.

ACME Group has reached a final investment decision (FID) on a $3.6 billion green ammonia project in Odisha, India, with an annual production capacity of 760,000 tons. The facility, scheduled for commissioning in 2029, will feature a 2,200-ton-per-day ammonia production loop designed by Thyssenkrupp Uhde. It will use renewable electricity to produce hydrogen through electrolysis for green ammonia production, targeting customers in India, Japan and Europe. Brookfield has committed up to $600 million to support ACME’s green molecules platform. The project is expected to avoid more than 1.5 million tons of greenhouse gas emissions annually. ACME has also secured green ammonia supply contracts in India and is developing green methanol projects.

Recent findings suggest that researchers in Chile have found that green hydrogen produced from curtailed solar electricity could achieve a levelized cost of hydrogen (LCOH) as low as $5.58/kg, compared with $7.27/kg for the most competitive wind projects. The study, “Green hydrogen from curtailment: Real data analysis,” assessed operational data from 56 solar plants and 44 wind farms with a combined capacity of 10.4 GW between July 2023 and June 2024. Curtailment occurred in about 25% of recorded hourly intervals, predominantly at low power levels. Using a techno-economic model based on proton exchange membrane (PEM) electrolyzers, the researchers identified optimal electrolyzer capacities of 5% to 13% of the renewable plants’ net effective power across the 10 best-performing projects, all located in northern Chile. The projects achieved LCOH values of $5.58/kg to $6.97/kg, with electrolyzer capacity factors of 25% to 30%. Deviations of up to 50% from optimal electrolyzer sizing increased hydrogen production costs by no more than 3.8%. The study, to be published in Energy Reports, found that curtailed renewable electricity could support competitive hydrogen production, although storage, compression and transport costs remain additional considerations. Chile has experienced significant renewable energy curtailment, particularly at solar plants in the north of the country.

Industry observers note that qair has inaugurated its Hyd’Occ renewable hydrogen production facility in Occitanie, France. The 20 MW plant is supported by a regional network of hydrogen refueling stations forming part of the European H2 Corridor. Qair opened its first hydrogen refueling stations in Béziers and Narbonne in spring 2026. A second development phase will double the plant’s installed capacity to 40 MW, increasing annual hydrogen production capacity to 5,400 tons. Total investment amounts to €130 million.

According to recent reports, plug Power has launched GenEco Scale, an integrated electrolyzer plant offering for utility-scale hydrogen production. Arcadia eFuels has selected the system for a 280 MW hydrogen facility at its Project ARC development in Texas. Plug Power remarked it has completed the project’s technical evaluation and front-end engineering design (FEED) study. Once operational, the facility is expected to support production of approximately 23.2 million gallons of electro-sustainable aviation fuel (e-SAF) annually. Plug Power previously signed a 280 MW electrolyzer supply agreement with Arcadia eFuels for a separate project in Denmark.

Protium has completed due diligence for two green hydrogen projects under the UK government’s second Hydrogen Allocation Round (HAR2). The South Tees Net Zero project in northern England and the South Wales Net Zero project have both advanced to the Invitation to Offer stage. The 70 MW South Tees facility is designed to produce up to 11,000 tons of green hydrogen annually, equivalent to about 433 GWh, for industrial consumers in Teesside. The projects will now progress toward Low Carbon Hydrogen Agreements, which provide revenue support to reduce investment risks. Protium is also developing other UK hydrogen projects, including a 15 MW electrolyzer project that secured support under the first Hydrogen Allocation Round.

#552. Early Americans spent over 10 hours making a single pumpkin pie

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1296 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Early Americans spent over 10 hours making a single pumpkin pie

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1296 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table.
  • It seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert.
  • Industry observers note that for generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s the late 1700s, and a pumpkin sits on a colonial kitchen table. The flesh has been cooked until soft. But the hard part is still ahead. To turn the pumpkin into pie, the cook must mash it, scrape it, and force it through a sieve, separating smooth pulp from stubborn strings and fibers. There is no can of pumpkin puree. No food processor. Just the pumpkin, rudimentary kitchen tools, and a lot of elbow grease. The work could take hours, all for an eight-person dessert. An 1876 Latest England cookbook, for example, instructed cooks to simmer pumpkin for six to eight hours, stirring frequently, before rubbing it through a colander.

It seems like an absurd amount of work for dessert. Pumpkin flesh doesn’t naturally break down into a silky puree. Cooking softens its tissues, but turning the squash into smooth filling requires additional mechanical work.

Industry observers note that for generations, cooks solved the problem with heat and muscle. Eventually, factories took over the work of cooking and processing pumpkins into puree. But the solution didn’t stop there. Growers also turned to pumpkin varieties with naturally smoother, less fibrous flesh, making the job easier before the squash even reached the factory.

Pumpkin was an crucial food in North America long before Thanksgiving became a national holiday. Indigenous peoples cultivated and prepared the squash in many forms, and European colonists adopted pumpkins as a plentiful crop. Colonists adapted their own pie-making traditions to the abundant squash, incorporating pumpkin into sweet and savory pies. By the 17th century, recipes for pumpkin-filled pies were appearing in English cookbooks.

In 1796, the first known American cookbook, Amelia Simmons’s American Cookery, included a recipe for “Pompkin Pudding” made with cooked pumpkin, milk, eggs, and spices. Before the pumpkin could be combined with the other ingredients, the recipe called for it to be strained, separating fine pulp from tougher material.

Thanksgiving didn’t take shape as a national tradition until the mid-19th century. Pumpkins were harvested in the fall and could be stored through the colder months, making them a natural ingredient for a holiday associated with the autumn harvest.

The story of the Pilgrims sitting down with Native Americans for the first Thanksgiving has some truth to it, too. In 1621, English colonists and members of the Wampanoag people did gather for a three-day harvest celebration. But the friendly, feel-good version passed down in schoolbooks leaves out a much more complicated history of colonialism and conflict.

It wasn’t until over two centuries later that Sarah Josepha Hale, a prominent magazine editor, campaigned for decades for a national holiday, and, in 1863, President Abraham Lincoln proclaimed a national “day of Thanksgiving.” She believed a shared day of gratitude, centered on family and community, could help unite a country increasingly divided by political conflict.

Hale also helped popularize the foods associated with the holiday, promoting a traditional Upcoming England Thanksgiving menu through her magazine. Pumpkin pie was already a regional favorite, but as Thanksgiving spread nationally after the Civil War, the dessert became part of the broader American tradition.

In a recent development, pumpkin pie became increasingly associated with the holiday meal during this era, drawing on its roots in New England’s seasonal cooking traditions. Preparing it remained labor-intensive, and results varied.

Industrial food processing offered a solution to the labor-intensive process of making pumpkin pie. Factories could cook and mechanically break down pumpkin in large quantities, producing puree without requiring every household to repeat the tedious process. Canning transformed pumpkin from a seasonal ingredient demanding considerable preparation into a convenient product that could be stored and used when needed.

John Coupland, Ph.D., professor of food science at Penn State, describes the work involved in preparing pumpkin by hand as “astonishing.” Industrial processing made pie filling far more convenient, eliminating the need to cook, mash, and strain a pumpkin from scratch.

It also gave bakers a reliable starting point, helping make pumpkin pie more consistent and cementing its place at the Thanksgiving table.

Recent findings suggest that making pumpkin puree is more complicated than simply cooking the flesh until soft. Pumpkin cells are surrounded by walls containing materials such as cellulose, hemicellulose, and pectin. Cooking softens the tissue, while mechanical processing breaks it into smaller particles. Together, these processes help determine the puree’s texture and moisture.

Sources indicate that the goal is a smooth puree that is neither watery nor full of tough fibers. The pumpkin variety matters, as do the heating conditions and mechanical methods used to break down its flesh.

Industry observers note that modern food processing allows manufacturers to control these variables on a large scale, producing batches with similar textures and moisture levels. That predictability is especially valuable in pumpkin pie, where the filling’s consistency helps determine the finished dessert.

But the food industry found another way to improve the process: start with a pumpkin better suited to the job.

That is where Libby’s, one of the country’s largest canned-pumpkin producers, and the Dickinson pumpkin enter the story.

Industry observers note that according to Libby’s, farmer Elijah Dickinson brought special Dickinson pumpkin seeds from Kentucky to Illinois in 1835. The variety became closely associated with commercial pumpkin processing, and Libby, McNeill & Libby acquired Dickinson & Co. in 1929, strengthening the company’s connection to the crop.

Dickinson pumpkins look different from the bright orange pumpkins sold for carving (often called field pumpkins). Their tan skin matters less to processors than the dense flesh beneath it. Relatively high in solids and sugars, Dickinson pumpkins are particularly well-suited to puree.

Industry observers note that many carving pumpkins, by contrast, have stringier flesh that makes them harder to process into a smooth puree. Coupland explains that they are not ideally suited to commercial food production because their fibers can be difficult to break down.

In a recent development, coupland describes Dickinson puree as having a “smooth, even texture,” adding that it means you won’t be “picking fibers out of your teeth.” Rather than trying to eliminate the stringiness of a carving pumpkin, processors can start with a variety whose natural characteristics make the job easier. The raw material itself becomes part of the technology.

Libby’s helped bring this approach into American kitchens through its canned-pumpkin business, pairing a suitable variety with industrial processing to deliver consistent puree to home bakers.

Industry observers note that interestingly, Dickinson pumpkins belong to Cucurbita moschata, a species that includes several varieties of winter squash. Many familiar carving pumpkins belong to Cucurbita pepo. Botanically, the distinction between pumpkin and squash is largely a matter of common usage rather than a strict scientific boundary. The FDA permits certain sweet, golden-fleshed squashes to be labeled as pumpkin in canned products, reflecting the longstanding overlap in how the terms are used in the food trade.

For pumpkin pie, what matters most is the flesh inside: how it tastes, how it breaks down, and how consistently it performs. Today’s Thanksgiving cooks no longer needs to work themselves to the bone because the food industry has learned to do the work first.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The findings, described in two latest papers published in the journal Nature, are based on recent analyses of H.
  • Sources indicate that scientists think H.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, homo erectus was thought to have disappeared from mainland Asia roughly 400,000 years ago. But newly discovered fossils suggest that the species survived there for much longer, possibly living in southern China as recently as 184,000 years ago. The fossils also show for the first time that H. erectus was capable of living in a tropical rainforest environment.

The findings, described in two latest papers published in the journal Nature, are based on recent analyses of H. erectus teeth. One paper finds that H. erectus persisted on mainland Asia for up to 216,000 years longer than previously thought, while the other indicates that the species was even more ecologically flexible than scientists assumed.

Sources indicate that scientists think H. erectus arose in Africa about 1.89 million years ago. It’s believed to be the first hominin species to have spread beyond the continent, with populations reaching what is now Georgia, on the border between Europe and Asia, by about 1.8 million years ago. The species continued spreading east into what is now China, eventually reaching the Indonesian island of Java.

Eugène Dubois, a Dutch anatomist and geologist, made the first discovery of an H. erectus fossil, in the early 1890s. He unearthed a skullcap and femur belonging to the so-called Java Man on the eponymous island.

Industry observers note that H. erectus had a more modern, humanlike body than earlier hominins, with long legs and short arms suited to walking and running over long distances. The species made increasingly sophisticated stone tools, probably used fire, and hunted and butchered significant game.

Scientists were excavating two limestone caves, located about nine miles apart in China’s Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, when they stumbled upon nine hominin teeth. They used computed tomography (CT) scanning and physical examinations to investigate the teeth, ultimately determining that eight belonged to H. erectus. The identity of the ninth tooth, however, remains unknown.

Researchers also recovered ancient protein from five of the teeth, including the mystery tooth. In the four H. erectus teeth, they found a version of a protein called ameloblastin that had only previously been seen in older Asian H. erectus fossils.

Recent findings suggest that the mystery tooth also contained ameloblastin, however, it didn’t match any known hominin. For now, that tooth remains unidentified, but Frido Welker, a molecular anthropologist at the University of Copenhagen who co-authored one of the studies, tells Scientific American’s Jacek Krywko that he thinks Denisovans, hominins who lived across Asia from roughly 400,000 to about 30,000 years ago, “would be the first option to consider.” He suspects the two species overlapped in what is now southern China, but cautioned that scientists will need to conduct additional research to definitively identify the tooth.

In a recent development, the researchers used numerous methods to date the H. erectus teeth, deducing that they’re likely between 324,000 and 184,000 years old. At that time, the region seems to have been a tropical rainforest—a upcoming and surprising ecosystem for H. erectus.

“Rainforests were thought to be a frontier that only modern humans could survive and cross,” Ben Marwick, an archaeologist at the University of Washington who was not involved with the newly introduced research, tells National Geographic’s Christina Larson. “But now it seems this idea of Homo sapiens exceptionalism may not be the true story.”.

Additional analyses of the teeth revealed that these H. erectus individuals traveled long distances, possibly coming to southern China from as far away as what is now northern Vietnam, some 155 miles away. Making that kind of journey would have required “a sophisticated understanding of the surrounding terrain, including regional landscape features and river networks that change with the seasons,” Ben Utting, an archaeologist at the University of Connecticut who was not involved with the new studies, tells CNN’s Katie Hunt.

In a recent development, together, the findings add to the growing picture of the species’ behavioral and ecological flexibility, Karen Baab, a paleoanthropologist at Midwestern University who was not involved with the new work, tells New Scientist’s Michael Marshall. “They seemed quite adaptable and flexible in general, because of the incredible range of niches they were occupying,” she adds.

Recent findings suggest that that flexibility probably helped H. erectus persist for roughly 1.8 to 1.9 million years—six times longer than modern humans—making it the longest-surviving known species in the Homo genus.

However, scientists still don’t know why the species went extinct between 108,000 to 117,000 years ago. The leading theory is that H. erectus couldn’t adapt when rainforests started encroaching on their final home, the island of Java.

Industry observers note that but the new findings turn that narrative “on its head,” Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University and the lead author of one of the studies, tells Reuters’ Will Dunham. “This ⁠opens up a new chapter on our understanding of H. erectus.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in some ways, Leila Wilson’s idyllic relationship with the American elm is a familiar story. “We had a significant elm on the hill of our driveway that we put a tire swing on when I was a kid,” says the U.S. Forest Service research ecologist, recalling her childhood home outside of Upcoming Haven, which is known as Elm City. Countless grandparents have a similar story to tell. What’s unique about Wilson’s recollection is the timing. Her childhood memories date back to the 1980s, and by then millions of American elms were gone—already felled by a fungus.

Wilson’s father, a forester, understood the significance of the family tree, which still stands. When she was in high school, he told her about the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s elm program in central Ohio, where researchers still fight Dutch elm disease—the office where she now works.

In a recent development, this summer, Wilson and her team, armed with vials of the fungus, laid the groundwork for significant breakthroughs by killing healthy elms. If the science holds—and with a little luck—researchers could identify more than two dozen genetically diverse American elms in the next few years to help restore forests. The USDA has been working toward this goal since it began screening elms for disease resistance around 1937; a genetically diverse population could better withstand Dutch elm disease and other future threats. Most homeowners don’t realize disease-resistant elms are already available, but this research could give the USDA its widest selection yet for restoring forests. Some of the trees may eventually reach nurseries for homeowners to plant.

It has been revealed that from the mid-1800s into the early 1900s, Americans planted millions of elms along streets and throughout public spaces, in part because the trees tolerated a wide range of conditions, including poor soil, compaction and urban pollution. “The village improvers, the first and most significant thing they do, project they undertake, is the planting of these elm trees,” noted Thomas J. Campanella, a historian of city planning and the urban built environment at Cornell University, during an October 2022 appearance on the podcast “This Old Tree.”.

Industry observers note that unlike oak or maple, elms have interlocking grain that makes their wood difficult to split, so loggers saw little value in them. Their appeal lay instead in their graceful, architectural form: a vase- or umbrella-shaped crown with limbs that arch up and outward. When elms grow on opposite sides of a road, their sweeping branches create the cathedral-like canopy over the street that became their hallmark. That branching is why Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux wanted rows of elms lining Central Park’s Mall.

“Other trees can do that, but to me, the elm has this movement that is really beautiful and almost like a dancer,” Wilson says.

Beginning around 1840, American elms shaded—and gave their name to—streets across the country. The USDA estimated that, at their peak, elms numbered 77 million in the urban landscape, a figure that excluded those in yards, like Wilson’s. Then by the 1950s, Dutch elm disease brought a real-life nightmare to Elm Street, killing the trees on a national scale.

Dutch elm disease likely originated in Asia and was first studied in the Netherlands in 1919. The disease probably reached the United States in 1930 through the port of New York in European elm logs destined for furniture veneer. Bark beetles and connections between neighboring trees’ roots spread the fungus, triggering blockages in an elm’s water-conducting vessels, severing the supply to the canopy. Leaves yellow, wilt and fall, and branches die back as the infection spreads, eventually killing the tree. The most common way to protect an elm is to inject it with a preventive fungicide every one to three years—not exactly a DIY task.

According to recent reports, in 1930, Curtis May, a research technician at the Ohio Agricultural Experiment Station, first identified the disease after receiving samples of trees from Ohio, collected by plant pathologist Paul Tilford in Cleveland and Cincinnati. Christine Buisman, a visiting Dutch scientist, confirmed the diagnosis.

Recent findings suggest that the disease traveled longer distances when people transported infested elm logs for firewood. Because the American elm’s native range is vast—stretching from Canada south to Texas, and from the East Coast across the Appalachian Mountains to Wyoming—the environmental loss has reached well beyond Main Street. The blight has killed more than 55 percent of the elm trees in the U.S.

According to recent reports, scientists have been trying to understand and outsmart Dutch elm disease since Franklin D. Roosevelt was in office. Those who went to school, walked their town’s main street, played in a local park or visited a government building in the 1960s may remember a big, old elm that got sick and had to be cut down—whether in one of those public spaces or in their own backyard. The research into restoring elms isn’t really about returning front yards and boulevards to prewar glory, though both places have benefited from the work.

American elm is a foundation species in river floodplain forests, stabilizing streambanks and feeding native insects, birds and small mammals. Dutch elm disease—which is still active—has left floodplains vulnerable to invasive species. “Elms tolerate these floodplains, and that’s a tough ecosystem that a lot of trees can’t tolerate,” says Benjamin Held, a researcher in the University of Minnesota’s plant pathology department who has been working to reintroduce elms. “A number of tree species grow in floodplains, but relatively few are well adapted to the periodic flooding and saturated soils that characterize that environment—elm is one of those species.”.

These large, long-lived trees helped shape the canopy, the conditions beneath it, and ecosystem processes like water use and nutrient cycling. The decline has become especially consequential in recent years, as the emerald ash borer, an invasive beetle, kills ash trees, one of the elm’s closest ecological substitutes.

This summer, scientists from the USDA and the Nature Conservancy walked through tidy rows of elms in Vermont fields. Carrying cordless drills and pipettes—essentially syringes—filled with the Dutch elm disease fungus, Wilson, fellow research ecologist Kathleen Knight, plant pathologist John Butnor, Nature Conservancy scientist Gus Goodwin and their teams went to work. The task was repetitive: bore a small hole in the trunk, squeeze in some fungus goop and move on. Researchers are testing 5,000 elms in Benson, near the Fresh York border, and 700 in Lemington, about eight miles south of Canada, deliberately infecting trees that range in age from 6 to 12 years old to identify the most disease-resistant survivors.

According to recent reports, and now comes the waiting. There is always a lot of waiting when dealing with plant pathology. The trees in these test fields took years to grow from seed. Now, Wilson and her team await the fallout. “We rate them for two years, so about summer 2028, we’ll dive into the data we collect early that summer and that’s when we make decisions,” Wilson says.

The USDA also has elm stock at two sites in Ohio, closer to Wilson’s office. Researchers infected those trees last year. “So we are already actively looking at the data, but it’s about two to two and a half years until we decide which trees will end up in seed orchards and serve as parents for progeny that can be used for reforestation,” she states.

Recent findings suggest that wilson and her colleagues at the U.S. Forest Service’s Northern Research Station are working to restore American elms across Newly introduced England. “For New England, ideally we’d have 30 [trees], which is the gold standard for tree species restoration,” Wilson indicates. With 30 or more trees, the team has enough genetic diversity to help repopulate the region. “Capturing a large amount of genetic diversity is notable to enable the population to adapt to future challenges, including changes to the Dutch elm disease fungus, and other changes, like new invasive species or changes in temperature.”.

Sources indicate that once researchers identify the ideal specimens, they will plant clones of the parent species in seed orchards in Shelburne, Vermont, and elsewhere in New England for further study. The trees will grow there for about 15 years before producing seeds to plant across the region. “It’s hard work, it’s hard science, it’s really slow, and the wins do not come easily or rapidly,” Wilson says. Nursery growers, researchers and scientists have identified about 20 disease-resistant American elms since the early 1920s. Homeowners can buy several of these Dutch elm disease-resistant cultivars, or cultivated varieties bred and selected for specific traits, though tracking them down usually requires going beyond a local garden center. These deliberately bred elms share similar growth traits and can grow two or more feet a year, reaching up to 70 feet tall and wide. Their trunks split into broad, arching branches that form a classic crown.

“Princeton” is the classic American elm: vase-shaped, with glossy green leaves. Found in a Upcoming Jersey cemetery in 1922, it was selected for its looks long before Dutch elm disease became widespread. “Jefferson,” descended from a survivor of the National Mall’s 1930s plantings, leafs out earlier and holds its foliage later than most elms. Sold as Prairie Expedition, “Lewis & Clark” thrives in the country’s coldest regions. And “St. Croix,” which the fifth-generation family-owned Bailey Nurseries introduced in 2015, traces its roots to a century-old elm in Afton, Minnesota. Beyond their similar shapes and sizes, these elms share a common origin: each cultivar is a naturally occurring genetic variation. Each tree sold under one of these names is a genetic clone of an original.

Did you know? Smithsonian Witness Elm.

Recent findings suggest that the Vermont test plots contain stock drawn from American elms that are adapted to climates across New England and have shown resistance to the fungus. “Dutch elm disease is killing the trees that are most susceptible, leaving trees that are less susceptible to breed,” Wilson indicates, adding that the progeny of those trees should have better disease resistance. Researchers produced the trees in the plots through controlled pollination, using four selections with proven Dutch elm disease resistance, including “Princeton” and “Valley Forge,” as mother trees and regional survivors as pollen donors. “That’s an advantage that science in the ’30s, ’40s and ’50s just didn’t have,” she adds.

But if scientists already have a handful of proven, Dutch elm disease-resistant cultivars, why not cross those? “We want as much of the genetic diversity that’s in the elm population to come forward with disease tolerance,” says Goodwin. “The idea of a super tree isn’t really what we’re after, because the idea is a population of trees that are adapted to our area that have higher-than-average disease tolerance.”.

Tinkering with the genetics also carries a risk of losing the very trait you’re trying to preserve. “I haven’t seen as many of the American elms be crossbred, and it could be that when you breed two together, the disease resistance falls out,” states Eric North, program manager of urban forestry at the Arbor Day Foundation.

Sources indicate that finding upcoming disease resistance from as many different cultivars as possible takes more time than breeding from a small pool of reliably resistant trees, but it also gives future plantings, both in the forest and your neighborhood, a better genetic chance at fighting Dutch elm disease. That emphasis on variety marks a shift from the old practice of lining streets with genetically similar trees. “Modern urban and community forestry is moving towards a diversified planting palette, because we don’t know what the next insect or pathogen that’s out there is going to be. So we need to hedge our bets environmentally and economically, because it’s a massive blow when you have huge percentages of your community forest dying in a very short amount of time,” says Ryan Murphy, a University of Minnesota researcher working on elms alongside Held.

It has been revealed that the USDA’s Vermont trials may be decades from restoring elms, but for Wilson, the work already brings her full circle, from that elm in Upcoming Haven that she swung from. “I think the elm is just beautiful, but the fact that it’s a workhorse and has such a large range that it can grow in almost any environment—it’s just so flexible, and for conservation, that’s a very useful tool,” she indicates.

While the aim of the work in Vermont is to restore forests and floodplains with disease-resistant elms, the benefits will eventually reach town squares and front yards.

Sources indicate that “We are interested in elms as an urban tree because of the historical legacy,” Wilson says. “I grew up right outside of ‘Elm City’…. It’s part of the city’s identity, and that resonates with me.”.

Sal Vaglica is a former editor at Serious Eats, Men’s Journal and This Old House magazine, where he first covered trees. He’s written about food, gear, gardening and travel for Saveur, The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Wired, Men’s Health and Better Homes & Gardens.

#545. Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1035 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Voyager 1 is officially one light-day away from Earth

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1035 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth.
  • William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.
  • According to recent reports, “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he says.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After traveling through space for almost 50 years, NASA’s Voyager 1 spacecraft should be one light-day away from Earth. The probe reached this record-breaking milestone at approximately 5:16:07 a.m. EST on Wednesday, November 18. Since takes about 24 hours to receive any signal from Voyager 1, NASA officially confirmed that it reached the distance on Thursday, November 19.

William Kurth, a research scientist at the University of Iowa who has worked on the Voyager mission since 1974 tells Popular Science that this mission is about more than just science.

According to recent reports, “The Voyager missions represent humanity’s curiosity and hunger to understand our species’ place in the universe,” he says. “They show that we are explorers and can work together to do wonderful things.”.

Astronomers often describe vast cosmic distances in light-years. It’s arguably the most famous unit of measurement when talking about the universe, in part because of its sheer incomprehensibility. A single particle of light travels at a speed of about 186,282 miles per second. Hypothetically speaking, if you fired a beam of light into the night sky at the outset of reading this story, it would travel around 44.7 million miles into space by the time you finished.

In a recent development, but even a unit like a light-minute isn’t particularly useful to astronomers. For them, cosmic measurements only start making sense on a scale of light-years. Voyager 1 is nowhere close to a light-year away from Earth, but a light-day (approximately 16,094,799,105 miles) is still basically impossible to envision as a distance. And since radio communications travel at nearly the speed of light, any messages to and from the spacecraft will require about 24 (Earth) hours to receive.

According to recent reports, “Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” Dave Gallagher, the director of NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, said in an emailed statement confirming the milestone. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward newly introduced frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”.

Even at one light-day from Earth, Voyager 1 isn’t done just yet. While several of its instruments are no longer functioning, it still routinely sends back invaluable information from its vantage point beyond the solar system.

Industry observers note that “Voyager 1 is telling us about our sun’s interaction with its galactic neighborhood. It has told us about the amount of galactic cosmic rays, unfiltered by the sun’s magnetic field,” says Kurth. “We are learning about the variation of plasma density in the interstellar medium just outside the heliosphere (sun’s extended atmosphere). We’re anxious to see where the direction of the magnetic field rotates from one similar to the heliospheric direction to that of the pristine interstellar medium.”.

In a recent development, “Though it might be a long shot, I hope to see Voyager 1 crossing into the predicted hot hydrogen wall,” Adam Szabo, a Project Investigator on Voyager’s Magnetometer Experiment, tells Popular Science. “The wall is composed of neutral hydrogen atoms, so it will not register easily, but it must have some magnetic and plasma wave signature.”.

Voyager 1 rolled out on September 5, 1977, heading for Jupiter and Saturn. Voyager 1 has 10 scientific instruments onboard, including two Golden Records engraved with sights, sounds, and depictions of life on Earth onboard—should the probe encounter any extraterrestrial life.

In March 1979, the Voyager 1 discovered a thin ring around Jupiter and two newly introduced Jovian moons: Thebe and Metis. When it reached Saturn in 1980, the spacecraft spotted five new moons and a new ring called the G-ring.

As part of a concept that NASA called the Grand Tour, the Voyager mission as a whole took advantage of a once-every-175-year alignment of the outer planets for a grand tour of the solar system. Its twin spacecraft Voyager 2 later explored Neptune and Uranus.

On February 17, 1998, Voyager 1 became the furthest human-made object in space, after overtaking NASA’s Pioneer 10 probe. It crossed into interstellar space in August 2012, and became the first spacecraft to cross the heliosphere. This boundary is where the influences from outside of our solar system are stronger than those from our sun.

Sources indicate that all good things must come to an end, of course. Voyager 1 is powered by three radioisotope thermoelectric generators (RTGs) fueled by decaying plutonium-23. The isotope possesses a 87.74-year half-life, so the batteries are presently operating at around two-thirds their original strength. NASA has slowly shut down onboard equipment in recent years to conserve energy, but there will come a time when there simply isn’t enough left in the RTGs for anything to operate. Barring any technical challenges, mission engineers expect to bid Voyager 1 a final farewell sometime during the 2030s.

The spacecraft may cease its work as a cosmic laboratory, but its very existence ensures it will remain a monument to humanity’s potential as it barrels forward for eons.

In a recent development, “Voyager 1 and its companion Voyager 2 have taught us time and again that nature is not as simple and predictable as we thought,” Kurth explains. “Voyager has always provided surprising differences from our best guesses as to what it will see in any newly introduced region.”.

Additionally, Szabo adds that it has an crucial lesson for anyone on Earth who has ever had a dream.

It has been revealed that “Do not be afraid to dream major. In 1977, even the Grand Tour seemed like a long shot,” he states. “We did not even conceive of making it into interstellar space. Dream big.”.

PATCH November 19 10:00 a.m. EST: An earlier version of this story said Voyager moves at 186,282 feet per second. It is 186,282 miles per second. We have updated unit of measurement and apologize for the error.

#543. Latest Update: Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (583 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Latest Update: Prickly pears can generate solar electricity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out.
  • Sources indicate that plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury.
  • According to recent reports, environmental biologists certainly did.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most plants rely on real-time photosynthesis for food, which means they aren’t generating energy unless the sun is out. Meanwhile, cacti like the prickly pear must get creative in order to survive the harsh conditions they live in. With high temperatures and little water, these plants and similar species like aloe and pineapple evolved a specialized process called crassulacean acid metabolism (CAM). The overall principles are the same, but instead of converting carbon dioxide (CO₂) and water into sugars solely during daylight, CAM allows a prickly pear to extend its photosynthesis over a full 24 hours.

Sources indicate that plants generally absorb carbon dioxide through pores in their leaves, but the prickly pear can’t afford such an evolutionary luxury. The desert heat would turn those same tiny openings into water drains. With CAM, a prickly pear only absorbs carbon dioxide at night, and subsequently turns it into malic acid. Photosynthesis later breaks down the acid—but only on the side of the plant directly exposed to sunlight. The shady side retains its malic acid, creating a pH concentration gradient. Interestingly, this pH imbalance is also one of the underlying principles for generating electricity…see where this is going?

According to recent reports, environmental biologists certainly did. In a study published today in the journal Plants, People, Planet, a team at the University of California, Santa Cruz, (UC Santa Cruz) detailed a fresh, interdisciplinary system that transforms the common prickly pear into a green solar panel. Although prickly pear voltages aren’t enough to deliver a noticeable jolt, they are strong enough to power the tiny sensors often used by farmers to monitor their crops. With some additional fine-tuning, their novel methods could offer a promising, sustainable adaptation to ongoing climate concerns.

Recent findings suggest that “It was just so nice to have 10 students in a room from all across campus working together on a single project. When we’re looking at climate solutions, that’s what we need,” Charlie Chesney, a UC Santa Cruz environmental scientist and study co-author, said in a statement.

Wiring a single spiky plant doesn’t do much, but linking them together adds up. As few as eight prickly pears are enough to generate 4.5 volts of electricity—nearly three times the charge of a commercial AA battery. That’s more than enough to power the common, low-energy sensors used to assess plants.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti [for] monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” explained UC Santa Cruz ecologist and study co-author Michael Loik.

He offered one such scenario, where wired prickly pears function as organic “sentinels” that monitor field conditions and relay the information back to a farmer’s office.

“This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue,” he added.

Industry observers note that the idea isn’t limited to the prickly pear, either. Any plant that uses CAM—aloe, pineapple, agave—could benefit from a similar battery upgrade. The team even assessed how the cacti performed under a standard desert challenge like drought. Even after 15 months without water, sample prickly pears weren’t simply surviving—they were still photosynthesizing. In some cases, the resultant voltages were higher than watered control plants.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is—it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” added Chesney.

  • “Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In bear life, as in human life, sometimes you just have to take a leap of faith. A brown bear (Ursus arctos) cub hanging around Anan Creek in Tongass National Forest in southeastern Alaska learned that this summer. Its mom, Gemini, was crossing the creek, and one cub jumped right in. But this cub? Not so sure. It stood waiting at the water’s edge, before jumping in.

For this forceful leap into the water, the park rangers have awarded Gemini’s little cub with the 2026 Yeet of Faith Award. For those keeping score at home, Gemini won this year’s helicopter mom award.

“Cubs learn at their own pace, and thanks to amazing recreation sites like Anan, we get to witness their tiny triumphs up close,” the rangers write.

Tongass National Forest’s rangers are awarding the Anan Bear Awards to the 39 bears spotted at the Anan Wildlife Observatory in Alaska over the summer.

Tongass is the largest national forest in the United States, and covers most of Southeast Alaska, including the state’s capital city of Juneau. The area includes Mendenhall Glacier (a popular destination for Alaskan cruises), numerous hiking trails, eagles soaring above, and plenty of bears on the hunt for food. One of the hotspots for wildlife is Anan Creek, home to one of the largest runs of pink salmon in Southeast Alaska. As such, the creek is a very popular dinner spot among black and brown bears.

In a recent development, according to Friends of Anan, 39 bears are known to feast on the salmon at Anan Creek. The population includes 31 black bears (Ursus americanus) and eight brown bears like Gemini and her cubs. Similar to their chubby counterparts farther to the north in Katmai National Park, the bears return each summer to gorge on salmon ahead of the long winter, and teach their cubs how to fish in order to survive. And also like the fat bears of Katmai, every bear around Anan Creek has their own habits and quirks.

According to recent reports, the U.S. Forest Service tracks and documents every bear spotted at Anan, while explore.org’s cameras broadcast live streams of their behaviors.

7 million pages of military records from the War of 1812 are finally online

  • It has been revealed that while archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the latest documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, after 16 years of painstaking work, the National Archives and its collaborators have finally completed digitizing over 180,000 pension applications submitted to the United States government following the War of 1812. The project is more than just preservation for preservation’s sake. The over 7.2 million pages contain long-forgotten and missing details about 19th century Americans, their families, and their everyday lives.

It has been revealed that while archivists previously digitized a similar collection related to the American Revolutionary War, the latest documents will help fill in knowledge gaps between early 19th century military events and the 1850 federal census. Patricia Oxley, president of the Federation of Genealogical Societies (FGS), explained the project was also incredibly time-sensitive.

“In the specific case of the War of 1812 pension records, there is an added priority due to their frail state where not acting may mean sacrificing these for future generations,” Oxley remarked in a recent announcement.

Industry observers note that the somewhat new United States of America declared war on the United Kingdom on June 18, 1812, citing objections to trade restrictions with France amid the Napoleonic Wars, as well as the Royal Navy’s impressment of American sailors. Although the conflict famously included a British attack on Washington D.C. that resulted in the burning of the White House and U.S. Capitol, little shifted geopolitically between the two nations following the ratification of the Treaty of Ghent on February 17, 1815. The U.S. tallied around 15,000 casualties, while the U.K. and Canada saw about 10,700 deaths. Another 9,000 Indigenous fighters died while enlisted between the two sides.

It has been revealed that today’s military records are meticulously documented and stored digitally, but applying for benefits such as pensions was a much more labor-intensive process during the 19th century. With the burden of proof on each applicant, veterans were required to supply lengthy accounts of their service. Each War of 1812 pension file is liable to contain not just combat information, but the names and personal details of fellow soldiers, family members, spouses, and countless other relations.

“Our users have been asking for the War of 1812 pension records for some time, and I expect this collection to be very popular based on the rich war time detail it contains,” added Brian Hansen, general manager at Fold3, Ancestry’s military records service and National Archives collaborator.

The collection also includes a full-text search feature using handwriting recognition technology. This lets consumers explore the files based on every named individual, and not simply the primary veteran applicants. The pension records are at the moment available for free on Fold3’s website, and are being added to the National Archives catalog on a rolling basis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Turn off reality TV and turn on the bald eagle cams. It’s all the drama you need.

According to recent reports, when internet-famous bald eagle Shadow seemingly welcomed a mysterious fresh female into his nest earlier this week, many fans have questioned the whereabouts of Kaydee. After the death of Shadow’s longtime partner Jackie in August, he had been spotted spending time with the 4-year-old banded female eagle named KD1 (later renamed Kaydee). It seemed like the eagles might head into mating season as a pair, but after the arrival of a new, large female, it’s unclear how the relationships will all shake out.

Sources indicate that since the appearance of the mystery female, nicknamed Significant Beautiful Visitor or BBV by some fans, Kaydee has disappeared from view of Friends of Big Bear Valley (FOBBV)’s two cameras. She was last spotted by the cameras on November 14 in the Roost Tree, according to FOBBV. Despite concerns that she may be injured or had left the area, wildlife photographers have continued to document Kaydee’s presence near Big Bear Lake as recently as November 18.

Photographer Alla Shumko shared photos of Kaydee perched near Big Bear Lake on November 18. Kaydee’s double bands are visible as she observed a scuffle between younger eagles fighting over fish.

Mating season is well underway, so viewers of FOBBV’s 24/7 livecams have been watching closely for signs that Shadow has selected a upcoming partner. Shadow has worked with both Kaydee and the new eagle on nest maintenance and shared “beaky kisses” with each female, both signs of bonding in bald eagles. Bald eagle mating involves a bit of aerial acrobatics—copulating pairs can be seen in what’s called a “cartwheel display,” in which they lock talons in mid-air while tumbling down to the ground. Male eagles do not have an external phallus, so mating occurs via a touch of cloacas. Vocalizations can typically be heard during the act, which lasts about 7 to 12 seconds, according to Raptor Resource.

As this is nature, we humans can’t predict or influence who Shadow will pick as a new partner. Or if he picks at all. All we can do is watch and wait and let nature take its course.

North Atlantic right whales named after Dolly Parton and Gonzo

💡 Key Takeaways

  • It has been revealed that “Naming right whales is a fun and creative activity for our research community, but it also allows an opportunity to connect with the whales on an individual level,” Amy Warren, an aquarium scientific program officer and name project coordinator, noted in Anderson Cabot Center’s announcement.
  • According to recent reports, the 2026 inductees also include Grand Slam (Catalog #3991) and Slide (Catalog #4991).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than 400 adult North Atlantic right whales (Eubalaena glacialis) still exist in the wild, making them one of the world’s most critically endangered species. Of those, 20 have officially received spiffy newly introduced names from conservationists at the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life. The researchers curate the annual North Atlantic Right Whale Catalog, and attach personable monikers to a select few baleen cetaceans in order to more easily monitor them. This year, it’s time to wave hello to Dodo, Volcano, and Dolly.

It has been revealed that “Naming right whales is a fun and creative activity for our research community, but it also allows an opportunity to connect with the whales on an individual level,” Amy Warren, an aquarium scientific program officer and name project coordinator, noted in Anderson Cabot Center’s announcement. “It can be hard to relate to Catalog #5299, but a whale named Nibbles is bound to be memorable.”.

According to recent reports, the 2026 inductees also include Grand Slam (Catalog #3991) and Slide (Catalog #4991). The sister whales have a mother named Fenway (Catalog #2791), who was also named in honor of the Boston Red Sox. Grand Slam earned her fresh name thanks to her three patches of raised tissue known as callosities that resemble the bases on a baseball field. Meanwhile, Slide received their name due to the curved scar on her back that recalls someone sliding through home plate. Other right whale names this year include Goose, Donegal, and even Gonzo for the beloved Muppet.

“Although the names are intended to help researchers at sea, they also give the general public a better understanding of the individual whales,” added Caroline Mowdy, a spokesperson for Whale and Dolphin Conservation (WDC).

Collaborators at the WDC also created some lighthearted, yearbook-esque biographies for each whale. For example, Dolly (Catalog #4191), whose callosity looks strikingly similar to the late, great country singer’s larger-than-life hair, apparently loves the song, “Jolene.” Then again, who doesn’t?

According to recent reports, “We see these whales and their families grow each year,” stated Mowdy. “Knowing them makes the tragedies even more tragic, but it also makes our determination to protect them even stronger.”.

On Monday, the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium announced that there are roughly 382 North Atlantic right whales, representing a 1.8 percent drop in population size from the 2024 estimate. Their primary threats remain getting tangled in fishing line and vessel strikes.

Recent findings suggest that however, even amid their struggles, the 2025–2026 right whale calving season saw the most calves born since 2009. A total of 24 calves were born, including a surprising late addition that was spotted in Canada in September.

#534. New electric comb from China regrew nearly 100% of hair (in mice)

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (795 w)
EV & Auto ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

New electric comb from China regrew nearly 100% of hair (in mice)

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (795 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that A potentially revolutionary electronic comb is generating some pretty hair-raising results.
  • Though the Detangle comb (named after the 2010 Disney film Tangled) hasn’t been tested on humans yet, the Chinese scientist behind its development notes the eye-grabbing results on our distant genetic cousins suggest it could play a role in the neverending quest to keep those luscious locks just a hair longer.
  • Created by a team led by Beihang University in Beijing, the comb initially looks like the chunky plastic kind adorning typical pharmacy aisles.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that A potentially revolutionary electronic comb is generating some pretty hair-raising results. The experimental comb has been used to successfully restore nearly all the hair in bald test subjects. But don’t chuck out that Rogaine just yet. The comb’s users were mice with shaved backs.

Though the Detangle comb (named after the 2010 Disney film Tangled) hasn’t been tested on humans yet, the Chinese scientist behind its development notes the eye-grabbing results on our distant genetic cousins suggest it could play a role in the neverending quest to keep those luscious locks just a hair longer.

Created by a team led by Beihang University in Beijing, the comb initially looks like the chunky plastic kind adorning typical pharmacy aisles. However, a closer look at its clear plastic handle reveals a green circuit board. Further down, one can see electrodes embedded in the comb’s teeth, which alternate between long and short. The team says that this height variance makes the comb’s pulsed electric field more than two and a half times stronger than it would be with evenly matched teeth.

Industry observers note that the shorter teeth also contain two experimental genetic treatments. One boosts blood vessel growth around the hair follicles. The other treatment  blocks dihydrotestosterone (DHT), a hormone known to shrink follicles. The electric field generated by the comb temporarily opens up skin so the treatments can get inside, reaching up to nine times deeper into the follicle region than a conventional cream.​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​.

According to recent reports, researchers performed a variety of tests on mice that had their backs shaved and were given testosterone to mimic pattern baldness. Over 28 days, the balding mice were treated with minoxidil or finasteride (the current standards for medical hair restoration), the comb’s electrical stimulation alone, and the comb combined with an experimental genetic treatment. Mice given finasteride regrew about 50 percent of their hair, while the ones on and minoxidil regrew 70 percent. Those numbers  honestly aren’t  too bad on their own, but the results were even better when Detangle got involved. Mice treated with the comb and both experimental treatments saw a staggering 97.85 percent hair regrowth. And all without having to book a flight to Turkey for a hair transplant.

“[T]hese results demonstrate that electrostimulation via the Detangle system promotes hair growth and follicle regeneration in a safe and effective manner,” the team wrote in their paper published earlier this month in the Nature Communications.

The potential market for a hair regrowing comb is sizable to say the least. Detangle’’s creators say androgenetic alopecia, the scientific term for pattern baldness, affects 1.5 billion people worldwide. Some studies suggest up to 80 percent of men will experience pattern baldness, with  some populations seeing symptoms before the age of 40. Somewhere between one fifth and two fifths of women may also experience pattern hair thinning. And hair isn’t just hair. Social expectations and norms around hair partly explain why hair loss can carry psychological baggage.

In a recent development, scientists and hair care providers know this, of course. Toupees, tonics, and tinctures promising to reverse nature’s balding date back thousands of years. Today, the standard medical treatment usually involves topical minoxidil (the active ingredient in Rogaine) and oral finasteride. Minoxidil generally works, but results vary widely from person to person and it requires constant, ongoing application.

Finasteride is often far more effective, with long-term studies showing it can preserve hair in most men for at least a decade, but it also carries the risk for much more intense side effects. The drug (which saw a surge in popularity thanks to online, telehealth services) has been linked to decreased libido and erectile dysfunction. Some patients have also reported anxiety, depression, and suicidal thoughts. While the side effects are uncommon, the risk presented a potentially steep trade off for a fuller head of hair.

In a recent development, those intrigued by the comb will unfortunately have to hold out quite a bit longer. The team says more research is needed before the device is tested on humans and, even then, there’s no guarantee the rodent results will translate. Testosterone-induced hair loss on a shaved mouse back is a far cry from human pattern baldness, which typically creeps in over years.

It’s also worth emphasizing that the electric comb, memorable as it is, wasn’t solely responsible for the best results. The pair of experimental genetic treatments used in the study (called SRD5A2 siRNA and VEGFA plasmids) also need to be tested in humans to ensure they are safe and don’t come with unintended side effects of their own. Wig stores, it seems, will live to see another day.

Fiona the hippo dies at age 9

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Cincinnati Zoo’s most famous resident Fiona the hippo has died at age 9.
  • Recent findings suggest that “We are in shock at the moment,” Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement.
  • It has been revealed that last week, a child’s knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Cincinnati Zoo’s most famous resident Fiona the hippo has died at age 9.

Recent findings suggest that “We are in shock at the moment,” Cincinnati Zoo director Dave Jenike said in a statement. “We did not expect this outcome. She fought until she couldn’t anymore. Our animal care team was heroic in their efforts to save her. They did everything possible, but her body couldn’t fight anymore. She was dearly loved by her Zoo family and countless others around the world. Her loss will be felt deeply by so many.”.

It has been revealed that last week, a child’s knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remained stuck in her digestive track. She had undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that highlighted intestinal bunching, indicating her body was trying and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests. Just yesterday, on November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers.

It has been revealed that “Fiona was such a gift,” stated Cincinnati Zoo Executive Chair of the Board Thane Maynard. “I have never known an animal so beloved in all my life. From the day she was born, she was like lightning in a bottle. And, she will be remembered and beloved many years from now.”.

It has been revealed that fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”.
