#526. The North Atlantic Right Whale Population Has Shrunk, Raising Concerns About the Future of the Critically Endangered Species

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (765 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

The North Atlantic Right Whale Population Has Shrunk, Raising Concerns About the Future of the Critically Endangered Species

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (765 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The North Atlantic right whale population shrank slightly in 2025, raising concerns about the future of the critically endangered species.
  • Scientists counted 382 individuals last year, according to new numbers released this week by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium.
  • Meanwhile, the number of reproductive females held steady at 73, according to the consortium, which is made up of scientists from the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The North Atlantic right whale population shrank slightly in 2025, raising concerns about the future of the critically endangered species.

Scientists counted 382 individuals last year, according to new numbers released this week by the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium. That’s a 1.8 percent decrease from the 2024 estimate of 389 whales.

Meanwhile, the number of reproductive females held steady at 73, according to the consortium, which is made up of scientists from the New England Aquarium’s Anderson Cabot Center for Ocean Life and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

In a recent development, north Atlantic right whales are massive marine mammals that can weigh as much as 140,000 pounds. They spend their winters in the shallow waters off North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia and Florida, where they give birth and raise their calves. Then, they swim more than 1,000 miles north to spend the spring, summer and fall feeding in the food-rich waters off New England and Canada.

Sources indicate that they’re one of three species of right whales, along with the North Pacific right whale and the Southern right whale. All three species are what’s known as filter feeders, meaning they use their baleen—flexible, comb-like plates that hang from their upper jaws—to tiny creatures called copepods from the water.

Commercial whalers hunted right whales to the brink of extinction by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, dubbing them the “right” whales to go after because they were relatively easy to kill and retrieve.

In a recent development, all three species have been protected under the U.S. Endangered Species Act since 1970. Still, the colossal creatures have been slow to recover—and their populations remain small today. Right whales can die or suffer life-threatening injuries after being struck by boats or becoming tangled in fishing gear.

“Imagine if you were wrapped in rope that moved as you moved … literally sawing into your body,” Philip Hamilton, a biologist with the New England Aquarium, tells CBC News’ Leila Beaudoin. “It is really painful. They don’t have arms. The pain is … kind of unimaginable.”.

Climate change, noise pollution and oil and gas development also threaten the whales. Rising ocean temperatures are particularly dangerous for the massive animals. As the North Atlantic heats up, copepods are moving toward cooler waters, prompting the whales to follow them into areas where they’re not protected from ship strikes and entanglements.

“We know that this population can and will move around to find food, and if we aren’t protecting them throughout their range, we may see another situation where we have this tremendous decline again,” Heather Pettis, chair of the North Atlantic Right Whale Consortium and a biologist at the Latest England Aquarium, tells Patrick Whittle of the Associated Press.

Over the past decade, North Atlantic right whales have been experiencing high rates of deaths and serious injuries, a period NOAA has dubbed an “unusual mortality event.” The primary causes have been vessel strikes and entanglements, with 177 total individuals getting killed or injured between 2017 and 2026. The true number is likely higher, as NOAA notes that only about a third of right whale deaths are recorded.

Sources indicate that the deaths are affecting the species’ ability to grow its numbers. The 2025 population estimate is 20 percent lower than the high of 483 in 2011, according to the consortium.

Sources indicate that did you know? Southern right whales.

Sources indicate that southern right whales are also struggling. Hundreds of calves have washed up dead along Argentina's coast in recent months, likely due to a bacterium that can cause skin infections.

In a recent development, scientists and conservationists are calling for stronger protections to prevent North Atlantic right whales from disappearing, including stricter vessel speed limits and measures to reduce entanglements in commercial fishing gear. “Right whales cannot afford to wait any longer,” Pettis notes in the statement.

There was one bright spot in the data: The 2025-26 calving season was the best since 2009, with 24 babies born. Three females gave birth for the first time.

Sources indicate that but Nora Ives, a marine scientist with the nonprofit conservation group Oceana, notes in a statement that “these whales can’t survive if the very safeguards and laws that protect them are constantly under attack. We must give them a fighting chance for a future.”.

#523. This Philosopher Was One of the First People to Donate His Body to Science. Nearly 200 Years Later, Researchers Are Still Learning From It

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (946 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

This Philosopher Was One of the First People to Donate His Body to Science. Nearly 200 Years Later, Researchers Are Still Learning From It

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (946 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a young man, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham vowed to donate his body to science, becoming one of the first people on record to make such a declaration.
  • Now, nearly two centuries later, Bentham’s body is still yielding new scientific insights.
  • It has been revealed that UCL researchers recently revisited Bentham’s remains, using computed tomography (CT) scanning to create a detailed, 3D model of his mummified head.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a young man, English philosopher Jeremy Bentham vowed to donate his body to science, becoming one of the first people on record to make such a declaration. And he made good on his promise. After Bentham died at age 84, his remains were publicly dissected, then transformed into an “auto-icon”—a lifelike display featuring his skeleton dressed in one of his suits, which has been preserved by the University College London (UCL) ever since.

Now, nearly two centuries later, Bentham’s body is still yielding new scientific insights.

It has been revealed that UCL researchers recently revisited Bentham’s remains, using computed tomography (CT) scanning to create a detailed, 3D model of his mummified head. They share the process and their findings in a short film called Bentham Revealed.

Sources indicate that born in 1748 in London, Bentham was a precocious child who enrolled at Oxford University at just 12 years old. Though he trained as a lawyer, he ultimately devoted his life to philosophy and writing. Bentham became best known as the founder of utilitarianism, a philosophy built around the idea that the best actions are those that produce the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.

According to recent reports, he applied this principle to a wide range of issues, advocating for prison reform, animal welfare, women’s rights, the decriminalization of homosexuality and the abolition of slavery—positions that were considered radical in 18th- and 19th-century Britain. His ideas inspired the founding of UCL, which opened to students in 1826.

But perhaps Bentham’s most radical act was his decision to donate his body to science. In his will, he bequeathed his corpse to his friend, British physician Thomas Southwood Smith, and asked him to arrange a public dissection of his body. Smith obliged, tasking anatomist Richard Dugard Grainger with carrying out the procedure five days after Bentham’s death in June 1832, according to a university statement. Smith then created the auto-icon, which he kept at his house until 1850, when he donated it to UCL. It’s right now on view at UCL’s student center.

Bentham coined the term auto-icon himself, defining it as “self image” or “self representation.” He hoped to inspire others to follow suit. “He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around,” Tannis Davidson, who led the recent research and serves as a curator at UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, tells Live Science’s Tom Metcalfe.

Smith tried to preserve Bentham’s head for the auto-icon, but his efforts ultimately failed, leading him to commission a wax replica instead. Bentham’s real head was displayed at the feet of the auto-icon for years, until it was stolen and held ransom for several days in 1975. After that, it was stashed away for safe keeping.

Bentham requested that his head be preserved in “the Latest Zealand manner.” He was referring to the preserved heads, or mokomokai, of the Māori, New Zealand’s indigenous inhabitants.

It has been revealed that bentham’s head is still used for research today. The team’s recent CT scans revealed that Bentham was missing several teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw, which likely caused excruciating pain. His tooth problems aren’t particularly surprising, given that the importance of regular dental hygiene was not yet widely understood. “Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today,” Davidson tells Live Science.

Industry observers note that it’s not clear whether Bentham knew about the arthritis in his jaw, but he was fully aware of his dental issues. He confided in an 1830 letter that he had “never been fond of having my teeth [extracted], but I have more than once submitted to the momentary torment to rid myself of the enduring one.” Bentham also described some of his home remedies, writing in another 1830 letter about heating a knitting needle, then applying it directly to an exposed nerve.

The recent investigation also sheds light on Smith’s attempts to preserve Bentham’s head for the auto-icon. He appears to have removed most of Bentham’s brain, but he left behind some of the dura mater, the thick, outermost membrane. Additionally, he drilled a hole through the top of Bentham’s skull, which was meant to attach it to the auto-icon using a metal rod. Smith also added highly detailed glass eyes—complete with an anatomically correct optic nerve—to the preserved head.

One of the team’s primary goals was to learn more about the mummification process, according to Bentham Revealed. They also hoped the CT imagery might serve as a baseline for monitoring the head’s condition over time and determining how best to preserve it.

It has been revealed that but, beyond that, they say the model of Bentham’s head could prove useful to a wide range of professionals, from healthcare providers and archaeologists to museum specialists. For example, a 3D-printed replica of Bentham’s skull could one day support teaching, research and conservation efforts.

And what would Bentham himself have thought of this modern study of his remains? That’s something the team seriously considered before embarking on the project, given the ethical sensitivities around studying human remains.

Given his beliefs about scientific inquiry and the specific directives in his will, Bentham likely would have “strongly approved,” Tim Causer, a philosopher who leads the university’s Bentham Project, claims in the statement.

“Bentham was of the view that you can’t advance knowledge without experimentation and observation,” Causer adds.

#521. Breaking: This Self-Charging Toothbrush Has Bristles That Generate Electricity to Help Kill Bacteria That Cause Cavities and Gum Disease

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (696 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Breaking: This Self-Charging Toothbrush Has Bristles That Generate Electricity to Help Kill Bacteria That Cause Cavities and Gum Disease

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers in China have reinvented a familiar tool: the toothbrush.
  • According to recent reports, brushing your teeth is an important part of your oral care routine.
  • Sources indicate that “Toothbrushes have undergone no substantive improvements beyond their mechanical function for about 1118 years to date,” the researchers write in the study.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers in China have reinvented a familiar tool: the toothbrush.

According to recent reports, brushing your teeth is an important part of your oral care routine. Both regular and electric toothbrushes rely on physically scrubbing away bacteria that can cause cavities and gum disease. But a latest design, described November 4 in the journal Science Advances, features bristles that generate bacteria-killing electricity when they bend, perhaps providing a long-awaited enhancement to the hygiene tool.

Sources indicate that “Toothbrushes have undergone no substantive improvements beyond their mechanical function for about 1118 years to date,” the researchers write in the study. “Conventional toothbrushes often fail to establish an antibacterial environment on the tooth surface, allowing bacteria to recover and recolonize. Here, we developed an innovative self-charged toothbrush that integrates daily tooth brushing with piezoelectric functionality.”.

In a recent development, piezoelectric materials generate electricity when put under mechanical stress, like being squeezed or compressed. In the new study, researchers applied this property to the toothbrush by creating bristles from polyvinylidene fluoride, a material that produces an electrical charge when it bends.

The electricity doesn’t directly zap oral bacteria, however. Instead, the charge creates highly unstable molecules called reactive oxygen species in the saliva. These molecules disrupt the membranes of bacteria in dental plaque—a sticky layer of the harmful organisms, along with food particles and spit.

According to recent reports, “The concept is great,” Nicholas Jakubovics, an oral microbiologist at Newcastle University in England who did not participate in the research, tells New Scientist’s Christa Lesté-Lasserre. “Basically, the mechanical forces recharge the surface, so it’s really innovative. Anything that even slightly improves the way dental care works could have a benefit, because oral disease is just so widespread.” Experts estimate that almost 3.7 billion people worldwide have oral diseases, such as gum disease and tooth decay.

In a recent development, the researchers first conducted lab tests of the piezoelectric toothbrush using two key oral pathogens: Streptococcus mutans, which causes cavities, and Porphyromonas gingivalis, which causes gum disease. The charge-producing bristles killed about half of the cavity-causing bacteria and more than half of the gum disease agent present, while traditional nylon bristles eliminated only about 9 percent and 8 percent, respectively.

According to recent reports, then, they moved to a human trial. The team enrolled 115 participants with tooth decay or mild gum disease, called gingivitis. They asked some people to use the electricity-generating toothbrushes and others to use nylon-bristled brushes twice a day for three months.

At the end of the study period, participants who brushed with the experimental tool had less plaque, gum inflammation and bleeding than regular toothbrush customers, the team found.

Early forms of toothbrushes, such as a “chew stick” with a frayed end, have existed since 3,000 B.C.E.

Sources indicate that “It’s great to have latest approaches that actually enhance the effect of mechanical cleaning,” Jakubovics tells Live Science’s Isha Ishtiaq. “The idea that the toothbrush surface itself is actively doing something is really interesting.”.

One of the limits of the research, however, is the clinical trial’s short duration, he notes. “We would want to make sure that it is safe on the tissues for long-term use.”.

Frank Scannapieco, a periodontist and microbiologist at the University of Buffalo who did not participate in the study, agrees that more research is necessary to prove the toothbrush is safe and effective, per Nature’s Elizabeth Gibney.

Sources indicate that this isn’t the first time researchers have taken a swing at upgrading toothbrushes. Previous designs have included bristles with antibacterial chemicals, but researchers aren’t sure if they have a lasting effect. Others produced charged particles to help clean teeth, but these require batteries.

“The toothbrush is humanity’s mightiest soldier in the battle against dental plaque,” according to a statement. The researchers behind the latest study “have now upgraded this warrior.”.

Still, there’s a long way to go before this upgrade can sit on pharmacies’ oral health shelves.

#519. Have Archaeologists Finally Pieced Together the 'Parthenon Puzzle,' One of Ancient Greece's Greatest Mysteries?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (977 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Have Archaeologists Finally Pieced Together the 'Parthenon Puzzle,' One of Ancient Greece's Greatest Mysteries?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (977 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, when the Parthenon was built some 2,500 years ago atop the Acropolis of Athens, one of the temple’s facades stood out for its striking imagery.
  • But no one alive today has ever looked upon the scene in its original glory.
  • Open this week at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt, Germany, “Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle” offers visitors a chance to see what the institution is calling the first-ever “archaeologically grounded proposal” for what the pediment once looked like.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when the Parthenon was built some 2,500 years ago atop the Acropolis of Athens, one of the temple’s facades stood out for its striking imagery. Stretching for nearly 100 feet above the building’s eastern entrance, the marble-carved pediment depicted Athena being birthed from the head of a nearly 13-foot-tall Zeus; they were flanked on either side by 37 other intricately sculpted figures, including gods and goddesses. For its fine craftsmanship and potent symbolism, the pediment is widely considered by scholars to be one of antiquity’s most famous images.

But no one alive today has ever looked upon the scene in its original glory. Sometime between the fifth century C.E. and 1670, the pediment was largely destroyed—fires, earthquakes and humans all played roles in its destruction. Only 20 percent of the ruins were recovered, and these fragments have since been scattered to museums across the world. Piecing together what the original artwork may have looked like has intrigued historians for centuries. Now, a team of researchers believe they have finally reached a solution to the Parthenon puzzle.

Open this week at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt, Germany, “Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle” offers visitors a chance to see what the institution is calling the first-ever “archaeologically grounded proposal” for what the pediment once looked like.

Recent findings suggest that “For around 200 years, archaeological research has sought to reconstruct the lost overall appearance of the Parthenon’s east pediment,” Philipp Demandt, the museum’s director, notes in a statement. “With this exhibition, we are presenting our findings to the public for the first time and inviting visitors to take a fresh look at and discuss one of the most significant works of art from antiquity.”.

A post shared by Liebieghaus Skulpturensammlung (@liebieghaus).

In a recent development, recreating the image took decades of dedicated research. The museum’s effort was led by Vinzenz Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, who are both archaeologists. They began by referencing the most complete, existing body of work about the pediment. In the early 20th century, Arthur Hamilton Smith, a curator at the British Museum, produced plaster casts of more than 200 small surviving fragments from the pediment and meticulously documented their known placements in relation to each other.

The duo created digital renderings of these pieces, which still left massive gaps in the overall pediment. They then began scouring archives around the world for unidentified clues to the original design. A breakthrough came during a trip to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg, Russia, in 2014. There, they observed an ancient Roman sarcophagus with a relief on its lid depicting the birth of Athena. The scene resembled nearly exactly what scholars envisioned of the pediment.

Brinkmann and Koch-Brinkmann are also noted for their painstaking work to accurately recreate the original color schemes of classical white marble statues. For authenticity, they used the same mineral and organic pigments available to the ancients.

“It was really a chance discovery,” Brinkmann tells the Art Newspaper’s Catherine Hickley. “We noticed a figural relief on the lid of a sarcophagus that was clearly closely related to the composition of the east pediment. It refers to the few surviving figures from the corners of the pediment, such as Helios and Selene with their chariots, but also to figures that have repeatedly been proposed as having belonged to the east pediment, such as the Horae [and] Moirai.”.

Industry observers note that brinkmann’s team studied nine sarcophagi in total, mostly in the Vatican Museum and elsewhere in Rome. “The Romans copied everything the Greeks did,” he explains to the Art Newspaper.

While no single sarcophagus showed the entire 39-figure scene, they each showed different aspects of the pediment, which the researchers were able to piece together digitally, with the help of 3D scanners. Earlier scholars noticed this connection between sarcophagi lids and the pediment, Brinkmann tells Deutsche Welle’s Katharina Abel. “But we really seized on the idea and never let go.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers searched for missing artifacts that could piece together the lost scene. On the surviving fragments they studied drill holes and the edges of broken shards for clues about adjacent pieces. They referenced ancient texts for possible descriptions of the pediment’s positioning. They identified lost sculptures and worked with international institutions to ask and answer latest questions as they arose.

“Piece by piece, the puzzle came together to form a fresh, archaeologically grounded overall picture of the Parthenon’s east pediment,” Brinkmann indicates in the statement.

It has been revealed that inside the exhibit, the reconstructed pediment is presented as a 13 foot-long, 3D-printed model, at a scale of 1:7.7 compared to the original. There are also life-size reproductions of the largely missing central figures, Zeus, Athena and Hera, based on surviving fragments and comparable sculptures. Casts of the well-preserved figures at opposite ends of the pediment—Helios, the sun god, and Selene, the moon goddess—mark the passing of time from day to night. A colorful animation created especially for the exhibition brings the tale to life through a retelling of the myth of Athena’s birth.

“Research belongs in the public sphere. In particular, a museum can demonstrate how scientific knowledge is generated by interpreting traces, asking questions and correlating different sources,” Ina Hartwig, who heads the city of Frankfurt’s Department of Culture and Science, notes in a statement. “The exhibition makes this process immediately comprehensible to visitors.”.

“Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle” is on view at the Liebieghaus Sculpture Collection in Frankfurt through July 25, 2027.

Christian Thorsberg is an environmental writer and photographer from Chicago. His work, which often centers on freshwater concerns, climate change and subsistence, has appeared in Circle of Blue, Sierra magazine, Discover magazine and Alaska Sporting Journal.

  • Power optimizers are DC-to-DC converters installed on the underside of solar modules to maximize power output.
  • According to the firm’s datasheet, each input supports up to 650 W, with an MPPT operating voltage range of 12.5 V to 57 V and a maximum continuous input current of 20 A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

SolarEdge unveiled its latest U.S.-made Duo power optimizer for commercial and industrial (C&I) solar projects this week at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas.

Power optimizers are DC-to-DC converters installed on the underside of solar modules to maximize power output. Unlike conventional optimizers, which typically connect to a single module, the SolarEdge Duo connects to two modules, with an independent maximum power point tracker (MPPT) for each.

According to the firm’s datasheet, each input supports up to 650 W, with an MPPT operating voltage range of 12.5 V to 57 V and a maximum continuous input current of 20 A. The optimizer has a maximum output voltage of 80 V, a maximum output current of 20 A and a weighted efficiency of 98.8%.

Sources indicate that solarEdge remarked the dual-module design reduces the number of optimizers required by 50% compared with its C651U model. Each optimizer features a short pair of wires for the nearest module and a pre-extended pair for the adjacent module, reducing cable slack and eliminating the need for field-installed jumpers. The Duo also supports dual-tilt racking configurations, allowing it to connect modules facing different directions.

The device measures 129 mm x 159 mm x 59 mm and weighs 1.2 kg, including cables. It has an IP68/NEMA 6P protection rating and an operating temperature range of -40 C to 85 C, with power derating above 65 C. The optimizer supports a maximum system voltage of 1,000 V and is compatible with specified SolarEdge commercial three-phase inverters.

Industry observers note that the Duo features SolarEdge’s optimizer-level arc fault detection technology, which uses each optimizer as an arc sensor as part of the manufacturer’s arc fault circuit interruption (AFCI) system. According to SolarEdge, this enables arc faults to be detected closer to their source rather than solely at the inverter. If one optimizer fails to detect an arc, a neighboring optimizer can detect it, the company mentioned. The system reportedly provides protection for strings with a total cable length of up to 1,000 meters between the inverter and optimizers.

SolarEdge reports that its Sense Connect technology also monitors temperature at every input and output connector to identify developing faults.

Sources indicate that the Duo comes with a 25-year warranty. Manufactured in Florida, it is designed to meet U.S. Domestic Content and Foreign Entity of Concern (FEOC) requirements.

The Duo power optimizer is available to order now in the U.S. through SolarEdge sales channels and distribution partners, with shipments expected to begin in January 2027. SolarEdge is showing the Duo this week at RE+ in booth N1516.

#517. The NIH Has Decided to Move Its Last Group of Retired Research Chimpanzees to an Animal Sanctuary Next Year

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

The NIH Has Decided to Move Its Last Group of Retired Research Chimpanzees to an Animal Sanctuary Next Year

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (721 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Roughly three dozen chimpanzees at the moment live at the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Bastrop, Texas.
  • “Completing their transfers will fulfill NIH’s commitment, revealed in November 2015, to retire all NIH-owned chimpanzees to sanctuary,” claims Jay Bhattacharya, director of the agency, in the statement.
  • The move has been a long time in the making.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Roughly three dozen chimpanzees at the moment live at the Keeling Center for Comparative Medicine and Research in Bastrop, Texas. They used to serve as subjects in scientific studies. Next year, however, these primates—the last federally owned chimps at an American research facility—will move to a retirement home at an animal sanctuary, according to an announcement by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) on November 18.

“Completing their transfers will fulfill NIH’s commitment, revealed in November 2015, to retire all NIH-owned chimpanzees to sanctuary,” claims Jay Bhattacharya, director of the agency, in the statement.

The move has been a long time in the making. In 2000, the Chimpanzee Health Improvement Maintenance Protection (CHIMP) Act established a national sanctuary system for chimps no longer needed for federal biomedical research. Then, in 2015, the NIH revealed it would end its funding and support of all research on the primate species. The agency committed to retire all its approximately 300 chimps and move them to Chimp Haven, a 200-acre federal sanctuary in Keithville, Louisiana.

Recent findings suggest that but the initiative proceeded slowly. In 2019, the NIH veterinary panel determined that the 44 federally owned chimpanzees at the Alamogordo Primate Facility in Latest Mexico were too old or ill to move. Many of the retirees were near the upper end of their life expectancy in captivity and had severe health problems like heart disease. Two years later, the agency decided the same for the 51 primates at the Keeling Center and the 11 at the Southwest National Primate Research Center in San Antonio, Texas.

However, in 2024, staffing changes at Alamogordo and public pressure—including a lawsuit filed by animal welfare organizations—forced the NIH to shift its prepares for the remaining chimps at the facility. They finally moved to Chimp Haven last year, meaning only the Keeling Center chimps remained at an NIH facility, given that the Southwest National Primate Research Center stopped receiving funding from the agency.

Although one elderly Alamogordo chimp died on the way to the sanctuary, the transfer prompted NIH leadership to revisit the potential transfer of Keeling Center animals, Bhattacharya states in the statement. “After careful analysis and internal consultations, NIH leadership decided to proceed.”.

Did you know? Chimps and humans.

Chimps, along with bonobos, are our closest living relatives. We share almost 99 percent of our DNA with these two species.

Animal advocacy organizations have welcomed the news.

It has been revealed that “This has been a long road and something that many people thought would never happen,” says Kathleen Conlee, vice president of animal research issues at the Humane World for Animals, to Emily Anthes at the New York Times. “It’s a really historic moment. This will be the end of the government’s use and confinement of chimps in labs.”.

Biomedical research groups, on the other hand, oppose the transfer. They argue that the aging chimps would be safer staying at a place with staff they know, reports David Grimm at Science.

“These are sensitive and intelligent beings with complex social histories that include strong relationships with their chimp and human families,” says Cindy Buckmaster, former chair of Americans for Medical Progress, an advocacy organization that supports humane animal research, to Science.

Industry observers note that at the Keeling Center, chimps have access to large, open enclosures, she says. “They have everything they need where they are. We should leave them be and let them live the rest of their lives in peace.”.

In a recent development, staff at Chimp Haven, for their part, are excited to welcome the animals. The primates from Alamogordo appear to be acclimating well, claims Rana Smith, the sanctuary’s president and CEO, to the Times. They hope to receive all the Keeling Center chimps by the end of next year, with some transfers beginning in January.

Industry observers note that “When that very last chimp arrives from the Keeling Center, I think that is a milestone moment,” Smith says. “We’re just happy to be a part of it and provide the chimps with their happy ending.”.

Sources indicate that sara Hashemi is a science writer and fact-checker at the moment based in Upcoming York City. Her work has appeared in Sierra, The Body, Maisonneuve magazine and more.

Industry News: See the Rare Baby Rhinoceros Born at England's Chester Zoo, an Adorable Boost for Its Vulnerable Species

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A zoo in England is welcoming an enormous upcoming baby: a greater one-horned rhino.
  • “The upcoming calf is gorgeous, big and active,” Emma Evison, team manager for rhinos at Chester Zoo, tells Smithsonian magazine.
  • It will be a few years before the calf gets its namesake horn, but otherwise, newborn greater one-horned rhinos “come out as almost perfect miniatures of their parents,” Evison states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A zoo in England is welcoming an enormous upcoming baby: a greater one-horned rhino. Video footage captured the moment of the calf’s birth at Chester Zoo on October 11, and since then, animal care teams have delighted in watching the baby grow.

“The upcoming calf is gorgeous, big and active,” Emma Evison, team manager for rhinos at Chester Zoo, tells Smithsonian magazine. “Every step of the process so far has been brilliant … and it’s a pleasure to see the calf becoming more confident and curious.”.

A post shared by Chester Zoo (@chesterzoo).

It will be a few years before the calf gets its namesake horn, but otherwise, newborn greater one-horned rhinos “come out as almost perfect miniatures of their parents,” Evison states. Their skin folds into plates in a way that resembles a coat of armor, and learning how to inhabit their bulky bodies takes some time.

“For the first few days, young rhinos have to work out how their legs are supposed to operate,” she adds. “There’s a bit of wobbliness.”.

The baby is healthy, though its sex and weight haven’t yet been announced. Greater one-horned rhino calves are typically around 99 pounds, per a statement from the zoo, and by the time it’s an adult, the animal will be about six feet tall at the shoulder.

The birth marks the fourth calf born to parents Asha and Beni at Chester Zoo. But after siring the calf, Beni died earlier this year from a sudden illness. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf,” Tom Garland, assistant manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo, claims in the statement. And Asha “has been a brilliant mum to all her youngsters,” he adds. This most recent pregnancy lasted 15 months.

The greater one-horned rhino’s scientific name is a nod to the animal’s single keratinous protrusion: Rhinoceros unicornis.

Tracking a rhinoceros pregnancy isn’t an easy task. With such thick skin, rhinos are tough targets for ultrasound machines. But caretakers were able to follow Asha’s reproductive cycle by measuring fertility- and pregnancy-related hormones—like estrogen and progesterone—in her dung.

Recent findings suggest that this technique also showed them when Asha was ready to breed, allowing them to safely introduce her to Beni. Rhinos are typically solitary animals outside the mating season, so knowing when they can come together is helpful for zoo scientists hoping to increase their population.

Greater one-horned rhinos once lived throughout the northern region of the Indian subcontinent. But at the start of the 20th century, after widespread habitat loss and relentless hunting driven in part by demand for their horns, only about 200 were left in the wild.

Thanks to decades of conservation efforts and strict protections, the rhinos have come back from the edge of extinction, with some 4,000 of them now living in the wetlands, forests and grasslands of northern India and Nepal.

According to recent reports, the species remains vulnerable to extinction, however, and the animals still face risks. Between January 2021 and December 2024, poachers killed nine greater one-horned rhinos in India, and another four were killed in Nepal, Spoorthy Raman reported for Mongabay last year. Many of the wild rhinos are concentrated in only a few national parks, a distribution that “makes them vulnerable to illness and environmental changes,” Mark Brayshaw, the Chester Zoo’s head of mammals, notes in the statement. Though the rhinos have more conservation guardrails than they once did, he notes, “they still need people to love and protect them.”.

It has been revealed that chester Zoo belongs to a breeding project across Europe that’s working to conserve the rhino species. And this calf is a key part of that effort, since it belongs to a genetically valuable lineage.

It has been revealed that “Asha is an key rhino, because her genetic line is not over-represented in this population,” Evison claims. Even though her species has seen recent success in the wild, “you don’t know what might happen down the line, so it’s important to have that insurance population of healthy individuals in human care.”.

“Every birth is important for the future of this species,” Garland says in the statement, “and it’s wonderful to see another healthy arrival.”.

Carlyn Kranking is Smithsonian magazine's associate web editor for science.

#514. Harvard Returns Two Skulls Likely Belonging to Enslaved Individuals, More Than 150 Years After They Were Taken From Brazil for Eugenics Studies

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1082 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

Harvard Returns Two Skulls Likely Belonging to Enslaved Individuals, More Than 150 Years After They Were Taken From Brazil for Eugenics Studies

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1082 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • More than a century and a half after their remains were removed from Brazil, sent to the United States and used in eugenics studies at Harvard University, the skulls of two people of African descent have finally returned to Brazil.
  • Last week, the Brazilian government formally repatriated the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, marking the transfer with official ceremonies in the cities of Rio de Janeiro and Salvador, according to a statement.
  • In a recent development, “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognizing the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, remarked at the ceremony, according to the Art Newspaper’s Gabriella Angeleti.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

More than a century and a half after their remains were removed from Brazil, sent to the United States and used in eugenics studies at Harvard University, the skulls of two people of African descent have finally returned to Brazil.

Last week, the Brazilian government formally repatriated the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology, marking the transfer with official ceremonies in the cities of Rio de Janeiro and Salvador, according to a statement. The skulls were carried aboard flights in padded boxes inside reinforced suitcases by Brazilian diplomats, concluding a four-year recovery campaign, the Guardian’s Tiago Rogero reports.

In a recent development, “The repatriation of human remains represents a fundamental step towards recognizing the memory, history and dignity of the Black population of our country,” Brazil’s minister of human rights and citizenship, Janine Mello, remarked at the ceremony, according to the Art Newspaper’s Gabriella Angeleti. “More than a century after they were taken from Brazil, these remains will return to the country to receive the dignified treatment to which they are entitled, in a process built on respect for memory, religious traditions and the communities involved.”.

According to recent reports, did you know? Slavery in Brazil.

Sources indicate that during the trans-Atlantic slave trade, over four million enslaved Africans disembarked in Brazil—more than in any other destination in the Americas. Brazil was the last country in the Western Hemisphere to abolish slavery, in 1888.

Sources indicate that eugenics emerged in the 19th century as the racist, pseudoscientific belief in the selective breeding of human beings. Universities like Harvard at times supported the eugenics movement, with faculty conducting since-discredited research into racial hierarchies. Exploiting enslaved people and their remains under the guise of science was “widespread,” historians Ayah Nuriddin, Graham Mooney and Alexandre I.R. White wrote in a 2020 Lancet article. “American medical education relied on the theft, dissection and display of bodies, many of whom were Black.”.

It has been revealed that the existence of the two Brazilian skulls at Harvard came to public light in 2022 through a book by historian Christopher D.E. Willoughby and reporting in the student-run Harvard Crimson, which found that the university held remains from at least 19 people likely enslaved in the United States, the Caribbean and Brazil, Rogero reported last year in the Guardian.

While a 2022 university report recommended the repatriation of the remains and Brazilian researchers continued to push for the skulls’ return, negotiations only gained momentum after Brazil’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs joined the talks in late 2024, historian João José Reis told the Guardian last year.

Sources indicate that one of the skulls, transferred to the Federal University of Bahia in Salvador, is believed to belong to an enslaved man of Nagô, or Yoruba, origin who fought and died in the January 1835 Malê Revolt, the largest urban slave rebellion in Brazilian history. During that uprising roughly 600 enslaved and freed African Muslims attempted to take control of Salvador before police suppressed the revolt, killing 70 participants. After the man died of his wounds at a Salvador hospital, U.S. diplomat and sugar trader Gideon T. Snow allegedly took his head and shipped it to Boston alongside a note laden with eugenicist beliefs, describing the unnamed man as “one of the chiefs in the affair,” per the Guardian.

Recent findings suggest that members of the Bahia Islamic Cultural Center in Salvador and the advocacy group Arakunrin campaigned for his return so he could receive a proper burial. “He is our brother and deserves to be buried under Islamic rites,” Sheikh Abdul Hameed Ahmad, the founder of the center, told the Guardian in 2025. Funeral rituals were often denied to enslaved individuals who died in Brazil, per researcher Hannah Romã Bellini Sarno.

Less is known about the second skull, which was entrusted to the National Museum of the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro. It had been held at the Peabody Museum since 1870, following a transfer from Harvard’s Museum of Comparative Zoology. Museum records indicate that it was obtained by Walter Hunnewell, a Harvard graduate who served as photographer on an 1865-1866 expedition to Brazil led by naturalist Louis Agassiz, with an accompanying note stating the remains had been “exhumed in the streets of Rio de Janeiro,” per the Art Newspaper.

Based on the skull’s size, Harvard researchers suggested it likely belonged to an adult woman. By cross-referencing 19th-century diaries, letters and maps, Bruno Véras, a historian at the University of Toronto Mississauga, concluded the remains may have been taken from Rio’s Cemitério dos Pretos Novos, a burial ground for newly arrived Africans who died during or shortly after arriving in Brazil. “To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” Veras tells the Guardian.

According to recent reports, “This return represents a historical responsibility for the museum,” Juliana Sayão, deputy director of the national museum, stated during the Rio ceremony, per the Art Newspaper. “We are confronted with the story of a person whose life was shaped by enslavement and the removal of her body from Brazil. Beyond assuming temporary custody, we are committed to treating this history with respect and responsibility.”.

It has been revealed that neither skull will be publicly exhibited or have its image released. Forensic anthropologists at the two Brazilian universities will conduct measurements and microscopic examinations—and, if authorized, genetic or dating analyses—to confirm the individuals’ sex and origins before both are laid to rest with religious rites.

Industry observers note that for Brazilian officials, the return marks both a reckoning and a beginning. “This history of slavery cannot be undone,” Irina Feisthauer Silveira, one of the diplomats who escorted the remains back to Brazil, tells the Guardian. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”.

#512. Efficient heating is not enough: Why the timing of electricity use matters for heat pumps

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (806 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Efficient heating is not enough: Why the timing of electricity use matters for heat pumps

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (806 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when discussing the cost-effectiveness of heat pumps, the focus is usually on the seasonal performance factor (SPF), flow temperature and building insulation.
  • Industry observers note that on very cold winter days, well-designed heat pumps often need to run almost continuously, leaving little scope for shifting heat production.
  • According to recent reports, even when a heat pump runs continuously, the electricity it consumes does not necessarily have to be drawn from the grid at the same time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when discussing the cost-effectiveness of heat pumps, the focus is usually on the seasonal performance factor (SPF), flow temperature and building insulation. While these factors remain crucial, the debate around dynamic electricity tariffs is too narrow if it focuses solely on how long a heat pump can be switched off. What matters is the overall flexibility of a household’s electricity consumption.

Industry observers note that on very cold winter days, well-designed heat pumps often need to run almost continuously, leaving little scope for shifting heat production. At milder temperatures, however, there is some flexibility: Buildings and hot water storage tanks can retain heat for several hours. For example, a home can be preheated overnight for the morning or during the day for the evening. Similarly, hot water production can be scheduled for periods when electricity prices are lower. How long this flexibility lasts depends on the building’s insulation, heating system and storage capacity, although it is generally insufficient to bridge entire days.

According to recent reports, even when a heat pump runs continuously, the electricity it consumes does not necessarily have to be drawn from the grid at the same time. A suitable battery storage system can charge from the grid when electricity prices are low and supply power later. In this case, it is not heat production that is shifted, but the timing of electricity drawn from the grid. This distinction is particularly relevant for households with photovoltaic systems and existing battery storage.

According to recent reports, in summer, PV systems cover a larger share of household electricity demand with self-generated solar power. In winter, heating demand increases while solar power generation declines, making households more dependent on grid electricity. An existing battery storage system, provided it supports grid charging and can be controlled in response to electricity prices, can therefore do more than store solar power. It can also take advantage of periods of low wholesale electricity prices.

Sources indicate that an analysis by Ostrom of average hourly wholesale electricity prices during the winter months of 2025 illustrates the importance of timing. At 2 p.m., the average price was €0.0832 ($0.0965)/kWh compared with €0.1462/kWh at 7 p.m. – a difference of €0.063. However, such a price difference alone is unlikely to justify investing in a battery storage system solely to optimize electricity costs. In addition to the initial investment, storage losses and the achievable utilization rate must also be taken into account.

Sources indicate that for households that already have battery storage, the economics are different. The key question is whether the potential savings from price differences outweigh additional storage losses, battery degradation and any costs associated with technical modifications. Even then, profitable operation is far from guaranteed. Average hourly prices also do not reflect the price differences that can actually be exploited on individual days. While the figures illustrate the importance of when electricity is drawn from the grid, they do not demonstrate actual savings.

Industry observers note that other flexible loads also play a role. Households charging electric vehicles, particularly in winter, often cannot rely solely on electricity generated by their own PV systems. Coordinated energy management can help shift charging to periods when grid electricity is cheaper. Even when solar generation is low, strong wind power output can drive down wholesale electricity prices.

For heat pumps, electricity prices are not the only factor affecting operating costs. With air-to-water heat pumps, outdoor temperatures also matter. If temperatures are higher around midday than in the early morning, the system can operate more efficiently. An intelligent control system should therefore consider electricity prices, outdoor temperatures and actual heating demand simultaneously. Producing additional heat simply because electricity is cheap makes little sense if that heat is ultimately wasted.

Good insulation and efficient hot water storage can help minimize these losses. Automated controls can make better use of periods with low electricity prices than fixed schedules. What matters is whether the different system components can communicate with one another and whether the resulting savings outweigh any additional costs.

Industry observers note that assessing the cost-effectiveness of heat pumps therefore requires looking beyond the efficiency of the individual unit. Particularly in winter, when heat pumps may need to operate almost continuously, it is worth considering the entire energy system, including thermal storage, battery storage, PV installations and other electricity-consuming devices. The key question is not how often a heat pump can be switched off, but how intelligently a household can source the electricity it needs.

Recent findings suggest that matthias Martensen is CEO and co-founder of Berlin-based green electricity provider Ostrom. The organization offers digital electricity tariffs and solutions for the intelligent management of distributed energy systems.

The views and opinions expressed in this article are the author’s own, and do not necessarily reflect those held by pv magazine.

#511. Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar by 2029 with policy reforms

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (715 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Pv-magazine

Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar by 2029 with policy reforms

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (715 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Pv-magazine

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indonesia’s cumulative installed solar capacity reached 1.59 GW as of the first quarter of 2026 (Q1 2026), according to the latest report from the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), a Jakarta-based think tank.
  • IESR’s Indonesia Solar Energy Outlook 2027 says the figure is equivalent to around 1.5% of Indonesia’s power generation capacity and 0.3% of electricity production.
  • In a recent development, rooftop PV currently accounts for the largest share of installed capacity, standing at 0.9 GW as of Q1 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indonesia’s cumulative installed solar capacity reached 1.59 GW as of the first quarter of 2026 (Q1 2026), according to the latest report from the Institute for Essential Services Reform (IESR), a Jakarta-based think tank.

IESR’s Indonesia Solar Energy Outlook 2027 says the figure is equivalent to around 1.5% of Indonesia’s power generation capacity and 0.3% of electricity production.

In a recent development, rooftop PV currently accounts for the largest share of installed capacity, standing at 0.9 GW as of Q1 2026. Utility-scale solar accounted for 0.33 GW, captive solar for 0.3 GW and installations in remote areas for around 0.06 GW.

With the country passing the 1 GW solar milestone in 2025, IESR says the current growth rate is “far behind the government’s ambition to make solar power one of the backbones of the national energy system”, as set out in the country’s 100 GW solar power program which President Prabowo Subianto has set a target of achieving by 2029.

The program officially rolled out in August with a first phase of 14 projects totalling around 5.2 GW, but only 526 MW of this capacity currently have targeted completion dates, IESR’s report reveals.

The think tank adds that deployments are at the moment held back by regulatory gaps, procurement uncertainty and limited grid access.

In a statement sent to pv magazine, IESR CEO Fabby Tumiwa remarked the 100 GW ambition needs to be reflected in updates to Indonesia’s 2025-2034 electricity supply business plan (RUPTL), with greater emphasis on utility-scale PV and battery energy storage systems (BESS), diesel replacement with solar-plus-storage and rooftop PV deployment.

IESR’s modelling suggests Indonesia could reach 96.7 GW of solar capacity by 2029 if development proceeds through multiple channels simultaneously.

The report says around 8 GW is already planned through RUPTL and Mentari GigaOne procurements, while a further 56 GW could come through procurements by Indonesia’s state-owned electric utility PLN. It suggests the remaining 33 GW could be developed through rooftop PV, diesel replacement, rural electrification, captive solar and other distributed applications.

IESR says five enablers that must move together – demand, rooftop access, procurement, grid and supply chain – will determine whether the 100 GW scales.

Under a high-electrification scenario, Indonesia’s electricity demand could be around 160 TWh higher in 2035 than under a business-as-usual scenario, according to figures from the report. Electrification of transport, industry, cooling, cooking and data centers, alongside potential electricity exports, could help create additional demand for solar generation.

IESR also suggests rooftop solar quotas be determined according to grid hosting capacity at the substation level, rather than through the current quota system, which it noted limits deployment.

Industry observers note that for utility-scale projects, the report recommends more transparent procurement schedules and reverse auctions. Projects are frequently tendered individually without a clear timetable, making it harder for developers, lenders and suppliers to prepare, IESR stated.

Industry observers note that grid and storage investment will also need to keep pace. Indonesia’s 2025-2034 RUPTL includes 42.6 GW of renewable energy and 10.3 GW of energy storage, but some transmission infrastructure needed to integrate solar is not scheduled until 2030-2034. IESR’s report recommends regulatory changes and incentives to encourage investment in storage.

Recent findings suggest that in the report, Tumiwa notes that Indonesia’s domestic solar supply chain is rising faster than demand. Solar module production capacity reached 27 GW per year in 2026, although the report notes more than half of it needs further verification due to relabelling allegations, while cell capacity now stands at 14.3 GW.

According to recent reports, it indicates that after 98.2% of Indonesia’s solar module exports went to the United States in 2025, US preliminary duties of about 104% in February 2026 cut Indonesian exports to the US by about 98%, from a peak of 2.2 GW in November 2025 to 34 MW in April 2026. Final duties of up to 268% followed in September 2026.

IESR states the 100 GW programme “could provide a market anchor [for the solar supply chain] if accompanied by consistent policy and project certainty”.

The 100 GW target must also be explicitly incorporated into revisions of the National Electricity General Plan (RUKN) and RUPTL, IESR added, with defined procurement channels, grid requirements, distributed solar roles and legal frameworks for project ownership and financing.

  • According to recent reports, the call is scheduled to open on Dec.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Commission is preparing to launch a €36 million ($39.5 million) funding call under the Horizon Europe program to support the development and industrial scale-up of advanced solar photovoltaic manufacturing technologies.

The Production technologies for solar photovoltaics beyond the state-of-the-art call is part of the European Partnership for Innovation in Photovoltaics (EUPI-PV). It aims to strengthen Europe’s competitiveness in solar manufacturing and support the development of more efficient, reliable and cost-effective solar cells and modules.

According to recent reports, the call is scheduled to open on Dec. 3, 2026, with an application deadline of March 31, 2027.

It has been revealed that the funding will target advanced manufacturing processes for high-efficiency PV technologies, including production equipment, automation, digitalization and scalable industrial manufacturing methods. Projects must demonstrate improvements over commercially available technologies while addressing production efficiency, product reliability and industrial scalability.

The initiative also aims to bridge the gap between technological development and commercial production by supporting pilot manufacturing lines and industrial demonstration activities.

The funding comes as Europe’s solar manufacturing sector continues to face significant challenges. A report by the EU’s Clean Energy Technology Observatory found that the bloc’s manufacturing capacity for solar ingots, wafers, cells and modules remains well below the targets set under the Net-Zero Industry Act. The report estimated EU production capacity at 12 GW for modules and 2 GW for cells, highlighting the need for coordinated policy support and investment in large-scale, automated manufacturing facilities.

The European Commission has also been supporting solar manufacturing through other funding mechanisms. In October, French manufacturer Holosolis secured support under the EU Innovation Fund for its planned 5 GW solar cell and module factory in Hambach, France. The project was among 77 net-zero technology initiatives selected for a combined €3.4 billion in funding, including investments in solar, battery and other clean-energy manufacturing technologies.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur regional government and Société du Canal de Provence (SCP) have completed what they describe as France’s first large-scale canal-top PV project in Saint-Maximin-la-Sainte-Baume, in the Var department.

Spanning 71 meters, the custom-designed installation covers the canal and its banks, demonstrating a upcoming approach that combines water transport and electricity generation on the same infrastructure. With an installed capacity of 299 kW and estimated annual generation of 404 MWh, the pilot project accounts for approximately 1% of SCP’s annual energy consumption.

Recent findings suggest that SCP has a long history in hydropower and presently operates 17 small hydroelectric plants, generating approximately 17 GWh per year. The company plans to expand this capacity in the coming years.

SCP aims to become a net energy producer, eventually generating more renewable electricity than its estimated annual consumption of 40 GWh. Since the early 2020s, the company has been adding solar PV to its existing hydropower portfolio.

It has been revealed that developed under the regional concession for the Canal de Provence, the pilot project also aims to help control water service costs. It makes use of existing infrastructure without requiring additional land development, while potentially improving water quality through the shading provided by the solar panels.

In a recent development, with nearly 70 km of open-air canals, the Canal de Provence, part of the Provence-Alpes-Côte d’Azur region’s hydraulic infrastructure, offers significant potential for solar PV development. SCP studies estimate that the canals could accommodate more than 50 MW of PV capacity, generating approximately 70 GWh of electricity annually.

However, deployment will be selective, with only 5% to 10% of the canal network considered suitable for PV installations due to technical and regulatory constraints.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, bolivia’s state-owned power utility ENDE has introduced an international tender for the engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) of the Contorno Bajo I solar plant, which will have a minimum nominal capacity of 40 MWac. The project will become the first large-scale solar power plant in the department of La Paz.

In a recent development, the tender, published on Nov. 16 under reference ENDE-KFW-2026-002, sets a 14-month implementation period from the signing of the contract. Construction is scheduled to begin in May 2027, with commissioning expected to be completed by June 2028.

The contract includes a 24.9/115 kV step-up substation, an approximately 800-meter-long, 115 kV interconnection line, and modifications to a bay at the Contorno Bajo substation, owned by ENDE Transmisión, to feed electricity into Bolivia’s National Interconnected System (SIN).

Industry observers note that bidders must demonstrate experience in five PV projects of at least 40 MW each and three solar power plants in South America that have been operational for at least two years. They must also demonstrate average annual revenue of at least €60 million ($65.93 million) and access to financial resources totaling €40 million ($43.96 million).

Recent findings suggest that A separate tender for consulting and project supervision services is also underway, with bids due by Dec. 21. The contract covers construction supervision, equipment quality control, plant commissioning and training for ENDE personnel.

As pv magazine Latam reported in June, the Bolivian government enacted legislation approving a loan of up to €34 million ($37.36 million) from German development bank KfW to finance the project.

According to information released by ENDE in July, the solar plant will occupy 34 hectares at an altitude of more than 3,700 meters above sea level and will have an estimated operational lifetime of 25 years.

Recent findings suggest that the original project design, announced in January 2023, included a lithium-ion battery energy storage system. However, the current tender notice makes no mention of a storage component.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) ran from 9 to 20 November 2026. On 11 November, at the side event “Clean Energy Systems: From NDCs to Implementation” – hosted by the Global Energy Interconnection Development and Cooperation Organization (GEIDCO) at the UNFCCC Capacity Building Hub – Floria Wang, Head of Global Branding at LONGi, delivered a keynote speech in which she shared the company’s practical achievements in advancing the global energy transition.

During her remarks, Wang introduced LONGi’s implementation practices across four dimensions.

For diverse industrial fields such as manufacturing, construction, and logistics, LONGi provides customized photovoltaic and energy storage solutions that help enterprises replace traditional fossil fuels with clean electricity, effectively reducing operating costs and carbon footprints while enabling low-carbon and intelligent industrial transformation and upgrading.

Recent findings suggest that LONGi actively promotes the “energy + rural revitalization” development model in many developing regions. For example, since 2024, Shaanxi Province has been rolling out the “PV+” rural revitalization demonstration project, under which the government provides overall coordination; village collectives establish village-owned new energy companies as the investment and loan entities; and farming households only provide rooftop space and bear no investment or loan risk. LONGi is responsible for the construction, operation, and maintenance of the power stations, while State Grid Shaanxi is responsible for grid capacity expansion and upgrading. Banks provide long-term green inclusive loans with an 18-year term. Power generation revenue is first used to repay loan principal and interest; after deducting loan repayments and operation and maintenance costs, net revenue is distributed between the village company and villagers at a ratio of 2:8. In addition, the project offers the option of installing air-source heat pumps, with dividend income from power generation covering heating expenses, allowing villagers to enjoy clean winter heating free of charge.

By integrating photovoltaic technology into urban buildings, public infrastructure, and transportation systems, LONGi helps cities build distributed clean energy networks, providing an energy foundation for smart city operations and bringing the benefits of green, low-carbon living to the wider public.

For remote regions with inadequate grid infrastructure, LONGi deploys off-grid and microgrid solar-storage systems, using clean energy to light up remote villages, ensure electricity for local healthcare, education, and people’s basic daily needs, and help address energy accessibility challenges in certain areas.

#495. Potatoes grown in moon dirt are as nutritious as Earth potatoes

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (570 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Potatoes grown in moon dirt are as nutritious as Earth potatoes

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (570 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates.
  • “We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, said in a statement.
  • It has been revealed that even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronauts living in the first permanent lunar base may see a sizable number of spuds on their dinner plates. In a study published today in the journal npj Microgravity, botanists at Oregon State University (OSU) proved it’s possible to grow healthy, edible potatoes in simulated moon soil with the help of everyday worms. Importantly, the team also identified the proper proportions of lunar regolith and compost needed to produce potato yields similar to those grown on Earth.

“We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter,” Aymeric Goyer, an OSU botanist and study co-author, said in a statement. “That’s an vital step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon.”.

It has been revealed that even in a controlled habitat, life on the moon will be physically demanding for astronauts. They’ll require carefully maintained, nutritious diets to keep them healthy, but it’s not as simple as sending them off packed with calorically dense prepackaged meals. Cargo room on spacecraft is limited and costly, and the desolate lunar surface isn’t exactly hospitable to agriculture. In addition to constant bombardment by cosmic and solar radiation, temperatures can swing anywhere between 250 degrees and -410 degrees Fahrenheit.

Recent findings suggest that indoor horticulture will also be challenging. Lunar regolith is an annoyingly powdery substance composed of sharp-edged, miniscule particles created over billions of years of asteroid impacts, but little else. With essentially no organic material at all, the dust alone isn’t capable of supporting plant life.

According to recent reports, while it is easy enough to combine that lunar regolith with agricultural additives, researchers weren’t sure if these could overcome moon soil’s heavy metals and irradiation. To test it, Goyer and his colleagues first obtained simulated lunar regolith made to resemble the samples collected during the Apollo missions. Regolith composition varies by region on the moon, so they selected five different types based on darker lunar mare dust and the lighter lunar highland soil. They then mixed the mock moon dust with vermicompost, the nutrient-rich soil created when worms break down organic materials. Next, they planted potatoes in various ratios of regolith and vermicompost, and monitored their growth. As a control, the team even planted potatoes in soil taken from Hermiston, Oregon, an area famous for some of the world’s highest spud yields.

The team found that composite soil with only 30 percent vermicompost was enough to produce potato crops comparable to those farmed on Earth. Their findings suggest the supplemental organics bind to the regolith’s heavy metals, which shield the plants and minimize any damage to their roots.

“We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith,” added OSU botanist and study co-author David Handy.

But bushels of moon potatoes only go so far if they lack any real nutritional value. Even here, the lunar simulations offered promising results, particularly when it came to glycoalkaloids. The naturally forming potato toxins can cause green skin discoloration, but analysis indicated no statistically relevant rise in glycoalkaloids for the lunar crops.

With the potato viability debate settled, Goyer’s team will next compare 10 specific spud varieties grown in simulated lunar regolith to determine the most nutritious and resilient options for NASA astronomers.

Industry observers note that what does it mean to encounter another living subject through architecture? The experience of observing wildlife is often understood in terms of proximity: how close we can get, how clearly we can see, and how much of an animal's world we are able to enter. Yet the desire to encounter wildlife also depends on maintaining a distance. Animals inhabit environments that are not organized around human presence, and their experience of these environments cannot be fully understood from the observer's position. Between the desire to see and the need to preserve lies a more complicated relationship, one that architecture is increasingly required to negotiate.

Industry observers note that at Shomari Wild Reserve in Jordan, the visitor center offers an opportunity to examine this relationship. Designed by Turath for the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature (RSCN), the building is more than a facility within a protected landscape. Its spatial organisation, viewing tunnels and relationship with the surrounding terrain establish particular conditions through which visitors encounter the reserve and wildlife.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

US electric vehicle and clean energy manufacturer Tesla has applied for a Texas property tax limitation for a proposed $3.1 billion polysilicon refinery near Robstown, Nueces County, saying it would not build the plant in the state without the incentive.

The application, filed with the Tuloso-Midway Independent School District under the state’s Jobs, Energy, Technology and Innovation (JETI) program, has been published by the Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts.

Tesla describes the plant as “under consideration for development” and as the “upstream component of Tesla’s vertically integrated domestic solar manufacturing platform.” It states that “in the absence of the agreement the applicant would not make the proposed investment in this state” and that it is assessing locations in other jurisdictions.

According to recent reports, the plant would produce ultra-high-purity polysilicon for single-crystal silicon ingots and N-type, high-efficiency solar cells. Its equipment list includes a hydrochlorination and trichlorosilane synthesis unit, chlorosilane distillation and purification trains, silicon tetrachloride recycling loops and Siemens chemical vapor deposition reactors. The filing does not state the plant’s production capacity.

In a recent development, an economic impact analysis prepared for Tesla by EY puts construction between 2027 and 2030. Of the planned capital spending, $1.5 billion is earmarked for engineering and construction, $1.4 billion for equipment and $183 million for utility infrastructure, with more than 80% spent in 2028 and 2029.

Industry observers note that tesla aims to hire 260 workers in 2030, rising to 515 once the plant is fully operational in 2032, at average total compensation of $130,000, according to the analysis. Construction would support an average of 550 direct jobs a year. EY estimates the project would generate about $63.5 billion in economic output in Texas through 2065.

Tesla said in the filing that more than 90% of the world’s solar-grade polysilicon is produced in China.

In a recent development, under the schedule in the EY analysis, the project’s taxable value for school-district maintenance and operations taxes would be cut to zero from 2028 to 2030 and halved from 2031 through 2040. The Comptroller must review the application, and both the Office of the Governor and the school district’s board must approve an agreement before it takes effect.

Recent findings suggest that the application follows Tesla’s JETI filing for Project Crystal Sun, a proposed solar cell and module factory in Fort Bend County, Texas, with planned investment of about $10.1 billion. That project cleared a key tax hurdle in September when the local school board backed its limitation.

The US government’s Section 232 tariffs and minimum import prices on polysilicon, which also impose a 15% duty on imported ingots, wafers, cells and modules, take effect on Dec. 4. The minimum import prices are designed to force foreign suppliers to match US production costs, raising the value of domestic feedstock in a market where US polysilicon production remains limited. Solar manufacturer Toyo secured US polysilicon supply to navigate trade barriers in January.

Recent findings suggest that tesla has been advancing a plan to build 100 GW of US PV manufacturing capacity by 2028, a target that has drawn scrutiny over whether Elon Musk’s solar ambitions are achievable. The company has taken a similar approach in storage, where it noted in 2025 that its 10 GWh lithium iron phosphate cell factory in Nevada was nearing completion as it reduced reliance on imported cells.

Reconciling Architecture with Nature.

The first Ambasz–MoMA Annual Prize for Nature–Reconciled Architecture frames the idea of architecture that repairs its relationship with nature. Created to recognize projects completed in the last 30 years, it was awarded to Kashef Chowdhury/URBANA for the Friendship Centre in Bangladesh, with the award shared with a reforestation effort by Fundación Gran Chaco in Argentina. Two projects join the same quest, each proposing a particular relationship with nature through the building itself. In Riyadh, JSWD was selected to design RIYMAR Towers, whose carved volumes and landscaped terraces draw on the Tuwaiq Mountains and the historic fabric of Diriyah. In Jakarta, SHAU's Microlibrary Taman Puring, now under construction, uses spiraling curved concrete to support a lightweight green roof within a park. The importance we give to this relationship will also shape how resilient our environments are in a context of climate change, a concern behind UN-Habitat and ICPAC's fresh El Niño guide for city leaders, which asks cities to turn climate forecasts into early, pre-agreed action.

BIG's "Refugee Future Cities" Proposes a Masterplan for 385,000 People in Bidi Bidi, Uganda.

Ver esta publicación en Instagram Una publicación compartida por SIGNIFICANT - Bjarke Ingels Group (@big_builds).

Una publicación compartida por BIG - Bjarke Ingels Group (@big_builds).

This week, the Copenhagen-based international firm MASSIVE - Bjarke Ingels Group unveiled a newly introduced project called "Refugee Future Cities" in Bidi Bidi, Uganda. Designed for to.org, a foundation "dedicated to scaling decarbonization, refugee empowerment, and human optimisation," the project is a masterplan to accommodate the nearly 230,000 refugees currently living in the area and 155,000 new residents by connecting Zones 1 and 2 of the existing refugee settlement. The design grows from a 250 m² family plot, with six plots forming a compound and compounds forming clusters through a repeating nested structure. The buildings are designed to be constructed with traditional materials such as sun-dried earth brick, laterite stone and bamboo. The masterplan layout also includes productive landscapes, schools, healthcare, markets, workshops and solar-powered infrastructure. The concept of a "city for refugees" has been highly controversial, stemming from the confrontation between the idea of the temporary and the actual average length of stay in a refugee camp. Despite local criticism of the firm's involvement, BIG states that the first part of the proposal is soon to take shape on site, with a prototype of the single-family base unit to be built at the Bidi Bidi Performing Arts Center.
