The U.S. Green Building Council (USGBC) has released two fresh resources aimed at accelerating the decarbonization of existing buildings: The Decarbonization Blueprint: Reducing Emissions and Creating Value in Existing Buildings and the Corporate Practice Toolkit for High-Performance Buildings. Drawing on data from nearly 11,000 LEED-certified projects across 90 countries, the blueprint examines strategies for reducing greenhouse gas emissions while improving building performance and long-term asset value. It addresses approaches such as energy-efficient retrofits and refrigerant management, outlining their role in reducing emissions across different building types and markets. Complementing the report, the Corporate Practice Toolkit provides guidance and model language through two resources, the Corporate Policy Guide and the Corporate Procurement Guide, helping organizations integrate sustainability, decarbonization, and resilience objectives into corporate policies, procurement decisions, and building operations.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Portable power station manufacturer Jackery and consumer energy aggregator Every Electric have partnered to roll out what they call North America’s first plug-in battery aimed at renters and apartment residents.
  • By aggregating behind-the-meter storage, the setup uses standard wall outlets rather than hardwired residential systems that require electricians.
  • The tie-up is part of an Every Electric program that has operated across Consolidated Edison’s Newly introduced York City service territory since September.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Portable power station manufacturer Jackery and consumer energy aggregator Every Electric have partnered to roll out what they call North America’s first plug-in battery aimed at renters and apartment residents.

By aggregating behind-the-meter storage, the setup uses standard wall outlets rather than hardwired residential systems that require electricians.

The tie-up is part of an Every Electric program that has operated across Consolidated Edison’s Newly introduced York City service territory since September. Roughly 2,000 portable power stations, mostly Jackery Explorer 2000 v2, are presently distributed across more than 1,000 households, providing 4 MWh of flexible storage capacity. According to the companies, nearly 50 MWh of energy has cycled through the units to date.

The companies are calling it the “continent’s first plug-and-play virtual power plant (VPP) distribution network based on self-contained, expandable portable power stations”.

Recent findings suggest that onboarding requires residents to register online, link their utility account, and plug a window or portable air conditioner into the drop-shipped battery’s passthrough outlet. Once connected to Wi-Fi via Jackery’s app, Every Electric’s cloud software automates charging during off-peak hours and discharges the battery to run the air conditioner during peak grid demand, while keeping backup capacity available for outages.

The setup is similar to how plug-in storage has worked in Europe’s balcony solar market, and requires no electrician labor, municipal permits, or other agreements.

Every Electric offers options, both tied to a portable battery and an air conditioning unit.

In the first option, the cost to the household is nothing upfront for the hardware, setup, or a monthly fee, and a refundable security deposit is $30. As part of the deal, Every Electric retains ownership of the battery, collects demand-response revenue through Con Edison’s Smart Usage program, and pays residents $100 to $150 per year per air conditioner.

In the second option, a separate ownership tier lets households buy a unit outright for $650, discounted from a $999 list price, to raise annual payouts to up to $250 per air conditioner while cross-subsidizing a free unit for a neighbor, alongside a zero-deposit waitlisted option for next summer.

A third option appears to be accepting a BYO battery as well, and Every Electric has details of operating with other brands outside of Jackery, with photos showing EcoFlow and Bluetti portable power stations.

Total seasonal payouts across participating Upcoming York homes are approaching $200,000. Every Electric reports a waitlist of more than 15,000 air conditioners looking to join the network.

“Traditional solar and storage require a roof, a garage or a permanent professional installation, which leaves renters and multifamily residents out,” remarked Andrew Wang, co-founder and CEO of Every Electric. “With Every Electric, adding grid services capabilities lets any household with a wall outlet earn on their bills while supporting the broader electrical infrastructure.”.

Both companies are demonstrating the platform at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas from November 17 to 19, where Jackery is also exhibiting its modular Explorer 5000 Plus system with smart transfer switch support.

  • Sources indicate that the team at Whiteface called the Upcoming York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, becky the basset hound is giving upcoming meaning to the term “man’s best friend.” On November 12, she walked to the Whiteface Lodge, a ski resort in Lake Placid, New York. The hotel staff immediately recognized the dog, but not because of her sparkling personality or floppy ears. Becky’s owner has dementia, and the unnamed man has disappeared before.

Sources indicate that the team at Whiteface called the Upcoming York State Police (NYSP), who contacted the Department of Conservation (DEC) Forest Rangers for assistance with the search. Four NYSP officers and 14 Rangers used drones and another dog (a bloodhound) to search for the missing person. According to Charlie Foutch, the lead Ranger on the search, it was about 25 to 30 degrees Fahrenheit overnight.

In a recent development, at 10 a.m. the next morning, a hunter who was searching just ahead of the group heard someone fall and scream. He found the missing man off to the side of a trail in a draining area with open woods. Ranger Sabo arrived on the scene shortly after. The 69-year-old man was not wearing gloves or shoes, and was suffering from some frostbite on his feet and hands. He was still alert and talking.

“We’re always looking for live people. That’s our goal is to find a live person,” said Fouch. “And a lot of people are really tough. This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning or mittens or gloves, so he had been out there for some period of time at night. And he still did okay. Sometimes if you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do okay.”.

It has been revealed that due to his injuries and the location off the trail, a hoist was the safest and quickest way to get him to safety. Ranger Martin used a cable to hoist him up to a helicopter, while NYSP Pilot Engle flew them to the hospital.

In addition to this coordination between hunters, the NYSP, and DEC, Fouch remarked that Becky the basset hound made this happy ending possible.

Recent findings suggest that “I think if the dog had not shown up at Whiteface, that gentleman definitely would have had a different outcome,” noted Fouch. “It definitely would have been much harder to find him. He may not have survived the rest of the day and probably not another night. The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so promptly.”.

#482. Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2454 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Popsci

Supersonic jets want a comeback. But can Americans stand the boom?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Popsci

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that but no one else would.
  • In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the spring of 1967, William Shurcliff began moonlighting on a project that seemed hopeless: urging the U.S. government to stop supersonic jets. By day, the Harvard-trained physicist ran experiments at the Cambridge Electron Accelerator. By night, he spent hours writing letters—to congressmen, federal aviation officials, mayors, and newspaper editors. It was not a job he wanted. “I was hoping and praying someone else would do it,” he told The Harvard Crimson.

Recent findings suggest that but no one else would. So Shurcliff launched the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom and took aim at the most expensive project in U.S. commercial aviation history at the time, the Supersonic Transport (SST) program. His opposition to the SST stemmed from research by Swedish scientist Bo Lundberg, who had written extensively on the perils of supersonic aviation, chiefly the sonic boom, which could impact hundreds of millions of people every day. Shurcliff’s goal was uncompromising. “Just as the only way to get rid of the smell of the skunk is to eliminate the skunk,” he told The New York Times, “we propose to attack the sonic boom by eliminating the SST.”.

It worked. In 1971, Congress cut off funding for the SST, and two years later the FAA banned civilian supersonic flight over U.S. soil.

Today, prompted by a 2025 executive order, the FAA is proposing to lift that ban before any community response tests of emerging supersonic technology have taken place. And even if new engineering designs can reduce the sonic booms at airliner scale, the economic and environmental costs that have plagued supersonic flight haven’t changed since Shurcliff’s day.

It has been revealed that during World War II, Shurcliff worked at the federal Office of Scientific Research and Development, helping keep the Manhattan Project’s atomic-bomb patents secret. In 1946, he witnessed firsthand the atomic tests at Bikini Atoll and wrote the official account, Bombs at Bikini. His son later told The Latest York Times that his father was so affected he spent the rest of his life atoning for that work.

It has been revealed that when supersonic aviation programs began heating up in the 1960s, Shurcliff was wary of the press, but he was clear about supersonic technology. “We all believe in progress,” he told the Crimson, “but some things just aren’t progress.”.

Industry observers note that the U.S. government-sponsored SST program was the culmination of supersonic military research that began on the heels of World War II. In January 1947, months before anyone had flown faster than sound, Popular Science described Bell’s experimental XS-1, also known as the X-1, which it said might someday reach 1,700 mph, more than twice the speed of sound and three times faster than a typical commercial jet. That October, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier in the X-1.

Fifteen years later, in 1962, Britain and France agreed to build Concorde, and the Soviet Union soon released its own supersonic airliner program, Tupolev Tu-144. The following year, President John F. Kennedy committed the U.S. to a faster, bigger rival, SST. Boeing won the contract in 1966. But even as the race heated up, an enormous problem trailed in its wake.

Sit in a closed room and the air feels perfectly still, but it isn’t. At room temperature, air molecules zip around at an average of about 1,000 miles per hour, each one bouncing off its neighbors billions of times a second. You don’t feel a gale because they’re flying every which way at once—for every molecule headed toward your face, another is headed away. What you’re feeling, without noticing, is the sum of all that pummeling—air pressure—about 14.7 pounds of it on every square inch (psi) of your body at sea level. You notice it only when the balance shifts, such as when the wind blows—a mass of air being pushed from high pressure toward low.

In a recent development, that restless jostling of air molecules is also how sound travels. A voice, a drumbeat, or a jet engine will shove the molecules, which pass along the shove like a crowd in a stadium passing along a wave even as every fan stays in place. The ricocheting molecules pass along vibrations somewhat inefficiently, which is why sound travels a bit slower than the molecules themselves, about 760 mph at sea level, and slower still in the frigid air at airplane cruising altitudes.

When a plane flies faster than the speed of sound, it outruns the air molecules carrying the wave. The air ahead gets no warning until the jet slams it aside, compressing it and creating a shock wave that trails the jet like the V-shaped wake behind a speedboat. But the shock wave’s wake is three-dimensional, spreading in a widening cone that sweeps across the ground below.

It has been revealed that A sonic boom isn’t a single bang that occurs the moment a plane “breaks the sound barrier.” It’s a continuous swath of jarring noise and pressure that follows the jet. Anyone in the cone’s path, or “boom carpet,” experiences it.

Industry observers note that in his 1970 explainer, S/S/T and Sonic Boom Handbook, Shurcliff estimated the boom carpet at 40 to 60 miles wide for the supersonic aircraft of his day. The jolt hits hardest directly beneath the flight path and weakens toward the cone’s edges.

Worse, Shurcliff warned, boom behavior was erratic. Swirls of wind and temperature could focus a shock wave so that one house took twice the jolt of its neighbor a few hundred feet away. That, he argued, meant people would never get used to sonic booms, just as people never get used to lightning and thunder.

On paper, booms don’t seem like they should be a big deal. A boom from supersonic passenger jets like Concorde raises air pressure at sea level about .014 psi relative to the normal 14.7 psi we live with—that’s just a 0.1 percent increase. It doesn’t seem like much, but relative to everyday sounds, it’s enormous.

It has been revealed that if you’ve ever stood near the speakers at a live concert and felt the bass or drum hit your chest, you’ve felt a pressure pulse like a sonic boom, but that bass is only 6.5 pascals, or Pa, a measure of air pressure. Now multiply that punch by about 15 and deliver it without warning. It’s roughly the shove of a 30 mph wind gust delivered in a fraction of a second and aimed at every wall and window of your house at once. That’s what the 0.1 percent of a supersonic jet actually represents.

In a recent development, what no one knew in the early 1960s, when supersonic research was barreling ahead, was how people would feel living under that boom carpet day after day. In 1964, the FAA decided to find out, picking Oklahoma City.

In a six-month trial that began in February 1964, Oklahoma City residents were subjected to eight sonic booms a day, starting at 7 a.m., to gauge how well they would accept the disruption, and whether they would grow accustomed to it. By the end, the Oklahoma City Council had requested a halt to the flights, and the FAA had logged more than 12,000 calls, mostly complaints, alongside more than 5,000 damage claims for broken windows, cracked walls and floors, and destruction of personal property.

Sources indicate that despite the fallout, the following year the agency pointed to a University of Chicago survey of Oklahoma City residents as vindication. Nearly three-quarters said they could live with eight booms a day indefinitely. The survey’s own numbers told a different story.

Nearly every resident surveyed, 94 percent, reported rattling walls and windows, and almost four in 10 believed the booms had damaged their homes. The longer the booms continued, the less people liked them. The share who felt more than a little annoyed rose from 37 percent to 56 percent, and those who mentioned they could live with the booms fell from 91 percent to 73 percent during the six-month trial. Anger over the FAA’s handling of damage claims eventually turned Oklahoma Senator Mike Monroney, one of aviation’s staunchest champions, against the SST program.

Although the residents of Oklahoma City delivered mixed results, the negative data emboldened the opposition. Shurcliff introduced the Citizens League Against the Sonic Boom (CLASB) in March 1967 with a handful of friends and colleagues. Their mission was to eliminate the SST program and keep its boom out of American skies. By June, CLASB had about 230 members in 18 states. What united them, Shurcliff told The New York Times, was that they were “human beings who don’t like to be hit over our heads without our permission being asked.”.

Sources indicate that SST opposition grew as the fight dragged on. Environmental groups joined in, along with economists who doubted the SST would ever pay for itself. For a man new to public relations, Shurcliff seized the moment, casting sonic booms in the language of a rising environmental movement, calling them “sonic pollution.” Atmospheric scientists began warning that SST’s high-altitude exhaust could erode the ozone layer.

Recent findings suggest that in 1971, Congress finally voted to cut off the program’s funding, ending America’s bid for a supersonic passenger airliner. But across the Atlantic, the European program was forging ahead.

In 1963, a plane flew to space. Why couldn’t we go farther?

In 1934, Chrysler bet big on teardrop-shaped cars.

Industry observers note that robotaxis almost happened in 1964—with help from the U.S. government.

Industry observers note that in 1871, cities almost got moving sidewalks. Why are we still waiting?

During WWI, a daredevil pilot helped invent the first ‘drones’.

In 1916, hybrid cars could’ve changed history. But Ford wouldn’t allow it.

Concorde began carrying paying passengers in January 1976, cruising at twice the speed of sound and crossing the Atlantic in about three and a half hours. But the U.S. overland ban confined it mostly to ocean routes. Only British Airways and Air France, both state-owned at the time, ever flew Concorde’s small fleet.

In July 2000, an Air France Concorde flight crashed on takeoff outside Paris, killing everyone aboard and halting flights for more than a year. In February 2002, Popular Science writer Bill Sweetman called the crash not only a tragedy but also “a metaphor for the sorry state of supersonic air travel.” But he also reported that a newly introduced supersonic race had “quietly” begun.

According to recent reports, private-jet maker Gulfstream wanted “a passenger jet for the rich that can smash the sound barrier yet is quiet enough to fly anywhere, anytime.” Controlling the boom was the chief obstacle. But in August 2003, over the California desert, a modified Northrop Grumman F-5 fighter plane demonstrated that a sonic boom could be reshaped and softened.

Two months later, Concorde made its last commercial flight, officially ending the supersonic era for passenger airliners.

The modern darling of supersonic flight is NASA’s X-59, a one-seat research jet built by Lockheed Martin’s Skunk Works. With a tapered nose that stretches roughly a third of its length, the plane’s shape spreads the shock waves so they reach the ground as a thump rather than a boom. The X-59 first flew in October 2025, went supersonic in June 2026, and a week later reached its target of Mach 1.4, or roughly 925 mph at 55,000 feet. Next, NASA intends to fly it over U.S. communities and ask residents how the thumps sound to them. In effect, we’re gearing up for Oklahoma City again, six decades later, albeit, with a gentler jolt.

Since Concorde’s retirement, a handful of private supersonic startups have come, and mostly gone. Denver-based Boom Supersonic flew its one-third-scale XB-1 demonstrator faster than sound three times in January 2025, claiming that no audible boom reached the ground. Its engineering innovation is to exploit atmospheric physics. Since sound travels faster in warm air near the ground than in the frigid air up high, a jet flying only slightly faster than sound at altitude is effectively flying slower than sound near the surface. So its shock waves bend back upward before they land, a phenomenon called Mach cutoff. Boom’s planned Overture jet, seating 60 to 80 passengers, would cruise at Mach 1.7 over oceans—leaving booms in its wake—but just above Mach 1 over land, where their booms would never be heard on the ground, just the distant rumble of their jet engines. The plane hasn’t been built, and its engine is still in development.

But Washington isn’t waiting for the data. A June 2025 executive order directed the FAA to repeal its 1973 sonic boom ban over land. In July 2026, the agency proposed a replacement. Civilian jets, both commercial and private, could fly supersonic over U.S. soil as long as their booms register no more than 0.11 pounds per square foot on the ground, about a twentieth of Concorde’s. That’s about 5 Pa, or slightly less than the pressure felt standing next to the speakers at a live concert (6.5 Pa). But airlines, airports, and Europe’s aviation regulator have questioned whether enough evidence supports the number, which the FAA set without the X-59 having flown over a single community.

It has been revealed that even if the boom fades to a thump, the environmental cost doesn’t. Flying faster than sound means fighting far more drag. According to a 2018 analysis by the International Council on Clean Transportation, a newly introduced supersonic airliner would “burn five to seven times as much fuel per passenger as a comparable subsonic jet.” Boom Supersonic indicates Overture will be able to run entirely on sustainable aviation fuel, but airlines, not manufacturers, decide what goes in the tank.

As Popular Science’s Bill Sweetman wrote in 2002, if you can afford a supersonic jet, “you’re not worried about a few lousy tons of fuel.” But everyone below will bear the cost of supersonic jetsetters’ small travel-time benefit in excess noise and climate-warming emissions.

Shurcliff saw this attempt to relax the rules coming. “Once they start flying, they’re going to want to fly them everywhere,” he told The Fresh York Times in 1967, warning that over-water routes would be “like a foot in the door.” Fifty-nine years later, thanks to the FAA, the door is swinging open. It’s up to us to decide whether we’re prepared to live with the repercussions or push back as Shurcliff did more than half a century ago.

In A Century in Motion, Popular Science revisits fascinating transportation stories from our archives, from hybrid cars to moving sidewalks, and explores how these inventions are re-emerging today in surprising ways.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • According to recent reports, after an exhaustive search, the manufacturer realized there was no reason to look beyond Northeast Arkansas.
  • Industry observers note that A variety of factors go into determining the ideal location of a steel plant, including proximity to large customers, good railroad and river transportation, and a solid local workforce.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in the early 2020s, U. S. Steel launched a nationwide search to find the best location for a newly introduced factory. The organization had recently completed its acquisition of the Major River Steel mill in Osceola, Arkansas. The goal of the expansion: Replicate the success of Big River Steel, which supplies the automotive, construction, and renewable-energy industries and can produce over 3 million tons of steel annually.

According to recent reports, after an exhaustive search, the manufacturer realized there was no reason to look beyond Northeast Arkansas. ​“We went to 48 states and narrowed the site selection down to 20, 10, five, and then three,” stated Dan Brown, U. S. Steel’s executive vice president of advanced technology steelmaking and CEO of Significant River Steel. ​“We built another plant one mile from where we’re at.” At close to $3.5 billion, the investment in what is now called Big River Steel 2 was the largest in U. S. Steel’s storied 125-year history.

Industry observers note that A variety of factors go into determining the ideal location of a steel plant, including proximity to large customers, good railroad and river transportation, and a solid local workforce. Arguably most important, however, is access to reliable and affordable electricity, because producing steel requires an enormous amount of power. ​“If that isn’t number one, it’s in the top two,” Brown mentioned. ​“You have to have a good electricity provider and a good electricity source.”.

The reliable, affordable energy source that will help power the growth of one of America’s most iconic manufacturers is solar and energy storage. To that end, the Steel River Energy Center, which broke ground this past July, is a 2.46-gigawatt solar and 2.94-gigawatt-hour battery storage facility that will be built in three phases and is expected to be fully operational in 2029. Cypress Creek Energy is developing, and will own and operate, what will be the largest solar project with energy storage in America.

The ambition to power American industry.

According to recent reports, the Steel River Energy Center is notable for a host of reasons. The grid-connected project represents $4.5 billion in private investment and is expected to create 1,400 construction jobs in its first two phases and generate $300 million in local tax revenue over its lifetime. Google also signed a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Cypress Creek Energy to secure the energy produced by the first two phases of the project. The Steel River Energy Center is the largest solar and storage project Google has sourced energy from worldwide.

Whether it’s the project’s size, offtake agreement, job creation, or tax revenue, much about the Steel River Energy Center attracts superlatives. But less obvious, and more meaningful for U.S. communities far beyond Mississippi County, Arkansas is the example it provides of solar and storage’s ability to power even the most energy-intensive industries and the many benefits of a robust domestic supply chain.

According to recent reports, “Ten years ago, solar was still pretty niche, and battery storage was hardly on the radar,” mentioned Kevin Smith, CEO of Cypress Creek Energy. ​“Steel River is proof that solar and storage have crossed a threshold. This is not niche energy dependent on incentives. This is the foundation of American industrial competitiveness, because we can beat alternatives on price and speed, both of which are critical to businesses that depend on affordable and reliable energy.”.

The Steel River Energy Center is unique because of its size and because the Entergy Arkansas utility can connect the facility effectively to its transmission grid. While that scale can’t be achieved everywhere, Smith said, the modularity and flexibility of solar and storage can meet the needs of industries anywhere in the country. ​“This is very replicable. Not every location can have gigawatts of solar, but it can be built in 100-to-500-megawatt blocks across Arkansas, the Midwest, the Southeast, the West, everywhere,” Smith said. ​“This should be a standard story going forward.”.

Industry observers note that what could also become the norm is the strong relationship between domestic manufacturers and their customers, so evident at the Steel River Energy Center. The domestic supply chain supporting Steel River is a significant departure from the situation just five years ago, when utility-scale solar plants relied heavily on cheap steel imported from China. By contrast, Steel River is being built with 100% U.S.-made structural steel. The first two phases of the project will be built on about 400,000 steel piles driven into the ground to support more than 3 million solar panels. Fabricated by PACO Steel in nearby Blytheville, Arkansas using coils produced at the Big River Steel 2 mill in Osceola, each pile bears a stamp reading ​“Proudly made in Mississippi County.”.

All the solar panels are being made at the First Solar U.S. factories, and trackers from California-based Nextpower are being built with domestically produced steel, much of it from Substantial River Steel. Battery storage systems provided by LG Energy Solution Vertech are assembled domestically using cells made in North America.

In a recent development, as much as the Steel River Energy Center is a story about domestic manufacturing and the ability of solar and storage to provide the energy major American industries need, it is also very much a local tale. After working in traditional steel manufacturing locations such as Indiana and Michigan, Brown has been in Northeast Arkansas for the past five years and has witnessed the transformation being driven by so much construction and manufacturing activity. ​“You can already see the difference,” remarked Brown, who lives just five minutes from the Big River Steel plant in Osceola. ​“People are spending money at the stores. There are more restaurants and more people in town.”.

In a recent development, it’s a story that is more likely to be repeated in rural communities across America because, as Smith pointed out, more utilities and corporate energy people are moving beyond the politicization of energy to focus on the financial benefits. ​“They are making decisions based on economics, and the economics of solar and storage are unambiguous,” Smith noted. ​“That’s why so much renewable manufacturing and deployment is going into red states. It’s not about ideology. It’s arithmetic.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

German solar module manufacturer Solyco has introduced a fresh full-black, glass-glass solar module for residential applications.

The Solyco Design R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect panel features a stainless steel cover for its connection cables, designed to protect them against mechanical damage, animal bites and ultraviolet (UV) radiation.

The module features 108 monocrystalline half-cut cells based on back-contact (BC) technology, delivering a power output of 485 W and a conversion efficiency of 23.8%. Under standard test conditions (STC), it has a maximum power voltage of 33.94 V and a maximum power current of 14.30 A. Its open-circuit voltage is 40.89 V, while its short-circuit current is 15.03 A.

According to recent reports, the back-contact cell design places electrical connections on the rear of the cells, reducing front-side shading and providing a full-black appearance. The module has a bifaciality factor of around 70%. It features three separate junction boxes, each equipped with a bypass diode, with an IP68 protection rating. The 4 mm² solar cables are 1.2 m long and fitted with Stäubli MC4-Evo 2 connectors.

In a recent development, the module measures 1,800 mm × 1,134 mm × 30 mm and weighs 24.8 kg. It features 2 mm tempered solar glass on both sides and a black-anodized aluminum frame.

Recent findings suggest that the operating temperature ranges from -40 C to 85 C, with a nominal module operating temperature (NMOT) of 42 C. The temperature coefficient is -0.26%/C.

Recent findings suggest that the module supports a maximum system voltage of 1,500 V and a maximum reverse current of 30 A. It can withstand front-side loads of up to 5,400 Pa and rear-side loads of up to 2,400 Pa. The manufacturer also claims resistance to hailstones measuring up to 30 mm in diameter at impact speeds of 23.9 m/s.

Solyco offers a product warranty of up to 30 years and guarantees 88.85% of the module’s initial power output after 30 years.

According to the manufacturer, the R-BG 108nBC.6 Protect is its first commercially available module featuring integrated protection against animal bites for its connection cables.

Berlin-based Solyco Solar has expanded its portfolio of high-efficiency PV modules and specialized solar technologies in recent years. In July 2026, the tech giant introduced a 500 W full-black back-contact module with an efficiency of 24.5%, following the launch of a 480 W back-contact panel in August 2025. The company has also developed a low-temperature solar cell interconnection technology designed to reduce material costs and vertical PV systems for green rooftops.

The inaugural two-day symposium brought together practitioners working in remarkably different geographic, social, and environmental contexts who are invested in implementing positive change for their communities. The event celebrated the recipients of the 2024 and 2025 Ammodo Architecture Awards, recognizing 49 projects that explore alternative approaches to architectural design, collaboration, and community engagement.

#477. A Drive Along the Coast of the Largest Greek Island Unfurls 2,000 Years of Ancient Culture, Channeling a Bronze Age Tourist

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (4949 w)
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smithsonianmag

A Drive Along the Coast of the Largest Greek Island Unfurls 2,000 Years of Ancient Culture, Channeling a Bronze Age Tourist

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smithsonianmag

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that some of the first great European road trips can be traced back to around 1500 B.C., when a mysterious people we know today as the Minoans built a network of stone-paved highways around Crete, their rugged and beautiful home island.
  • In a recent development, the journey must have been unforgettable.
  • Sources indicate that thus refreshed, these pioneer tourists would have proceeded to the palace itself.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some of the first great European road trips can be traced back to around 1500 B.C., when a mysterious people we know today as the Minoans built a network of stone-paved highways around Crete, their rugged and beautiful home island. A Bronze Age traveler would likely have headed first to the island’s grandest site: the Palace of Knossos, a wonder of the prehistoric world.

In a recent development, the journey must have been unforgettable. Landing by ship from Egypt, say, at a port on Crete’s southern coast, voyagers would have made their way to the main highway to begin the 30-odd-mile chariot ride through the island’s mountainous interior, past cultivated vineyards, olive groves and fields bursting with flowers. Just south of Knossos, many would have likely paused at a small, elegant structure known today as the Caravanserai—now excavated, the remains of one of the world’s oldest known surviving hostels. There travelers could have stabled their animals, washed away the dust of the road in a shallow pool or enjoyed a full scrub in the adjoining bathhouse, all fed by stone and terra-cotta pipes carrying water from a nearby stream. Travelers would then have repaired to a pleasant adjacent loggia, decorated with colorful frescoes of birds, where fresh meals were served with fine Cretan wine.

Sources indicate that thus refreshed, these pioneer tourists would have proceeded to the palace itself. “Picture to yourself all the kings’ palaces you ever saw, set side by side and piled on one another,” Mary Renault wrote in her classic 1958 novel, The King Must Die. “It was a palace within whose bounds you could have set a town.” The massive structure consumed an entire ridge and “clung to its downward slopes, terrace after terrace, tier after tier of painted columns, deep glowing red,” with “porticoes and balconies gay with pictured walls.” Although the book is “impressionistic, not scholarly,” said Vassilis Petrakis, a prehistoric archaeologist at the National and Kapodistrian University of Athens, it captures something of the thrill a Bronze Age traveler must have experienced seeing Knossos for the first time. “I read Renault’s description to my students every year to inspire them.”.

As summer approached, I made my own pilgrimage to Knossos, although in a rental car instead of a chariot. The stark Aegean landscape was bathed in golden afternoon light, and I could see why modern Greeks regard Crete as one of the most dramatic, colorful and extreme corners of their lovely country. To avoid the crowds, I’d chosen a late hour to visit the palace; few travelers realize that in summer the site is open until 8 p.m., near dusk. I approached the entrance gate and found myself one of the last stray visitors. A drowsy guard waved me into the ruins, where the only sound was now the buzz of cicadas in the olive trees.

Petrakis had explained that what I would see in Knossos was, in fact, largely the product of imagination—specifically, that of Arthur Evans, the eccentric British aristocrat and archaeologist who rediscovered the site in 1900. It was Evans who had named the palace’s ancient inhabitants “Minoans,” after the King Minos of Greek mythology, and Evans who first evoked an alluring vision of an innocent and Edenic society populated by peaceful and nature-loving people who preferred flower-strewn religious rites, dancing and the sport of “bull-leaping” to the glorification of armed conflict. Evans found that Knossos had no fortifications—its defensive walls were the sea—and that the Minoans left no major military citadels, no images of battle, no graves full of weapons or heroic depictions of warriors. Instead, they filled their frescoes with scenes of idyllic beauty.

Recent findings suggest that but in excavating and “reconstructing” Knossos, Evans took heavy-handed license, including using modern building techniques like reinforced concrete and iron girders, and enlivening walls and columns with bright paint, methods that Petrakis and other scholars today roundly reject as guesswork that did more harm than good. They have also shown that some of his restored frescoes were cobbled together from fragments to suit his often fanciful theories. The most egregious example depicts a young man known as “the Prince of the Lilies,” who wears a loincloth and a headdress of flowers, which was later found to comprise small sections from at least two separate frescoes. Meanwhile, many Minoan women he reconstructed with the help of Swiss artists suspiciously resemble Art Nouveau fashion models. In recent decades, ongoing excavations around Crete have added yet more nuance—even touches of darkness—to Evans’ idyllic picture.

In a recent development, even so, the classicist Mary Beard argues that Evans’ excavations at Knossos, managed by methodical Scottish field assistant Duncan Mackenzie, who had extensive archaeological experience, were “by the standards of the time, extremely careful.” Evans’ colorful vision of a pacifist, artistic Minoan society still dominates the popular images of Minoans. Because we cannot decipher many written records discovered at Knossos, however, the history and culture of the oldest known civilization in what we now call Europe remains bathed in mystery. Still, Crete is rich in clues about the origins of its prehistoric civilizations, including the Minoan archaeological sites encrusting its northeastern coast and, near the island’s farthest eastern point, an outpost called Palaikastro, where Minoan culture persisted in the mountains despite outside influences. And so to try to untangle the Minoans’ 2,000-year saga, I set out on a Bronze Age road trip, taking what novelist Henry Miller called a “vault into the blue.”.

According to recent reports, planning an itinerary was both daunting and alluring. At 160 miles in length and 37 miles north to south, Crete is by far the largest of the Aegean isles, more than 100 times the size of Santorini. Its coastline is scalloped by gold-sand beaches, while its rugged interior contains semi-deserts that evoke North Africa and mountain ranges that are often capped in snow. Adding to the attraction, the island is also overlaid with grandiose relics left by a parade of invaders—Roman temples, Byzantine churches, Venetian fortresses and Ottoman Turk villages.

But the central site is still Knossos, with its alleyways and frescoed halls. Evans described it as a “palace,” though recent research has shown that it was not actually a royal residence but a ceremonial complex for Minoan religious rituals, social gatherings and administration, a bit like Vatican City. It was the grandest of many complexes that dotted Crete in the Bronze Age, ruled by a wanax, or lord. Evans devised the site’s evocative names—“The Room of the Chariot Tablets,” “The Hall of the Double Axes”—which endure today, even though, for example, there is no evidence that a royal ever sat in the “Throne Room.”.

This article is a selection from the December 2026 concern of Smithsonian magazine.

With theatrical flair, Evans linked Knossos to the most beloved Greek myths set in Crete. Most famously, he declared that it was the home of King Minos, who, legend said, demanded tribute from Athens of seven young men and seven young women to be sacrificed in the underground labyrinth to a monstrous half-man, half-bull, the Minotaur. The practice only ended when the Athenian hero Theseus slew the beast with the help of the king’s daughter Ariadne.

It’s easy to see why the labyrinth connection seemed plausible to the first Edwardian tourists who flocked to the site: At its peak around 1500 B.C., the compound spanned nearly 150,000 square feet and had more than 1,000 connected residential areas, storerooms, ceremonial halls and archives for administrative records inscribed on clay tablets. Some structures, made of mortarless stone, were multiple stories high, with roof terraces for hot summer nights. Knossos also houses one of the world’s oldest-known and most elaborate gathering spaces, a rectangular courtyard with tiers of seats for 500 spectators.

The world’s largest collection of Minoan artworks, including most of the original frescoes from Knossos, resides at the Archaeological Museum in Heraklion, Crete’s capital city, some four miles away on the north-central coast. There I learned that Minoan civilization is broken by historians into four broad stages (although arguments continue over dates): the Early Minoan Period, covering the culture’s rise from around 3000 to 1900 B.C.; the Early Palatial Period, from 1900 to 1700, when the first complexes were built and destroyed; the Second Palatial Period, from 1700 to 1450, when a second wave of palaces was built in the golden age of Minoan prosperity; and the  Post-Palatial Period from 1450, covering the long decline to its final collapse around 1200.

Sources indicate that the most alluring artworks date from the cultural apex after 1700 B.C., when the Minoans had unique cultural and political influence over a vast swath of the Aegean. I inspected intricately filigreed gold earrings, brooches in the shape of shells, cups decorated with harmonious geometric patterns and bulbous urns painted with starfish, octopus tentacles and strands of seaweed. There were also many everyday items with refinements that have been compared to those of samurai-era Japan. A board game found in Knossos was lined with gilded ivory and rock crystal cut in a daisy pattern. (We don’t know how it was played.) An oil lamp decorated with lotus designs was crafted from veined red porphyry. Other cases held the inscribed clay tablets of Europe’s oldest written language, separated into two distinct strands dubbed Linear A and Linear B. While Linear B, which recorded the earliest known Greek language, was finally deciphered in 1952, we are still unable to read the older, purely Minoan Linear A. As a result, our knowledge of Minoan culture is formed from the physical remains of settlements across Crete (as well as some in Egypt).

Recent findings suggest that evans’ belief that the Minoans were a pacifist, sometimes matriarchal society was clearly not without basis. One of the finest Minoan statuettes appears to depict the supreme deity, a mother goddess of fertility who has sacred snakes climbing up her arms and was worshiped by female priests on mountaintops and in grottoes. Unlike in later classical Greece, where free citizen women were sequestered, Minoan women appear to have been strikingly independent, seemingly taking part in public life and “bull-leaping games.” I tracked down the most renowned Minoan artwork of all, the Taureador Fresco, which depicts young acrobats. One girl confronts a charging bull as another waits to help, while a boy somersaults over its back. Imagining these prehistoric bullfights (closer in spirit to bloodless Portuguese touradas than to the lethal Spanish variety), Renault again offers a poetic description: “beauty and pain, skill and glory, fleetness and fear and grace and blood, all that fierce music.”.

Just 25 miles east, the Palace of Malia once stood by the sea at the edge of a fertile agricultural region. The shore has shifted so that the site now sits inland, but the palace’s higher sections still offer glimpses of the vibrant Aegean.

Malia was one of five major palace complexes recognized alongside Knossos as UNESCO World Heritage sites in 2025, all built around a distinctive rectangular central court. Observing the similarities between some of these sites, Evans had argued that the Minoans across Crete were ruled from Knossos by a hereditary “priest-king,” but modern scholars disagree, suggesting they were related but separate, a bit like the American Colonies before the United States was formed. “The Minoans were a group of quite separate cultures across Crete,” Petrakis explained. “The palace-states remained independent but traded and cooperated with one another closely. The Minoan elite saw themselves as a community. All of the palaces are connected by a common sense of identity and artistic style.” Judging from the lack of fortifications, discoveries of Minoan artifacts around the eastern Mediterranean and the plethora of imported relics found in Crete, Evans believed that the palace-states at their height also built powerful navies, protecting the island from invasion. This enforced a “Minoan Peace”—sustained more by the threat of retaliation than actual warfare—similar to the later Pax Romana and creating an international trading network across the eastern Mediterranean and beyond. The work of Minoan artists has been found in the far deserts of the Nile, and cylinder seals from Mesopotamia have been unearthed in Crete.

It has been revealed that excavations at Malia’s cemetery, nicknamed the “pit of gold,” have yielded artistic treasures such as a gilt pendant with what looks like two symmetrical bees—an exquisite item now sold in reproduction at chic jewelry stores across Crete. Another discovery threatened to dent the Minoans’ peaceful reputation when what appeared to be defensive walls were found deep in the Malia site, adding to several warlike finds across the island, including long swords, shields emblazoned with images of bulls and helmets adorned with curved boar tusks. “We shouldn’t jump to conclusions,” stated Jan Driessen, an emeritus Mediterranean archaeologist at the University of Louvain in Belgium. “I don’t think the Minoans were hippies or flower-lovers, but they weren’t constantly at war either. There is relatively little evidence for violence, and they may have felt remote enough that they didn’t need walls.” Some researchers believe the fortifications date from the Pre-Palatial Period, and Driessen suggested they could have been built because of earlier intercity conflicts. Later, perhaps, the Malians felt safe enough to build over them. Evans’ idyllic image of the Minoans frayed more definitively in 1979, when children’s bones were unearthed at the North House in Knossos and an adult was found nearby at Anemospilia showing signs of knife cuts suggesting human sacrifice and even possible cannibalism. Many Greek scholars initially dismissed the idea of such gruesome practices, but more conclusive evidence was found in 2017, when archaeologist Maria Andreadaki-Vlazaki excavated a site beneath the modern city of Chania called Kastelli Hill. There, she discovered among the bones of more than 40 sheep, goats and other livestock the remains of a teenage girl whose skull had been carefully split by a knife sometime in the 13th century B.C., a clear example of sacrifice. Andreadaki-Vlazaki explained that such ceremonies were fundamental to ancient cosmology: “It seems barbaric and shocking to us today, but it was a ritual offering. The Minoans surrendered the best and most valuable life among them, a young virgin, to placate the chthonic gods”—the deities of the underworld and those who resided in and beneath the earth—“and to ask for protection from disaster and evil.”.

According to recent reports, andreadaki-Vlazaki considers the discovery a message from the distant past to add depth to our image of the Minoans. “The site was miraculously intact,” she mentioned. “It was as if the ancients were saying: This is us; please understand us.”.

Driving farther east, I entered the serene Cretan landscapes that Miller, who visited in 1939, wrote “can hush the mind.” After 18 miles, I pulled up in Agios Nikolaos (St. Nicholas), a picturesque port that tumbles down a hillside to the Gulf of Mirabello—justly named “Beautiful View” by the Venetians. At first, it seemed a drowsy provincial outpost where blue-and-white tavernas lined the waterfront, so I was surprised to find a gleaming archaeological museum, expanded in 2024, with marble halls, mood lighting and state-of-the-art video presentations. On display were finds from nearby Minoan shipwrecks, including olive oil amphorae, bronze statuettes with surfaces cracked like bark and a carved ivory representation of a crocodile, more evidence of the reach of the Bronze Age trading network.

Sources indicate that modern Cretans’ pride in the Minoans runs far beyond the tourism industry. For 15 years after its liberation from the Ottoman Empire in 1898, the island was an independent country, eventually voting to join Greece in 1913. Its government has always made a point of keeping its heritage intact instead of sending relics to Athens. “To see the finest Minoan artworks,” Petrakis declared, “you have to come to Crete!” The voluble islanders maintain their unique identity in other ways, with their own Greek dialect and pronunciation and unique cultural traditions—distinctive Cretan folk music (often played on a local lute), song (including a cappella verses known as rizitika), dances, embroidery, pottery and jewelry. Crete feels connected to the rest of Greece yet also separate from it.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps the most pleasurable continuity with the Minoan past involves food and wine, as I found after the museum in Agios Nikolaos, when I settled into a Cretan banquet in a taverna located so close to the waves that I could have fished from the table. The cuisine includes ingredients little changed for thousands of years: For example, dakos salata (Cretan salad) uses barley rusks and a soft anthotyro cheese instead of the feta of the classic Greek salad. Minoan-era traders brought garlic from Central Asia and pomegranates, almonds and cumin from the Middle East. And Cretan wine is descended from a viticultural tradition begun at least four millennia ago. Excavators have found wine presses and clay storage jars known as pithoi for fermentation. Aficionados consider it the finest in Greece, with tongue-twisting (for me) varietals like thrapsathiri, kotsifali and mandilari.

Sources indicate that beyond Agios Nikolaos, the thinly trafficked road became an explosion of color. White oleanders and purple bougainvilleas overflowed from the red soil to create tunnels of brilliant petals. Olive groves stretched across the hills, their leaves shifting in the wind from pale green to silver in shimmering waves as if caressed by a ghostly hand.

It has been revealed that this same coastal route was followed more than a century ago by Harriet Boyd, a strong-willed 28-year-old Bostonian heiress and pioneer archaeologist. After arriving in Heraklion in April 1900, Boyd was bitten by the Minoan bug at Knossos and resolved to lead her own dig. On advice from Evans and other archaeologists, she made the difficult muleback journey east along the southern coast to meet with poor farmers who had found artifacts in their fields. While she was excavating in 1901, a peasant led her to a hillside called Gournia. Her small team uncovered a hitherto-unknown Minoan town with a palace at its summit. Increasing her crew to more than 100, Boyd revealed that Gournia was one of the Minoans’ busiest industrial centers, with broad cobbled streets leading to blacksmith forges, carpenters’ workrooms, metalworker shops, olive oil production sites, and factories for dye and perfume. The Philadelphia-based Institute for Aegean Prehistory Study Center for East Crete continues to support excavations in Gournia today.

I hiked up the steep streets to the ruins of the palace, which offer panoramic views over agricultural fields to a bay that was once filled with vessels from around the Aegean. It was a fitting vantage point to ponder a string of disasters that threatened the Minoans’ golden age. Around 1600 B.C., a volcanic eruption on the island of Santorini, 70 miles north, blanketed Crete with ash and pumice and sent a giant tsunami to the coast. From the heights of Gournia it was easy to picture the residents watching puzzled as the sea withdrew, stranding their boats on the sands, and their terror at the approaching tidal wave.

Sources indicate that minoan society was then threatened by a period of upheaval. To understand it, I drove the mile and a half to the fishing village of Pachia Ammos (“Thick Sand”), set in a wineglass-shaped inlet, where an international conclave of academic “Minoanophiles” was ignoring the fine summer’s day and crowding into a former customs house for a conference on 15th-century B.C. Minoan pottery. The dedication of the attendees was impressive. Driessen, the Belgian archaeologist, told me that he fell in love with Crete as a child and had been excavating there since he graduated from college, and I noticed one young PhD student with a Minoan gourd tattooed on his calf.

Still, I feared the conference might be wildly arcane, but I was soon captivated by ceramic shards with inventive patterns and aquatic imagery. “If you look at other cultures around the Mediterranean in this period, there is nothing to compete with Minoan pottery,” said Tom Brogan, the executive director of the Institute for Aegean Prehistory, who is set to begin an appointment as the director of the American School of Classical Studies at Athens in 2027. “It’s like porcelain.” The analysis of even the tiniest fragments reveals surprising amounts about Minoan trade, he added, since, thanks to Crete’s varied geology, the origins of the raw material can be traced. “We don’t have texts we can read from this era, so this is one way to tell the Minoan story.”.

In a recent development, did you know? Washington, D.C. has its own minotaurs.

During a break, Driessen repaired with me to a seafront cafe to outline his theory about the 15th-century crisis, first propounded in The Troubled Island, a 1997 book he co-wrote with Colin F. Macdonald of the British School at Athens. “The Minoans had a strict religious system,” Driessen mentioned. “Religion was everywhere! Then suddenly we see evidence of natural disasters—earthquakes, tsunamis, eruptions, weather incidents—which had dire effects on humans, animals and crops. And we start to see a breakdown of the system.” As sea spray wafted over us, Driessen suggested that the Minoan populace lost faith in their leaders, who had presumably angered the gods and lost their favor. “Almost all of the palace complexes were damaged. Cave sanctuaries were abandoned. There was a general wave of destruction that may have been from popular rebellions.” Although the Minoan elite recovered from the burst of anarchy and rebuilt the palaces, they were weakened and failed to erect fortifications when a latest threat emerged.

Journeying east of Pachia Ammos felt like falling off the map. A narrow road zigzagged for 60 miles through the tawny Ornon Mountains, then plunged back to beaches with vodka-clear waters and pebbles the size of dinosaur eggs. On a sun-blasted headland, a ragged Greek flag flew above the remains of the Palace of Zakros, a site that filled a museum in the village of Sitia with treasures. It was here that I paid closer attention to the brown clay tablets covered in the Minoans’ two elegant scripts, Europe’s oldest known written languages. The tablets had been housed in the archives of palaces all over Crete and then accidentally fired by conflagrations. Evans had dubbed the older script, dating from 1900 to 1450 B.C., “Linear A.” The second he called “Linear B,” dating from 1450 to 1200 B.C., which he believed was simply another purely Minoan language. When Linear B was deciphered in 1952, 11 years after Evans’ death, the news made world headlines—and revised entirely Evans’ view of the Minoan twilight.

The breakthrough was made by an English autodidact, Michael Ventris, who had become obsessed by the Minoans as a teenager when he heard Evans lecture in London. Although he became an architect, Ventris was also a brilliant cryptologist, and he used grids to cross-reference the characters in place names to discover that Linear B was actually not Minoan but an ancestor of classical Greek, which called into question Evans’ belief that the Minoan Peace had gently faded from history.

It has been revealed that thanks to the linguistic evidence of Linear B and recent excavations that show widespread destruction of palace complexes, many archaeologists have postulated that around 1450 B.C., an invading fleet swept across the Aegean from the state of Mycenae, near the Peloponnese, a southern peninsula of the Greek mainland. “The Mycenaeans were an aggressive, expansionist people,” remarked Paul Cartledge, an emeritus ancient historian at the University of Cambridge. “They were later responsible for what we call the Trojan War,” featured, of course, in Homer’s The Iliad and The Odyssey. These seasoned warriors easily conquered Crete—“the Minoans were defenseless,” Cartledge said—and the invaders burned all their palaces save Knossos, which they used as a power base. But Crete was too significant to dominate solely by force, and they ruled the island in cooperation with their subjects, blending the two cultures. Linear B was a script used by the conquering Mycenaeans, who co-opted Minoans’ writing and administration skills to govern. “In a single stroke, Ventris added 600 years to the history of the Greek language,” Cartledge said.

It has been revealed that today, the older, purely Minoan script remains a mystery. “Deciphering Linear A is the Holy Grail for linguists,” Cartledge said. “We need a Rosetta Stone, with parallel texts in other languages.” Excavations still yield tantalizing clues, most recently an ivory “scepter” unearthed in 2024 near Knossos, with a round ring and handle inscribed with some 119 Linear A symbols, the longest chain of the text ever found. (“Despite the name, the ‘scepter’ wasn’t royal,” said Thomas Palaima, former director of the Program in Aegean Scripts and Prehistory at the University of Texas at Austin, who is participating in a detailed joint study on the relic, expected to be published in 2027. “It was a religious ceremonial piece, so experts just call it ‘the ivory.’”) And this June, an amateur linguist in Newly introduced York claimed to have used artificial intelligence to interpret 40 symbols from Linear A and compile a 408-word lexicon, although the results have gone no further. Still, Palaima has no faith that A.I. can ever crack the arcane script. “There’s insufficient data,” he said with a shrug; the text cannot be cross-referenced with any other script.

My Minoan road trip ended at Palaikastro (“Old Fort”), hidden at Crete’s easternmost tip. To reach it, I followed an unpaved road around a desolate harbor to modest ruins, which lay beneath a tabletop mountain called Petsophas (“Skin Eater”), known as a peak sanctuary that was once the location of a Minoan shrine. Even this far-flung outpost had a rich past: In 1899, a farmer unearthed two ornate stone molds once used for casting bronze plaques with images of women and double axes. Excavators soon realized that Palaikastro was the site of a strategic Minoan port: One of its villas had more than 20 rooms, and among the treasures unearthed was a now-famous vase painted with a swimming octopus that looks at the viewer with wide, friendly eyes.

The haunting spot was an appropriate place to ponder the ultimate mystery: the reason for the final demise of the blended Mycenaean-Minoan culture. Carbon dating shows that the Palace of Knossos burned for the last time around 1350 B.C. and was abandoned, but we don’t know whether this was the result of warfare, popular revolt or natural disaster. Nor do we know why Crete ended up sliding into a dark age around 1200 B.C. “Then it was all lost!” noted Brogan. “We don’t know why. We’re fascinated by how they reached this cultural height and then declined. The rise, the peak and the fall.”.

A steep hill near Palaikastro attracted refugees who kept the Minoan culture alive into the early Iron Age. In The Odyssey, which is thought to have taken its final form around the eighth century B.C., Homer notes that a mixture of languages was spoken on Crete and refers to one linguistic group as Eteocretans. Archaeologists have also found a few inscriptions in a non-Greek language dating from the seventh to around the third centuries B.C., at a time when Doric Greek dominated the island. By 100 B.C., evidence of these Eteocretans had disappeared. Some assume that the Eteocretans spoke a language derived from Minoan, but neither Minoan nor the Eteocretan language has been deciphered.

Industry observers note that the windswept isolation of this eastern port had a mournful air, prompting meditations on the limits of archaeology and our ability to rescue the distant past. Despite more than 125 years of dedicated research, we know relatively little about these Bronze Age people. I recalled one of Petrakis’ philosophical musings: “We would know even less about the Minoans without their clay tablet records, but those tablets only survived by accident, because their palaces were burned and the clay was hardened. What records would survive from our own civilization if our hard drives were lost and our paper books disintegrated over time?”.

And yet, Petrakis added, in a deeper sense, the Minoans are very much with us today. Their palaces vanished, but the Greeks kept a collective memory of a powerful and sophisticated civilization that had thrived in deep antiquity and then vanished, possibly inspiring Plato’s enduring legend of Atlantis. Many Minoan stories were passed on by oral tradition and transmuted into Greek legends. In addition to King Minos, Crete was where the mother goddess Rhea gave birth to Zeus in a cave to hide him from his jealous father, Cronus. Most enduring is the Minotaur, which has inspired Western artists for millennia.

As I began the long drive back to Heraklion, I saw that our ongoing fascination with the Minoans may be fed by their elusive nature. “Every day we get closer to the Minoans,” Driessen had told me in Pachia Ammos. “With every excavation we find more information, but will we ever solve their mysteries? I don’t think we really want to. We’ll never fully know the Minoans, but the mystery is also the attraction.”.

Follow him on Instagram @TonyPerrottet.

According to recent reports, myrto Papadopoulos is a photographer and documentary filmmaker. Her work has appeared in Le Monde, Time, and the Wall Street Journal, among others.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A research team led by scientists from Chinese perovskite solar cell manufacturer MicroQuanta Semiconductor has achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% for a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module, setting a new world record.

The researchers noted the result was enabled by cooling the wet perovskite precursor film before vacuum treatment to slow crystallization and reduce the fill factor losses associated with scaling up from cells to modules.

In a recent development, “What makes our result special is that the world record is achieved at the module level, rather than in a small laboratory cell,” corresponding author Dongchen Lan told pv magazine. “Solar cells often lose efficiency when scaled up into modules.”.

The result was certified by the National PV Industry Measurement and Testing Center (NPVM) of China’s Fujian Metrology Institute.

Lan noted the team identified a major cause of these losses and demonstrated a way to mitigate them while helping modules maintain their performance over time. “This addresses a key challenge in bringing next-generation solar technologies closer to practical use,” he said.

Industry observers note that the researchers first compared laboratory-scale perovskite solar cells with mini-modules fabricated under matched processing conditions in previous studies. They used Shapley value analysis, which averages the contribution of each parameter across all possible orders of substitution, to quantify the contributions of open-circuit voltage, short-circuit current density, and fill factor to the measured efficiency loss.

After accounting for current losses in inactive areas created by laser scribing, they found that fill factor was the largest contributor to the efficiency drop from cells to modules.

Recent findings suggest that to reduce that loss, the team spin-coated a perovskite precursor onto indium tin oxide (ITO)-coated glass carrying two hole-transport layers (HTLs). Immediately after coating, they cooled the wet film for 15 seconds to 0-10 C, transferred it to a vacuum chamber within about five seconds, and vacuum-flashed it for two minutes before annealing it at 110 C for 30 minutes. They then applied a surface passivation layer and deposited the electron-transport layers (ETLs) and silver (Ag) electrode. Measurements during film formation indicated that cooling slowed the conversion of an intermediate phase into perovskite, yielding films with larger, more uniform grains.

The researchers used slot-die coating to fabricate a 19.48 cm² perovskite mini-module consisting of eight subcells connected in series through laser scribing. The device was built on a glass substrate coated with indium tin oxide (ITO), nickel oxide (NiOₓ), and a self-assembled monolayer known as 3PATAT-C3. It featured a formamidinium-cesium lead iodide (FA₀.₉₅Cs₀.₀₅PbI₃) absorber with an ethylenediammonium diiodide (EDAI₂) surface passivation layer, a fullerene (C₆₀) electron transport layer, a bathocuproine (BCP) buffer layer, and a silver (Ag) electrode.

Sources indicate that according to the team’s measurements, the mini-module achieved a certified steady-state efficiency of 23.9% and a fill factor of 83.3%, which the authors reported as the highest for a perovskite module. It also had a geometric fill factor of 97%, meaning 97% of its aperture area was photoactive. In separate aging tests under continuous one-sun illumination at open-circuit, the efficiency loss attributable to declining fill factor was less than one-third as large in modules made with the cooling step as in control modules.

Industry observers note that “The resulting fill factor advantage is retained across device scales and during operation, revealing a shared parameter-level pattern between scale-up loss and operational decay,” the group concluded. “Hence, preserving fill factor offers a unifying optimization target for developing efficient, stable and scalable perovskite photovoltaics.”.

The cell was described in the study “Retarding efficiency loss upon scaling in perovskite photovoltaics as fill factor becomes the bottleneck,” published in nature communications. Researchers from China’s MicroQuanta Semiconductor, Zhejiang University, China Three Gorges Renewable, Zhejiang Provincial Key Laboratory of Optoelectronic Functional Materials and Devices, and the Australian Centre for Advanced Photovoltaics.

In January 2025, MicroQuanta achieved a certified efficiency of 21.86% for an 810 cm² perovskite solar module. The company has also been developing a gigawatt-scale perovskite production line in Quzhou, Zhejiang province, with looks to manufacture large-area modules measuring 2.88 m² and targeting 20% efficiency and a 25-year lifespan.

More recently, MicroQuanta introduced a perovskite-silicon tandem module for building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV) at The smarter E Europe 2026 in Munich, Germany. The four-terminal MQ-α² series features a reported efficiency of 26% and power outputs ranging from 65 W to 165 W. The modules are available in customizable colors and finishes.

  • Constantine’s march on Rome in 312 set a template for what Williams calls “muscular Christianity in Europe.” Charlemagne’s forced conversion of the Saxons in northern Germany was followed by the slow, bloody Christianization of Scandinavia over three centuries.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in 1107, after the First Crusade, Christians held Jerusalem, and Norway’s King Sigurd set sail to defend the city with 60 ships and around 5,000 men. In northern Spain, Sigurd ended up ransacking the fortress at Compostela, one of Western Europe’s holiest sites. He went on to sack Lisbon, storm Ibiza and Minorca, and then team up with King Baldwin of Jerusalem to conquer the port city of Sidon, in modern-day Lebanon. A grateful Baldwin gave Sigurd a fragment of wood from what he said was Jesus’s cross.

Recent findings suggest that sigurd was the first Christian king to lead a military campaign in defense of the Holy Land, but his expedition, sometimes known as the Norwegian Crusade, looked a lot like an old Viking raid. That unexpected collision of traditions is the subject of a upcoming book, God’s Hammer: A History of the Viking Crusades, by historian Thomas Williams, a former curator at the British Museum. The book closes the gap many of us imagine between the culture of the Viking raider and that of the Christian crusader—and vividly explains how pagan warrior traditions entered the Christian age.

Constantine’s march on Rome in 312 set a template for what Williams calls “muscular Christianity in Europe.” Charlemagne’s forced conversion of the Saxons in northern Germany was followed by the slow, bloody Christianization of Scandinavia over three centuries.

According to recent reports, williams has a knack for bringing unfamiliar medieval figures to life. Take Vladimir of Kyiv, who replaced Jesus on coins with his personal emblem: “Christ was employed to serve Vladimir, not the other way around,” Williams writes. In God’s Hammer, the cross was a convenient way to pursue power.

The book’s turning point comes in 1147, toward the start of the Second Crusade, when Pope Eugenius III empowered Scandinavia’s now-Christian kings to pursue a crusade right at their doorstep, with the prospect of the same spiritual rewards promised to the crusaders in Jerusalem.

In a recent development, two decades later, in 1168 or 1169, the Danes besieged and burned the temple at the Slavic fortress of Arkona, in modern Germany. The surrender terms required the Arkonans to free Christian prisoners, accept the faith, give pagan lands to the church and supply troops to the Danish army. In a symbolic move, the idol of a pagan deity was chopped into pieces and fed into the army’s cooking fires. This, Williams writes, was “as much a political and cultural act as a religious one.”.

Did you know? Who were the Teutonic Knights?

The Teutonic Knights were a Catholic military-religious order founded during the Crusades, originally to care for sick pilgrims—and later to wage war and establish Christian rule in Northern Europe, particularly against the Balts and Finns.

Unlike the famously red-crossed Knights Templar, the Teutonic Knights garbed themselves in white mantles emblazoned with black crosses.

In 1525, their grand master, Albert of Brandenburg, converted to Lutheranism, relinquished his position and transformed the order's Prussian territory into a secular hereditary duchy.

Thomas Williams tells the story of how the Vikings took up arms in the name of Christianity.
